The *Vālmīki-Śrīvāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, together with its commentary titled *Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Vāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa, edited by Vāsudeva Śarman, son of Paṇaśīkara Upāhv Lakṣmaṇa Śarman.

The Second Chapter: On the Conduct of One Seeking Liberation (Mumukṣuvyavahāraprakaraṇam).
The First Canto. Vālmīki said:
When these words had been uttered with a great sound by those present in the assembly, [the earth shook].
Viśvāmitra addressed Rāma, who stood before him, with affection.

I bow to that which is unborn, undecaying, beginningless, and one; which bestows upon the heart the essence of the Self—the nectar-elixir of the Upanishads—in which all other joys are rendered insignificant by its own innate bliss.

Having described the perfection of the means even through the words of Śrī Rāma and others, the venerable Vālmīki, beginning the second chapter to instruct them by analyzing individually how those seeking liberation (mumukṣu) should accomplish that perfection while engaged in worldly activity, and how they may attain rest in reality (tattva-viśrānti) through it, said: śrīrāmādivacanamukhena varṇitāpi sādhanasaṃpanmumukṣubhiḥ kena krameṇa vyavaharadbhiḥ saṃpādyā kathaṃ ca tayā tattvaviśrāntilābha iti pratyekaṃ vivicya teṣāmupadeśāya dvitīyaṃ prakaraṇamārabhamāṇaḥ śrīvālmīkiruvāca ||— Although the perfection of the means has been described through the words of Śrī Rāma and others, [Vālmīki], wishing to instruct them by analyzing individually how those seeking liberation should accomplish that perfection while engaged in worldly activity, and how they may attain rest in reality through it, began the second chapter, saying:
Although he was told by his father, Śuka did not believe it even when the Fully Awakened One spoke it himself;
rather, through his father’s words, he is celebrated as one who found rest in reality.

In this regard, first of all, so that those whose dispassion and other qualifications are weak might not engage in hearing [the scriptures] and so forth under the delusion that they have suddenly attained the requisite qualification, the Teacher— showing the characteristics of the ripening of such qualifications through the narrative of Śuka and citing the Vedic text, "Knowledge, having been known from the teacher alone, reached Aśiṣṭha"— [approaches] the family preceptor.
In order to instruct Śrī Rāma, Viśvāmitra, hastening to remind him of the previous events, spoke first; thus it is said: "iti.
[He addressed] those who had arrived at the assembly, who were standing before him, and who were situated at the limit of their authority.

Because primary qualified authorities are difficult to find, because Rāma possesses the highest knowledge of aesthetic flavor (rasa), and out of affection for the discussion of Brahman that is about to take place. || 1 ||
O Rāghava, best among the wise, there is nothing further for you to know;
by your own subtle intellect, you have understood everything.

That which is to be known must necessarily be known because it has not yet been known; it is the entire secret of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. Thus, by means of an intellect intent on discriminating between the essential and the non-essential, that which constitutes the ultimate essence—the indivisible, non-dual Consciousness—is merely cleansed, requiring only a slight application of effort.
In the mirror of your own intellect, which is eternally pure by nature, [all things are reflected]. || 3 ||

To the question "In that case, why is there no final rest [in that alone]?", he says: "merely" (*kevalam*). "Cleaning" (*mārjanā*) means merely the removal of the stains of distrust, doubt, and impurity. The meaning is that even when something is known by one's own intellect, there is an absence of conviction without corroboration from authoritative sources (*pramāṇa*), teachers (*ācārya*), and so forth. And thus they have said:
"Even for those who are highly trained, the mind lacks conviction regarding the self. (3)
Like the intellect of Śuka, the son of the Blessed Vyāsa, your mind,
though it has already known all that is to be known, requires only internal rest.

[This is] of the Blessed Vyāsa. Here, Vyāsa and Śuka are understood to have been born at the end of a previous Dvāpara age, since it is well known that there is a distinct manifestation of Vyāsa at the conclusion of every Dvāpara age. (4)
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, how was it that Śuka, the son of Vyāsa,
did not find rest even at the outset regarding that which is to be known, and yet found rest through his intellect once again?

"Even though the reality is capable of being known through one's own investigation regarding the object of knowledge, [it is better] when it is confirmed by the intellect through the instruction of a guru.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O Rāma, this account of my own life, which I am now relating, is equal in significance to your own."
Listen to the account of the son of Vyāsa, which is the cause of the end of births.
"Equal to one's own condition" means similar to one's own life story. "The end of births" is liberation (mokṣa). || 6 ||
This venerable Vyāsa, who resembles a mountain of collyrium and possesses the radiance of the sun, is seated upon a golden throne at the side of your father.
The mountain known as Añjanaśaila, or Nīlādri, is a boundary range (varṣaparvata). Seated there, resting upon a seat (viṣṭara), he had a son of moon-like countenance who was skilled in statesmanship.
Named Śuka, he was possessed of great wisdom and stood firm like the sacrifice (yajña) personified.
Skilled in policy and knowing all the treatises, he was endowed with a physical form as well-established as a sacrifice.
As he reflected upon this worldly course of existence within his heart,
this very same discernment indeed arose in him just as it had in you.
Discernment is investigation; it is of this nature. || 9 ||
Therefore, by means of his own discernment, that high-minded one himself investigated for a long time what is beautiful and attained that which is the truth. (10)

He has attained—that is, he has known—that which is the ultimate truth, whose nature is the non-dual pure consciousness that is the reality of the Self; for the attainment of that [truth] consists in nothing other than knowledge itself. || 10 ||
Though he had personally attained the supreme reality, his mind remained unsettled;
he did not gain the conviction within himself that "this is the reality. (11)
The cause of non-rest is lack of trust. || 11 ||
His mind alone ceased its restlessness regarding enjoyments— which were fraught with manifold calamities— just as a cātaka bird ceases from the rain-showers that are full of frequent interruptions.
He ceased—that is, he desisted; in other words, he became dispassionate toward the manifold waves of the many sufferings of destruction.
Once, that one of pure wisdom, with devotion, questioned his father, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, who was dwelling in solitude on Mount Meru. (13)
To Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa. || 13 ||
O Sage, how has this grand spectacle of saṃsāra arisen?
How does it come to rest? To what extent, for whom, and at what time does it occur? || 14 ||
He asked: "How and by what process did this artificial display of pretension for the sake of deceiving others arise?

Whose is this saṃsāra—is it of the body, or of the senses, or of the mind, or of the vital breath, or of the aggregate, or of something else that is subject to modification, or of the changeless pure consciousness?"
The connection is with what precedes. || 14 ||
Thus questioned by his son, the sage Vyāsa, who knows the self, explained everything that was to be said to him clearly and exactly as it is. 15.
The grammatical connection is that Vyāsa, having realized the Self, has correctly related everything exactly as it ought to be told. || 15 ||
"I already knew this before," said Śuka to his father with his auspicious intellect; he did not hold that speech in high regard.

The word division is *ā ajñāsiṣam*. Now, if this particle *ā* here has the sense of recollection (*smaraṇa*) of something previously known through one's own prior inquiry, then—since the rule *aṅitaḥ* excludes particles from being included—the particle *ā* would not be subject to the *an-aṅ* condition; consequently, by the rule *nipāta ekājanāṅ*, its status as a *prakṛtibhāva* (original form) would be proper. True. Nevertheless, previously...

Because the connection with the verbal root (*kriyāyoga*) is intended to be expressed—since the prefix *āṅ* serves to illuminate the excellence of the meaning of the root by signifying "having known in every respect" (*āsamantād viśiṣya ajñāsiṣam*)—the prefix *āṅ* is included therein through the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a group of identical items).

This is because, in the rule *nipāta ekājanāṅ*, the view of a simple prohibition (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)—namely, "excluding *āṅ*" (*āṅ-varjya*)—is accepted; and as it is said, "prohibitions are more powerful."

Because the *Mahābhāṣya* states that the designation *pragṛhya* is prohibited [in this case], the sandhi is indeed correct. Now, immediately after the instruction, the connection is as follows: Śuka, with a mind free from fear, did not say much more than "I have understood" (*ājñāsiṣam*)—the word *anu* being used here in the sense of "following" or "subsequent to"—in response to his father's words. || 16 ||
The venerable Vyāsa, having understood his son's intention to be such, replied again to his son: "I do not know [this] in its true essence. (17)
There exists on the surface of the earth a king named Janaka;
he knows that which is to be known exactly as it is, and from him you shall obtain everything.
Perceiving his son's intention and following that very thought, he replied: "I do not know.
The implication is: "other than what was said [by you]. || 17 || 18 ||
When his father had spoken thus, Śuka departed from the earth of Sumeru and reached the city of Videha,
which was protected by Janaka.
There is a country named Videha; its capital city is Mithilā. || 19 ||
O King, he was announced by the staff-bearers to the high-souled Janaka:
"The son of Vyāsa, Śuka, stands here at the gate."
By the gatekeepers who were staff-bearers and armed with staves. || 20 ||
Thinking, "Let this inquiry of Śuka remain as it was," Janaka spoke thus with disdain and then remained silent for seven days.
Janaka, having learned the news regarding Śuka, acted with sudden disregard for the instruction—as if it were the word of Vyāsa—lest there be a failure in his purpose.

This was for the sake of inquiring into Śuka’s means for detachment (*vairāgya*) and so forth, as well as his faith and steadfastness; [the term] *avajñayā* means with contempt or indifference. || 21 ||
Then Janaka had Śuka enter the courtyard;
there he remained for exactly seven days, dwelling in that same state of dejection.
*Aṅgaṇa* means the courtyard within the house. *Unmanāḥ* means one whose longing for the desire to know reality has caused all other disregard to be forgotten;
that is to say, [he was filled with such eagerness]. || 22 ||
Then Janaka had Śuka enter the inner apartments;
for seven days, the king was not seen at all.
There, Janaka cherished Śuka, whose face was like the moon, with intoxicated beauties, foods, and an abundance of enjoyments.

The connection with the following verse is as follows: under the pretext of saying, "As long as you are not honored with food and other offerings, the king will not be seen," he pampered him there in the inner apartments for seven days with an abundance of enjoyments. || 23 ||
Those enjoyments or those sorrows did not shake the mind of Vāsuputra,
which was as immovable as a mountain with its base firmly fixed, like gentle breezes failing to move a tree rooted deep in the earth.
Neither the Ajas nor the Vicakras could shake it; its pedestal was fixed and its roots were firm. || 25 ||
Perfectly equanimous, self-composed, silent, and joyful in mind, Śuka remained there like the full moon. (26)
The word *kevalam* is used for emphasis. He is perfectly equanimous toward both enjoyment and disregard; therefore, he is established in his own self (*svastha*). The reason for this is as follows:
King Janaka, having beheld Śuka—who had realized his true nature and arrived with a joyful heart—prostrated before him. (27)

"Having been thus thoroughly examined, you have reached the culmination of the vision of reality; you are established in the state where the desire for deliberation and the like has ceased, having exhausted all worldly activities and attained every heart's desire.
'What do you wish for?'—thus he spoke to him, having quickly offered a welcome. (28)

One by whom all the well-known duties in this world—those tasks that must necessarily be performed and which are the means for attaining the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*)—have been brought to completion without remainder; such a person is meant by the term "one who has accomplished what was to be done" (*kṛtakṛtya*).
Since all forms of happiness are included within the bliss of the Self (*ātmasukha*), it follows that upon the attainment of that [Self-bliss], all desires have been fulfilled.
Śrī Śuka said:
O Teacher, how has this grand spectacle of worldly existence arisen? How does it come to rest? Tell me this correctly and quickly.
"Saṃsāra" has been explained previously. || 29 ||
Viśvāmitra said: When Janaka was thus questioned, he then related that very same account which had previously been told to him by his high-souled father regarding Śuka.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: when thus questioned by Janaka, his father, that very thing which had been spoken previously in the past was related by Śuka. || 30 ||
Śrī Śuka said:
"This very matter was previously understood by me through discernment;
and it was likewise explained by my father when he was questioned about it. (31)
It has been fully proclaimed and correctly explained through appropriate illustrations and logical arguments. || 31 ||
O best among those skilled in speech, you too have stated this very same point;
and this indeed is the meaning of the sentence as it is observed in the scriptures. (32)

The meaning of the exposition (*vyākhyārtha*) is the meaning of the great sayings (*mahāvākya*) found in all the Upaniṣads. It is determined by the following [verse], which establishes their intended purport (*tātparya*):

"Just as this [world] arises from one's own conceptual construction (*svavikalpa*), it perishes through the complete dissolution of that very conceptual construction; thus, the certainty is that the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), once burnt away, is devoid of essence. (33)

It is called *vikalpa* because it conceptualizes variously within the Self as conditioned by ignorance; it consists of the infinite tendencies of desire and karma, and—remaining as the collective and individual impressions (*saṃskāra*)—it is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that has dissolved into the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) and serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the beginningless state of being a living being (*jīva*). From that [internal organ], through the reversal of the order of dissolution...
It proceeds as follows: by the mere performance of the combination of ritual action (*karman*) and meditation (*upāsana*), the state of being an individual self (*adhyātmika-vyaṣṭi-bhāva*) ceases.

Through the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*) produced by the ripening of hearing and other means, the ignorance consisting of cause and effect, along with its latent impressions (*savāsanā-kāryakāraṇāvidyā*), is destroyed.

The word "burnt" (*dagdha*) here implies censure. Alternatively, it is so called because it is poorly situated within the self-luminous Self (*svaprakāśātman*) and because of its falsity (*mithyātva*).

It was already mostly burnt even before, and for that very reason it is devoid of essence; therefore, the certainty that it is "devoid of essence" is held either to prevent the suspicion of its sprouting again and again through the fire of dissolution at the time of direct realization, or [simply] because it is so. The phrase "of those who know reality" (tattvavidām) is to be supplied as the subject. || 33 ||
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, tell me this truly and unswervingly;
for my mind, wandering through the world, finds rest only in you.

This very truth has been previously understood by me through my own reflection; therefore, tell me what it is so that it may become firm and indubitable within my heart. I am being led astray by you—my mind wandering in doubt, revolving among various objects of the world, wondering whether this or that might be the reality.
That is to say, through trust in your words; I attain rest, that is, stability, in that very state. || 34 ||
Janaka said:
"O Sage, there is no other certainty higher than this;
you have known it yourself and have heard it again from a teacher. (35)
Therefore, from this which has been fully understood by you, the object to be ascertained must be determined. || 35 ||
In this world, there exists only the one Person whose nature is uninterrupted consciousness, and nothing else;
bound by the power of his own volitions, he is liberated when free from volition. (36)
He speaks again for the sake of firm conviction regarding that very point: "uninterrupted," etc. (verse 36).

By this, it is clearly known that for you, that great soul, all that is to be known has been realized; thus, detachment from enjoyments—whether from the visible or from what was previously seen—has arisen here in its entirety.
The phrase "of you, O Great-Souled One" is the ellipsis. "Prior to enjoyments" means before the experience of objects; "here" refers to this state of certainty;
"from the visible" means from the mere appearance of objects. || 37 ||
O young great hero, your mind has turned away from enjoyments which are like long-lasting diseases; what else do you wish to hear? (38)
Though a child, he is a great hero because of his courage in renouncing sense-objects.
The fullness of the great treasury of omniscience did not arise for your father while he remained in extensive asceticism in such a manner as it has for you. (39)
The praise is for the sake of strengthening [the conviction] that "just as fullness has arisen in you, it has not [likewise] arisen in your father";
so too in what follows. || 39 ||
"I am indeed superior to Vyāsa; you are his disciple and thus his son.
By the attenuation of your desire for enjoyment, you have become even more distinguished than I."
Everything that was to be attained has been attained by you, whose mind is now full.
O Brahmin, you do not fall into the visible world; you are liberated, so cast away delusion. 41.

You do not fall into the visible external object, because falling into the perception of the visible is itself the fall into saṃsāra; for the Śruti says, "He who perceives any difference therein becomes afraid. [Abandon] delusion—either the delusion that there exists some other object of knowledge, or the delusion of perceiving the visible. || 41 ||
Having been thus instructed by the high-souled Janaka,
Śuka remained silent, established in the pure, supreme reality.

Having been thus instructed—"You are that aforementioned one, the single, uninterrupted conscious Self"—that Śuka [remained] in the pure [state], which is free from the impurity of the visible world. || 42 ||
Free from sorrow, fear, and exertion, devoid of worldly desire, and with all doubts severed,
he went to the faultless peak of Mount Meru for the sake of meditative absorption.
Because it is presided over by sattvic deities, it is irreproachable due to the absence of causes for distraction; that is to say, it is conducive to meditative absorption (samādhi). || 43 ||
Having remained there for ten thousand years in non-conceptual meditative absorption, he was extinguished within himself like a lamp without oil.
He was pacified and became liberated from the body. || 44 ||

Pure, with the stain of temporal succession removed, that great-souled one himself attained oneness within his own stainless and purifying self, just as a drop of water merges into the ocean once its latent tendencies have dissolved. (45)

*Kalanā* is the state of being oriented toward the visible; *kalaṅka* is its root, which is ignorance (*ajñāna*). Upon the departure of both of these, [one attains oneness] with the supreme reality of the Self. In the case of the water droplet, *kalanā* is the state of being separate; *kalaṅka* is the dark cloud. And it is said in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "When the ignorance that produces differentiation has gone to absolute destruction, [the Self...]"
"Who will create a non-existent difference in Brahman? Thus [it is said]. 45.

Thus ends the first canto, titled "The Departure of Śuka," in the section on the Conduct of the Seeker of Liberation within the *Mokṣopāya* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* tradition.
Thus ends the first canto, titled "The Departure of Śuka," in the Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Second Chapter.
Viśvāmitra said:
[This is] merely the cleansing of the impurity of that son of Vyāsa.
O Rāma, it is used by you exactly as much as is required. || 1 ||
Here, the enthusiasm of Viśvāmitra— the wise one who was requested by [Brahmā] for the purpose of instructing Rāma— is proclaimed.
Applying the story of the parrot to the present context in order to prompt Vasiṣṭha to instruct Rāma, [the author] says:

"In whatever manner instruction joined with logical reasoning is employed, in that very same way it is employed and appropriate for you as well"—this is the connection. [The phrase] "it was employed" means...

It should not, however, be explained as being merely supplementary to the preceding sentence, because that would contradict the rule prescribing the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* within the same sentence. || 1 ||

O lords of sages, by this [knowledge] everything that is to be known has been understood without remainder; for him, worldly enjoyments do not provide pleasure, just as diseases do not please one of sound intellect. (2)
The address "O Lords of Sages" is used to support the stated meaning by means of the consensus of all sages.

"They please" (svadante) means they are pleasing or agreeable. For this Rāma; the dative case is used because of the rule "rucy-arthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ" [Pāṇini 1.4.33], which prescribes the dative for the one who is pleased by things that cause pleasure. || 2 ||
This is indeed the characteristic of a mind that has known what is to be known:
that all varieties of enjoyments no longer taste sweet. (3)
Through the contemplation of enjoyments, bondage born of unreal things attains firmness;
through that same contemplation being stilled, bondage in the world reaches attenuation.
By means of cultivation—that is, by means of habitual impression—one brings about attenuation, which is to say, reduction.
O Rāma, the attenuation of latent impressions (vāsanā) is called liberation by the wise;
the firmness of latent impressions regarding objective entities is designated as bondage. (5)

To the extent that the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding objects are exhausted, to that extent one is liberated; the sense is that when they are exhausted in every way, there is liberation from everything. || 5 ||
O Sage, for most men, the realization of the truth of their own self occurs only after they have become weary of sense objects due to the hardships of worldly existence.

Approaching [the teacher] results in intuitive knowledge (*āpātajñāna*), which generally arises even with little effort such as limited hearing [of the teachings], and not from the hardship of indirect perception (*aparokṣa*). || 6 ||
He who perceives correctly is a knower of that; having known what is to be known, he is a wise man.
To that great-souled one, enjoyments do not become palatable by force.
In that case, what is the use of mere detachment? To this he says: "Properly" (*samyak*).

He who sees in such a way that it remains unobstructed by passion and the like—he alone is the knower of that; he is the one who possesses the fruit of the destruction of ignorance born from the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), and he is the wise man who has known what is to be known.
But one who perceives only the surface does not see it as such because of the non-removal of his ignorance; this is the intended meaning. || 7 ||
He for whom worldly enjoyments no longer hold any appeal on this earth, even without such causes as fame and the like, is called one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 8 ||
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*prabhṛti*), honors, gains, and so forth are understood. [The phrase] "without a cause," meaning without a motive or a fruit;
thus, the meaning is that there is no attainment of the desired goal through hypocritical renunciation of enjoyments and the like. || 8 ||
As long as that which is to be known has not been fully understood, so long does dispassion toward sense objects fail to arise in a living being, just like a creeper in a desert land.
Through the mutual assistance of the growth of dispassion (*vairāgya*), awakening (*bodha*), and cessation (*uparama*), there occurs the ripening of knowledge (*jñānaparipāka*).

As long as [the truth] is not fully understood, so long does a lack of attachment toward sense objects (*viṣayeṣvarati*) fail to arise; thus, from the excellence of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), the excellence of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is indicated. "Even his taste [for worldly things], having seen the Supreme... (*raso 'py asya paraṃ dṛṣṭvā*)...
The intention is that [the world] ceases to exist, according to the words of the Blessed One. || 9 ||
Therefore, know that this scion of Raghu has already known what is to be known;
for these delightful realms of enjoyment do not delight him. (10)
The objects of experience are the planes of enjoyment. || 10 ||
O lords of sages, having heard from his own mouth that "that which Rama knows within himself is the true reality," one surely attains peace of mind. 11.

If Rāma is already a knower of reality (*tattvajña*), then for what purpose is the request to Vasiṣṭha to be made hereafter for the sake of instruction? To this he says: "Rāma. [The meaning is: from the mouth of the existent Vasiṣṭha; the ellipsis is that "anyone else who is qualified would certainly obtain [this knowledge] as well. Thus, the meaning is that the request for instruction is for the benefit of all. Alternatively:
That which Rāma knows as the inner reality, Rāma alone [perceives] due to the absence of firm conviction; he merely awaits rest in the state of absolute oneness (kevalībhāva),
for the intellect of Rāma is indeed like the autumnal splendor seeking repose.

He explains that very point clearly with the words "kevalam" (only/alone). "Resting in the state of isolation" means the remaining of non-dual pure consciousness alone upon the elimination of duality. The word "khalu" (indeed) is used for the sake of certainty; it means "with conviction. || 12 ||
In this matter, may the illustrious and venerable Vasiṣṭha provide a method for the repose of the mind of the high-souled Rāghava.
He is the eternal lord and family preceptor of all the descendants of Raghu;
he is omniscient, the witness of all, and possesses stainless vision of the three periods of time.

To the objection, "Why do you yourself not teach this?", he replies with the words "of the Raghus" (*raghūṇām*). [He is the witness] of those characterized by the Raghu lineage—meaning, of the descendants of Raghu. He is the *sākṣin*, one who sees directly both in reality and through the power of yoga, part by part. The suffix *-in* is used here according to the rule *sākṣāddraṣṭari saṃjñāyām*. The reason for this is that he is stainless (*amalam*)—that is, unobscured by delusion—with respect to all three periods of time.
He whose mind is the means for [attaining] vision. || 14 ||
O venerable Vasiṣṭha, do you perhaps remember what was done previously by yourself for the sake of pacifying the enmity between us and for the welfare of those of great intelligence? (15)
The word "kaccit" is used in the sense of an inquiry regarding welfare; it connects with the subsequent phrase "of the sages of great intellect. (15)
On the peak of Mount Niṣadha, which was crowded with sages and Sarala trees,
much knowledge was taught by the Lord Brahmā.
On the ridge, that is, on the level plateau; *sarala* refers to a specific species of tree; "much" means either excellent in quality or abundant by way of its occurrence. 16.
O Brahmin, by that reasoned knowledge indeed this worldly latent impression surely comes to rest, just as darkness does before the sun.
By which knowledge; [it consists of] reasoning, logical proof, and one-pointed concentration. || 17 ||
O Brahmin, quickly instruct that very same reasoning to Rāma, who dwells at the end of the path, so that he may attain rest.
And this is by no means a hardship, for Rāma is one whose impurities have been removed; just as a face reflects effortlessly in a stainless mirror.
It yields little fruit, involves great effort, and is a source of affliction. || 19 ||

That knowledge, that meaning of the scriptures, and your own irreproachable skill— O virtuous one, whatever is taught to a good disciple who is free from attachment, that indeed is what is truly taught.
This is not a reproach; on the contrary, because it brings about the fulfillment of the purpose of the higher knowledges, compassion, and so forth, it is indeed an excellence.
Thus he says: "That... *Vidagdha* means a learned person; the state of being such is *vaidagdhya*. It is "blameless" (*anindita*), meaning praiseworthy.
The sense is that if there were no application toward worthy recipients (*pātra*), it would be useless and thus indeed blameworthy. || 20 ||
Whatever is taught to one who is not a disciple or who lacks dispassion becomes impure, like cow’s milk poured into a dog’s skin-bag. (21)
A *dṛti* is a leather bellows.
Free from passion, fear, and anger, devoid of pride, and with their sins dissolved—wherever those like you speak, here the intellect finds its rest. (22)

Since passion and the other afflictions have their root in ignorance, it is only through the destruction of that [ignorance] that one becomes free from passion and so forth. "Galitainasaḥ" means those whose sins have fallen away, i.e., who are sinless. "Iha" means in this very state of instruction; or, it refers to this very reality of the Self which is not beyond perception. || 22 ||
When this was said by the son of Gādhi, those sages, headed by Vyāsa and Nārada, honored him for that very matter, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! (23).
By Viśvāmitra, the son of Gādhi; they honored and praised him. || 23 ||
Then the illustrious sage Vasiṣṭha, possessed of great splendor and standing by the side of the king like Brahmā’s son Brahmā himself, spoke.

Since he is the son of Brahmā and, like Brahmā himself, is distinguished by qualities such as great majesty, the sense is that he spoke even before the divine great sages just as Brahmā would. || 24 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O sage, I shall carry out what you command without obstacle;
for who, even if capable, is able to transgress the word of the virtuous?

As if instructing those who possess the knowledge of reality through their own conduct by means of qualities such as humility (*amānitva*) and other characteristics, he promises to explain the matter requested through humble words, beginning with "O Sage" (*mune*), etc.; "you command" (*ādiśasi*) means you give an order. || 25 ||
For I shall quickly dispel the darkness of mind of the princes, Rāma and the others, with knowledge, just as one dispels the darkness of night with a lamp. (26)
The word "immediately" (aśu) is used to indicate that there is no delay in the cessation of ignorance once knowledge has arisen. || 26 ||
I remember it all without omission for the sake of pacifying the delusion of saṃsāra—
that knowledge which was formerly proclaimed on Mount Niṣadha by the Lotus-born One.

I remember all that knowledge which was previously proclaimed by the Lotus-born [Brahmā], unimpaired and uninterrupted, both in its textual form and its meaning; or rather, I remember it as unimpaired—that is, continuously—or I maintain it in my mind. Vālmīki said:

Having spoken thus, that Great-Souled One, Vasiṣṭha, whose oratorical splendor was enhanced by his firm resolve, explained this— solely for the awakening to the supreme state and for the pacification of ignorance.

Having clearly declared and promised, "This great-souled one is Vasiṣṭha," he— engaging in the employment of examples, narratives, means of valid knowledge, logic, and other methods for the purpose of awakening and pleasing his disciples— shone just as a hero or an actor shines when prepared with the array of ornaments, garments, weapons, and other accoutrements.

Having assumed and taken hold of the splendor— the specific brilliance— of speakers and commentators by means of binding on the armor of courage and other virtues, he, being thus constituted, makes known this single, primary awakening to the supreme state, which will be described hereafter, for the sake of pacifying the ignorance of all the worlds— that is, for its total eradication at the root.
He taught the scripture for the purpose of awakening to that. || 28 ||
Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Words of Viśvāmitra," in the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa* of the *Tātparyaprakāśa* commentary on the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
*** In the *Ārṣa Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* of Vālmīki, within the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa*, this is the second canto, titled "The Words of Viśvāmitra. (2)
The Third Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That knowledge which was previously spoken by the Blessed One, the Lotus-born [Brahmā], [is now to be related].
At the beginning of creation, for the sake of the peace of the world, I shall relate this very [account]. || 1 ||

The object of inquiry— the inner conscious self— is established through the superimposition and subsequent removal of the world, beginning with gross objects, under the guise of dispelling Rāma’s doubt.
Having thus recalled everything from the past in detail, he who desires to speak of that [subject] first recollects the True Guru (*sadguru*).

By stating, "For the sake of pacifying all the sufferings of saṃsāra, I shall explain this very scripture which has been declared as the knowledge and the means for attaining that knowledge, and nothing else," the purity of the tradition (*saṃpradāya*) is established. || 1 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, you shall indeed relate the extensive compendium on liberation;
however, first dispel this doubt that has arisen in me for a moment.

Thus constrained by his promise, Rāma— since it was impossible for him to attend to the inquiry into truth while there was another inquiry to be made, as the desire for truth had not yet arisen— spoke, seeking to dispel the doubt that had first arisen according to the maxim of the needle and the kettle:

"You shall tell"—the sense is: "after the cessation of this doubt. This doubt arose because Vyāsa was seen alive by the world of the learned (śiṣṭas), while Śuka was heard to have attained liberation without a body (videhamukti). || 2 ||
Śuka’s father was the omniscient and high-minded preceptor Vyāsa, who was liberated while in the body (videhamukta); how then could his son not be liberated? How indeed could he not be liberated? (3)
He demonstrates that very point with the word "father. Now, one might object: "Is this doubt not ill-founded? No;
for the fruit of knowledge is indeed liberation consisting in the absolute cessation of suffering, and if even Vyāsa, the omniscient one, did not achieve it—[then how could others do so?]"

The state of being the fruit of knowledge would thus be rendered impermanent. Furthermore, if ignorance were completely eradicated by knowledge, then—as in the case of Bhṛgu and others—continued life would be impossible, because when the material cause is destroyed, the persistence of its effect is untenable; and if there were no continued life, [liberation would follow immediately].

"Because there is no one to initiate the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), the tradition has been interrupted. If it has not been interrupted, then why is it not manifest? [It does not bear fruit because it is not something to be performed. It bears fruit because its nature as the indivisible Self is perceived throughout the three periods of time.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The motes of dust within the three worlds, which arise again and again only to dissolve within the light of the supreme sun, do not admit of any calculation.

Thus questioned, the venerable Vasiṣṭha thought: "As long as Rāma does not understand that bondage is rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), the true nature of ignorance, and the nature of consciousness (*cit*) which is its witness, undivided, and the support of all, he will not have confidence in liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*); therefore, I shall first establish those points and subsequently provide the resolution. With this in mind, he spoke.

He demonstrates the superimposition of the succession of gross manifestations through the three verses beginning with "paramārkā... (the supreme sun), based on such scriptural passages as: "There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars;
by its light the sun shines, kindled with splendor," because [Brahman] is the illuminator of all things, including the sun and everything else.

The motes of dust (*trasareṇu*) that constitute the infinite millions of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) which support the three worlds—having arisen again and again, and having remained and remained—are dissolved; they do not admit of calculation. The meaning is that they cannot be numbered.
By this, it is indicated that Vyāsa and others as well are beyond numbering. || 4 ||
And as for those millions of multitudes in the three worlds that exist at present,
not even one of them can be counted by anyone.

Regarding the phrase "they exist as present": "presentness" is defined as being commenced but not yet completed, while "existence" is the connection with the time of utterance; thus, there is no tautology. || 5 ||
There will be waves of world-creations in the supreme ocean of consciousness;
indeed, there is no way at all to enumerate them.
The Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is that very ocean; those who will come into being—them [it refers to]. "That" is well-known; "story" (*kathā*) is the activity of speech.

By this, the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the world upon the Supreme Self—the substratum for the origination and so forth of all that is born throughout the three periods of time—is demonstrated. (6)
Śrī Rāma said:
It is appropriate to investigate those successions of world-creations that have occurred and those that will occur; but what indeed are those that are currently present?

Overlooking the matter asked about and speaking of something else, the Guru—whose intention was hidden—indicated his own skill to encourage Gora by saying, "I have understood it correctly myself. Rāma, pointing out some specific distinction within those chapters, said:
"Although they are innumerable in their individual forms, nevertheless, in terms of time, they are thus..."

The sense is that because both banks [of the river] are visible, their number is known to be fewer when compared with past and future creations; thus, they are already understood. "What are they like? Of what nature are they? Are they yet to come?"—since there is not even a similarity between these two [past and future], it is not appropriate to include them in that enumeration. Likewise, regarding the infinite adventitious [entities]...
The sense is: "I have understood that you have shown them the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) as infinite, one, non-adventitious, and of the nature of consciousness. || 7 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Whether one is an animal, a human, a god, or another, that name by which he is known perishes; at the very moment and in the very place where it ceases, he perceives this [new state].

Thus, encouraged by that specific description which reveals his hidden intention, Śrī Vasiṣṭha—desiring to demonstrate that what was previously described as the gross manifestation of grossness is in fact merely the subtle phenomenal world—spoke the verse beginning with "Tiryañca" (Animals). "Animals" refers to beasts, birds, and so forth; "men" refers to humans; and "gods" are well known.

The meaning is this: within that collection of living beings of which [the body] is the primary constituent, whichever individual soul perishes or dies in a particular place at a particular time, that very self beholds this threefold world—which is about to be described—in that same place at that very time, and not elsewhere, nor after a delay. || 8 ||
Within his own heart, by means of the subtle body known as the *ātivāhika*, the unborn one experiences the three worlds in the void through his ethereal mental form.

Regarding what equipment he possesses and what his nature is when he sees [the truth], he says: "The subtle body consisting of latent impressions (vāsanāmaya-sūkṣma-śarīra). *Ativāha* means carrying across—that is, the conveyance to the other world by the deities presiding over the paths such as smoke and light; that which is suitable for this is the *ativāhika*. By name, it is the subtle body composed of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). With this, he sees.

Within his own heart, in the internal void— the *dahara-ākāśa*— he experiences the three worlds as consisting solely of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) through delusion, or he sequentially attains various bodies composed of such impressions. In reality, however, he is of the nature of space, having the aforementioned form of the consciousness-space (*cidākāśa*), and for this very reason, he is unborn (*aja*).

The meaning is that [the Self] is devoid of modifications such as birth and so forth. Now, an objection is raised: "By that light, this Self departs—either from the eye, or from the head, or from other parts of the body;
as it departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) departs after it; whether it is departing or staying... and so on, with many such scriptural passages.

If it is asked, "How can this be said?"— it is true that those statements from the Śruti and Smṛti are made from the perspective of conventional practice corresponding to ritual action and meditation (*karmopāsanā*). But here, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), [the earth and heaven] are "contained within this very [Self]" (*asmin dyāvāpṛthivī antareva samāhite*), just as the scriptural statement says they are contained within the heart (*hṛdi*).

The conception of another world is now explained. Because the self is all-pervasive, it is not confined to the heart; having set aside the limitation of the heart, [the text] establishes that the phenomenal world is devoid of action and consists merely of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and that even such things as departing and going to another world are likewise [mere impressions] therein.
There is no contradiction, because it is intended [to be understood] that [the world] is established even by mere conceptualization (kalpanāmātra). || 9 ||
In this way, millions have died, are dying, and will die—those beings who individually pursued various hopes for the world. (10)

He demonstrates that the principle established in one instance applies everywhere with the word "evam" (thus). The grammatical connection is: "the crores of beings. At the time of death, the worlds—the various objects of perception—become dissolved within the latent impressions (*vāsanās*) of those worlds;
whichever specific hope or impression (*vāsanā*) corresponds to whichever particular impression in which the ripening of karma has occurred—[those dissolve therein].

The meaning is that those very [states] flash forth and attain them; the sense is that this is established by such scriptural and traditional texts as, "Whatever they become, that they become," and "Remembering whatever state... and so forth. || 10 ||
Like a creation of mere imagination, like the play of a kingdom of the mind, and like a succession of magical illusions, it is like the appearance of the meaning of a story. || 11 ||

Thus, regarding the fact that the world consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he describes its ultimate nature as being illusory from the perspective of the highest truth (*paramārtha*) through six verses beginning with *saṃkalpa*. The distinction is this: in the case of mental worship and the like, palaces made of jewels and so forth are constructed with effort within the realm of imagination (*manorājya*), whereas [in the case of the world] they are produced without effort.

Regarding the reading "nirvāṇam," *nirvṛti* (cessation) is *nirvāṇa*, which is the bliss born from embracing an imaginary woman and the like; that very delusion in which it appears is like a garland fashioned by a magician’s trick (*indrajāla*). || 11 ||
Like a young piśāca trembling during a violent wind and earthquake;
like a string of pearls in a clear sky; like a tree and a vehicle motionless [in stillness]. 12.

A "durvāta" is a specific type of wind; by it, the illusion of an earthquake is produced. Just as a *piśāca* (demon) is imagined for the purpose of terrifying a child, so too is the pearl-string (*muktālī*) a cluster of pearls. It is well known that for those on a boat, when the vessel moves, there is an illusory perception (*bhrānti*) of the trees standing on the shore moving along with it. || 12 ||
Like a city perceived in a dream, or like a sky-flower born of memory,
the world-process within one's own mind is experienced by oneself once one has died.
"Consciousness" (saṃvitti) means perception. "Born from memory" refers to that which is imagined, like a flower in the sky;

likewise, the world-process (jagatsaṃsaraṇam)—which ends in the nominative case—is an illustration by way of analogy with the preceding nominative examples, and it also serves as an indicator for that which has arisen [from memory]. || 13 ||
There, through extreme transformation, that very [space] attains density;
thus, this world manifests within the space of the living soul (jīvākāśa). (14)
In that case, how is it that the Sūtra of the venerable Bādarāyaṇa, "And because of dissimilarity, [the dream body] is not like a dream," is to be understood?
Regarding the dissimilarity of the enjoyer there with respect to a long duration, the fixed nature of worldly transactions, and the conviction of its reality, he says: "Therein.
"Excessive transformation" means long-standing familiarity. "Solidity" means firmness through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*).
And thus, the sense is that the conventional usage of "dissimilarity" and so forth is produced by that very [difference]. || 14 ||
Furthermore, in that very state, one who experiences birth, death, and so forth, imagines a supreme world; having died there, he likewise imagines it again.

He says "furthermore" (*punar*) in order to show that the world is false (*mithyātva*) also because its nature is unstable (*anavasthitasvabhāvatva*). "Effort" (*īhā*) refers to activity from after birth until death. (15)
Within that are other persons, and within them others, and likewise yet others;
thus these appear in the cycle of existence like the layers of a plantain tree.

Within the end of latent impressions (vāsanā), there are other persons and bodies; by the term "persons," even animals and so forth are included. There are neither the collections of great elements such as earth, nor the sequences of the world for those who have died; yet even there, they possess the delusions of a world. (17)
Thus, having established that [the world] is false, and intending to show that the existence of the Self is established by the negation of that [world], he says:

"Not earth, etc. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "[they] are not destroyed without knowledge. In this way, the existence of the remaining Self is established through the negation of the phenomenal world (prapañca). || 17 ||
For this ignorance alone is infinite, possessing manifold expansions; for the dull-witted, it is like a river of long duration, a surging stream of successive creations. 18.

Intending to show that its cessation cannot be accomplished by mere denial without the cutting off of its root, he states that it is to be destroyed by ignorance (*avidyā*) alone, saying: "Ignorance itself.
For the dull-witted and deluded, it is long-lasting—that is, difficult to cross—by those who are crossing, i.e., moving forward.
With its cantos, it is like a river possessing waves. || 18 ||
O Rāma, in the vast ocean of ultimate reality, the waves of creation arise again and again—both those very same ones and many others in great abundance. (19)

He shows that [the Self] is the substratum for all conceptual constructions such as ignorance and so forth—by the words "paramārtha" (ultimate reality) and so on. Those [constructions] are both former and new. 19.
Some are similar in every respect—by way of family lineage, conduct, and qualities;
some are similar by half; and others are entirely distinct.
There, I remember this sage Vyāsa as the thirty-second,
by means of the vision of knowledge that appears according to its capacity.

Having established the order of the world and the subject matter of the present treatise by way of an introductory digression that resolves a relevant doubt, he begins the resolution of that doubt with the words "imam" and so forth, [referring to] that which is being observed by the authors of the Purāṇas, the Mahābhārata, and other such works.

The connection is as follows: "I remember this thirty-second [chapter]"—referring to those waves within the creation of Vyāsa which are characterized by their renown, by their appropriate origin and birth, by their wisdom consisting of knowledge of the scriptures and so forth, and by their vision consisting of the knowledge of Brahman. || 21 ||
Among them, twelve were of small intellect and equal to others in their family forms; ten were all of uniform appearance, while the remaining ones were distinct from their families.
Regarding these as well, he states the internal distinctions with the word "twelve": among those renowned as the Knower of Brahman (*brahmavit*),

the Excellent Knower of Brahman (*brahmavidvara*), the More Excellent Knower of Brahman (*brahmavidvarīyān*), and the Most Excellent Knower of Brahman (*brahmavidvariṣṭha*), because one does not rest at the fourth station, there are those of small intellect— such as Vyāsa and Vālmīki— who will likewise continue to appear even now.
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Pulastya, as well as others likewise.
The meaning is that they are just like the previous ones in some respects, yet different from them in other respects, being characterized by those distinct features. || 23 ||
Men, the hosts of celestial sages, and the gods, having come together in great numbers,
are born and at times dissolve individually.
I know that there have been, are, and will be seventy-two Brahmās in the Tretā ages; I know who he was, who he is, and who he will be, as well as the worlds, you, and me.

The Brāhmī [age], which constitutes a part of the Brāhma-kalpa, is currently the Tretā; and it has existed thus in every kalpa. This tenth incarnation of this sage Vyāsa, of wondrous deeds and far-sighted vision, is clearly perceived in this manner. (26)
Of this Vyāsa standing before [me], the soul of Vyāsa. || 26 ||
We have been joined with Vyāsa and Vālmīki many times;
we ourselves have also appeared individually in many different ways.
"We alone have become these; know that we are similar to others. We alone have become these, diverse in form yet identical in intention. (28)
The others are dissimilar; "vidaḥ" means those who possess knowledge. || 28 ||
Indeed, he must once again manifest here his own eightfold incarnation;
furthermore, he will compose the work named Bhārata, together with the Itihāsas. (29)
"He will do this"—this is the ellipsis. || 29 ||
Having divided the Vedas and established the fame of this lineage through him,
and likewise having performed the office of the Brahman priest, the liberation of the people of Videha must be brought about.

The fame (*prathām*) of the family, of one's own lineage, or of the Bharata dynasty; the state of Brahmā (*brahmatvam*), meaning the office of Hiraṇyagarbha; and the liberation of Videha (*vaidehamokṣaṇam*), meaning the attainment of liberation while in the body (*videhamuktatām*).

The word "remnant" (*śeṣaḥ*) refers to that which has been attained by one who has reached liberation in the disembodied state. The form *bhāvyam* is a gerundive (*kṛtya*) used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*). Alternatively:

The liberation of the Vaideha [Rāvaṇa] is to be brought about; it is to be attained. The root *bhū* meaning "to attain" is conjugated in the Ātmanepada; from it, the kṛtya suffix is applied in the sense of the object (passive). || 30 ||
Free from sorrow and fear, possessing peaceful nirvāṇa, with all conceptual construction gone, this Vyāsa is described as one liberated while living, having conquered his mind. || 31 ||

He now demonstrates his state of liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*) with the verse beginning "vīta-": "Nirvāṇa" means one who has gone out from the bond of delusion (*moha-bandhana*). Since the root *gam* (to go) is used here in the sense of motion, the suffix *kta* denotes the agent. In the rule "nirvāṇo vāte," the final *ṇ* is substituted for *t*.
It is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "he who is both peaceful (*śānta*) and liberated (*nirvāṇa*). For this very reason, [the word] "gone" (*gata*)...
He for whom there is no conceptual construction of the superimposition of "I" and "mine," and for this very reason, he is free from sorrow and fear. || 31 ||
Beings may at times be equal in terms of wealth, kin, age, action, learning, wisdom, and conduct; yet they are never truly so.
But those two minds are not identical; this is the logical conclusion. || 32 ||

[The word "kvacit" connects with both what precedes and what follows: At times, through hundreds of creations, these [worlds] come into being or do not; yet at no time is this illusion ever thus devoid of an end.
They occur only occasionally and at certain times. || 33 ||
This vast succession of beings perpetually yields perversion, like a heap of seeds that is being replenished again and again. (34)

The succession of beings refers to the multitude of living creatures. Just as a heap of seeds, such as grain and the like, when repeatedly filled into a measure like a *prastha* and then made into a heap again, does not remain with its seeds arranged in their previous order, but rather undergoes a transformation and is scattered—so it is with this. (34)
In that very same configuration, and again in another, the forms of creation proceed repeatedly like waves from the ocean of time. (35)
Arrangement (*saṃniveśa*) is either a specific configuration of parts or a sequence. (36)
With his inner heart consoled, with conceptual constructions stilled, consisting of the essence of his own true nature,
and satisfied by the nectar of supreme peace, the wise one remains free from all veils.
Even when one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) assumes various bodies for the sake of qualification through the power of yoga, there is no change in the nature of liberation;
for the cause that brings about everything is unobscured (*nirāvaraṇa*).
This is because [liberation] is not characterized by the lack of confidence in conceptual constructions, nor by being composed of the body and so forth, nor by a lack of peace or satisfaction.
And that [attainment] is the fruit of knowledge; the sense is that it is not partial. || 36 ||

The Fourth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as water remains water whether it is in the state of gentle droplets or in the state of waves;
The liberation of the sage from the body is like the sameness [of the sky] within the ocean. || 1 ||
In this context, no distinction is proclaimed between liberation and the experience of liberation;
rather, both scriptural authority and human effort are praised for the sake of strengthening the foundation.

For the Self, whose nature is eternally liberated, bondage consists solely in the obscuration of ignorance; liberation is simply the destruction of that [ignorance] by means of knowledge. Once ignorance has been destroyed, worldly activity—even though it is being experienced—is like a painted tiger: it serves only for amusement and not for harm. Thus, there is no difference between one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and one who is liberated after death (videhamukta).

Having resolved the previous doubt and desiring to teach the present reality of the Self in detail, [the author] first establishes the necessity of human effort for the sake of strengthening the foundation, beginning with the words "O gentle one" (*saumya*). O gentle one, O one of pleasing appearance: in the state of being water—that is, in the state of being motionless water—it is indeed even, not uneven; likewise, it is bodiless.
Liberation exists neither with a body nor without a body within the realm of objects;
for one who has not tasted enjoyment, how can there be experiences of what is to be enjoyed? (2)

Nor is liberation dependent on objects; for if liberation were dependent on objects like heaven and so forth, then it would likewise be variable due to the variation in those objects—this is the sense. Now, one might object: "Even so, there is certainly a distinction based on being an enjoyer or a non-enjoyer, since the maintenance of the body exists for the sake of enjoyment. To this, he says:

—“Un-tasted”: by means of the notion that worldly enjoyments are real and the conceit of being an enjoyer. For while a distinction produced by enjoyment might exist for one who tastes enjoyment, it does not exist for one who perceives the oneness of the Self as unattached and indifferent; this is the sense.
We behold before us that best of sages, liberated while living, who is indeed like a solitary object; there is no further obstacle within his inner being.

If so, how can he possess a body? To this he says: "the one liberated while living" (jīvanmukta). We see Vyāsa, the best of sages, before us as if possessing a body, like any other object. The words "by our own imagination" are to be supplied [to the end of the sentence]. The sense is: "due to the internal disposition [of the observer]. || 3 ||

What difference can there be between those liberated with a body and those liberated without a body, since they are both of the nature of pure consciousness? It is just like the case of water and its waves: though they differ in form, their essence is the same.
For it is indeed non-awareness (*abodha*) that creates differentiation; when that has vanished and only pure awareness (*bodha*) remains, what differentiator could there be?
This is the meaning. "In gentleness" means in clarity through stillness. "That water" means that very water itself. || 4 ||
There is not even the slightest difference between liberation while embodied and disembodied liberation;
just as air, whether moving or still, remains simply air.

He supports the statement that "even in water there might sometimes be a distinction caused by lack of clarity and so forth" by means of another illustration, saying: "not even slightly" (na manāk). || 5 ||
Whether with body or without body, liberation is not an object of valid cognition;
for us as well, there exists that indivisible self-identity.
In this regard, in some manuscripts it is read:
"I have declared the state of Kevalin, whose life consists of the remembrance of that [Truth];
for one both with body and without body, equanimity alone is always auspicious."

Thus, an additional verse is recited; its meaning is as follows: Now, it may be argued that air is characterized by motion (*saspaṇda*), is cool, is the cause of the trembling of trees, waves, and so forth, and is perceptible by the sense of touch (*tvagindriya-vedya*); whereas non-motion (*aspanda*) is the opposite of that.
Therefore, since a distinction certainly exists even there, how can it serve as an example for the absence of that [distinction]? To this, he says:

"May I... O Rāma, you should understand by way of analogy that which has been stated everywhere—that which is intended—as the very life and essence of the recollection of those respective illustrations: the state of isolation (*kevalībhāva*), characterized by the non-deviation from the true nature of reality;
and not that which is unintended [or that which merely produces the desired effect].

The meaning is: "imagine" (kalpaya) refers to imagining a distinction (*vailakṣaṇya*) produced by a difference in effects (*kāryabheda*). Thus, the point is that the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) applies to one aspect (*ekāṃśa*), not to every aspect. Here, the object of comparison (*upameya*) stated is the unity of the embodied and the disembodied.

That which is intended to be expressed is remembered for the sake of its similarity; that remembrance is the means of comparison (*upamāna*), whose life is the manifestation of similarity with the object of comparison (*upameya*). Furthermore, even the worldly discourse regarding the bondage and liberation of the body and the non-body is merely a conceptual construction from the perspective of the ignorant.

Regarding the phrase "the vision of ultimate reality," he says: "whether with body or without body. For us—Vasiṣṭha, him [Śuka], and Vyāsa as well—liberation, whether with body or without body, is not the locus or object of valid cognition, that is, of the vision of ultimate reality; rather, it is non-differentiated and devoid of duality.

Since there is only the oneness of one's own Self, and because there is no distinction in the fruit of knowledge—which consists in the attainment of that [oneness]—there is no room for the suspicion of the defect of impermanence in the fruit of knowledge; nor does the consequence of the fall of the body follow upon the arising of knowledge.
This is because only that portion which is opposed to the Self is sublated by knowledge, while the maintenance of the body persists as the result of *prārabdha* (commenced karma).
The point is this: because it is not contradicted by knowledge— due to its similarity to knowledge and its status as that upon which knowledge depends—

just as the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a dream persists for some time even after the sleep (the material cause) has been destroyed, so too, even when ignorance (*avidyā*) is severed, the appearance of the body and so forth remains possible for as long as the prārabdha karma lasts.
Therefore, listen to this very subject at hand, which is an ornament for the ears—
the knowledge being taught by me, which destroys the blindness of ignorance.

Thus, having dispelled the doubt, he shows the occasion for the subject at hand with the words "Therefore": "Ignorance (ajñāna), that is, ignorance itself, is blindness; its destruction [is the goal]. (7)
For in this world, O descendant of Raghu, everything is always obtained by everyone through human effort when it is properly applied.

[Objection: But how can the hearing [of the scriptures] by others in the present day bear fruit, given that it was fruitful for Śuka and others who were endowed with the means such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*), since those means are difficult to accomplish? [Reply: This is not so;
everything is always obtained. If that is so, why is effort seen to be fruitless in some cases? To this, he says:
"Rightly" (samyak) means precisely non-cessation; it is "attained" (samavāpyate), that is, fully reached. || 8 ||
For here, like the moon, a cool refreshment arises in the heart;
yet, in the attainment of the fruit of one's exertion, it comes from human effort alone and from nothing else.

"Exertion" (*parispanda*) refers to action (*karman*) in the form of the movement of body, speech, and mind as prescribed by the scriptures. Its fruit is knowledge, attained through the purification of the mind; when that is attained, there is the bliss of Brahman, which is cool and free from desire, anger, and other such afflictions. As for the phrase "of the learned one (*śrotriya*) who is unaffected by desire," there is also the traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "And whatever happiness is found in desires..."

Whatever great divine happiness exists in the world, these do not equal even a sixteenth part of the happiness arising from the destruction of craving. Thus, since all of that arises solely from human effort and nothing else, the sense is that one must apply oneself with total reliance to human exertion alone. || 9 ||
Human effort is seen through direct perception to lead to results like the ripening of a fruit;
as for "fate," which is imagined by the deluded and the dull-witted, it does not exist at all.

Now, one might object: "Is it not seen that human effort (pauruṣa) is rendered futile when fate (daiva) is adverse? And since there is the common saying that 'prosperities are beset by many obstacles,' there can be no confidence in attaining their fruits.

Anticipating this doubt, and intending to explain the inclusion of fate within human effort as well as its relative weakness—which will be discussed later—the author refutes that [objection] independently.

—Regarding the term "pauruṣam" (human effort): human effort, such as walking or eating, is perceived through direct perception as it leads to or brings about another place or satisfaction by means of movement; thus, the word *nayat* connects with the preceding clause. Alternatively, the connection occurs with the subsequent clause through a word-split (*pada-bhaṅga*), meaning that whatever is not seen to be caused by fate does not exist [as such]. || 10 ||
Whatever movement of mind or body is performed according to the path well-taught by the virtuous, that is manly effort; that alone is fruitful, while anything else is the behavior of a madman. (11)
He states what that manly effort is which is praised: "Excellent! (sādhu). The mention of the limbs (aṅga) is also indicative of the voice (vāk). || 11 ||
Whoever desires a particular object and strives for it in due order will certainly attain it, provided he does not turn back from his purpose. (12)

"He strives" means he exerts effort. The word "in due order" (*kramāt*) is stated to indicate that in some cases there may be an obstruction by obstacles (*vighna*) precisely due to a deviation from the sequence prescribed in the scriptures. The underlying sense is that there is an invariable rule (*niyama*) that the fruit necessarily arises from a ritual action performed with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*). || 12 ||
Indeed, by means of human effort, a certain distinguished being attained the state of Śakra— the status of Indra, the bull among gods— possessing the beauty of sovereignty over the three worlds. (13)
He confirms that very rule repeatedly through corroboration with four verses beginning with "By human effort" (pauruṣeṇa).
Only a certain radiance of consciousness, by means of human effort alone, suddenly ascends to the state of Brahman, which has its abode in the lotus.

"Having occupied the lotus-seat," that is, the abode of the lotus; the ellipsis "having occupied" is to be supplied. "Brahmanhood" refers to the state of being Hiraṇyagarbha, or liberation consisting in attaining a form similar to that of the Guṇamūrti. The same applies to the two subsequent [verses]. 14.
By his own essential human effort alone, a certain man indeed has attained the state of Puruṣottama, he whose banner bears Garuḍa. || 15 ||
Through human effort alone, a certain embodied being here, whose form was once encircled by women, has attained the state of having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
Know that human effort is of two kinds: that pertaining to the past and that pertaining to the present. That of the past is quickly overcome by present human exertion. (17)
By human effort—that is, by manly exertion—it is conquered, meaning it is overcome. || 17 ||
By those who exert effort, possess firm practice, and are endowed with wisdom and enthusiasm, even Merus are swallowed; what need is there to mention former human achievements?
Now, one might ask: how can the infinite past karmas accumulated over infinite millions of kalpas be destroyed by a small amount [of practice] today?

The meaning is: by persons who have attained the state of being deities presiding over creation and dissolution. Although the karmas are indeed infinite, nevertheless, because they share a single root, their destruction is easily accomplished; intending this, he says:
"What is it? || 18 ||
The supreme manliness of a person is that which is governed by the scriptures;
for it leads to the attainment of the full weight of desired fruits, whereas otherwise it leads to misfortune. (19)
Concluding the matter thus stated, he describes the harm that results from its failure, saying: "By the scriptures...
That human effort alone which is restrained and regulated by the scriptures—namely, the Vedas and so forth—is supreme and must necessarily be undertaken;
for it alone leads to the accomplishment of the full weight of desired fruits. Otherwise, [effort] not based on the scriptures...
The meaning is: "for your own ruin. || 19 ||
In one state, due to the power of his own internal distress, a man perceives many drops of water from a single cup pressed slowly by the tip of a finger;
in another state, he perceives the world as consisting of oceans, mountains, cities, and intervening islands.
If one does not provide the appropriate distribution of shares to those who must be supported, the earth shall no longer be considered "pṛthvī" (the generous). || 20 ||

Now, one might ask: how can those with limited wealth, power, and intelligence attain the fruit of human effort—which is accomplished by great wealth, power, and intelligence—either in this very life or in another birth through the attainment of such great wealth and other resources? For it is not the case that a person's misfortune or prosperity remains constant; having considered this, [the text speaks] regarding the results of scriptural exertion and its relaxation.

He demonstrates the great difference with the words "in some [cases]": because a person’s own hand and so forth are not under their own control due to the lack of scriptural effort, even the contraction of the fingers—which is accomplished by squeezing and is itself produced through pain—is used to pour water from a single handful, measured by the palm, into the mouth; that is, it is cast therein.
Thus, even a single drop of such a kind, when added as an infusion, becomes highly esteemed because of its rarity; for when that very [drop] reaches a state of firmness through scriptural effort,
there arises an excellence of merit, as in the case of Priyavrata and others during their tenure as sovereigns of the seven continents.

The division of inheritance and so forth is appropriate for those who must be supported, such as sons and others; if that were done, the earth would not become a great mass of water—that is to say, it would not be highly esteemed. For it is well known in the Purāṇas: "We two, Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, are indeed the two sons of Snuhī. || 20 ||

Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Section on Human Effort," within the "Section on the Conduct of Those Seeking Liberation" in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis; and thus concludes the fourth canto in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Fifth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: First of all, there is the active engagement of those who conduct themselves according to the scriptures.
She is like light to the various colors, the accomplisher of all rites. || 1 ||

Since human effort is predominant here as well, and since there is an inevitable connection with the fruit even in the case of destiny, a logical argument supported by an illustration is now set forth.

He undertakes to support with logical arguments everything previously stated—that destiny does not exist apart from human effort, that human effort is more powerful than destiny, and that the attainment of the goals of human life comes from human effort alone—by stating:
"It is activity itself... [referring to] those who act without transgressing the scriptures through speech, mind, and body.
The intention is that for the accomplishment of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), initial engagement itself is the primary cause—just as in the case of blue, yellow, and so forth.

This is because of such traditional texts (*smṛti*) as: "For you, [knowledge of] the means of valid cognition is the authority in determining what is to be done and what is not to be done; for the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the cause. (Gītā 2.39). || 1 ||
That which is desired by the mind but not accomplished through action according to the scriptures—such is this intoxicating sport; it is delusive and not a means for achieving one's purpose.

[Objection: Since knowledge has a visible fruit—just like satisfaction and the like—what is the use of scriptural rules regarding its means? To this he replies: "By the mind," etc. This [practice] is mere "matta-līlā," i.e., the behavior of a madman. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "it is accomplished by that. Therefore, it is not a means for attaining human goals; on the contrary—

Delusion (*mohanī*): Even when the fruit is already perceived, one exerts oneself through non-scriptural means; by whatever means one strives, it is experienced accordingly as one's own karma alone. Thus it remains, and there is no other distinct "divine eye" (*daiva-dṛk*) apart from this. (3)

Since it is established that the fruit of scriptural effort is indeed scriptural, and the fruit of non-scriptural effort is indeed non-scriptural, one might wonder if by chance both could be the opposite; to this he says: "As... [yathā].
Now, one might object that by chance both could indeed be the opposite; to this he says: "There exists another, distinct vision, not the vision of fate" (āste 'nyā vyatiriktā na daivadṛg iti).
The meaning is that past karma alone, when in the state of fruition, is called "destiny" (daiva); no destiny is observed apart from that. || 3 ||
Human effort is traditionally held to be of two kinds: that which is contrary to the scriptures and that which is in accordance with the scriptures.
Of these, that which is contrary to the scriptures leads to misfortune, while that which is in accordance with the scriptures leads to the supreme goal.
He clarifies the very meaning already stated with the words "contrary to the scriptures" (ucchāstram). "Śāstritam" means regulated by the scriptures.
The suffix *kta* is applied after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in the sense of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), following the rule for the causative (*ṇic*). || 4 ||
Two human aims, both equal and alike, fight like two rams; the one pertaining to this life and the one pertaining to the past—whichever possesses less strength therein is subdued.
*Huḍau* means two rams; sometimes they are equal, sometimes they are unequal. *Attra* means "in the midst of these two. || 5 ||
Therefore, a person should strive by every possible means through human effort,
so that by means of this tantra and right yoga, he may quickly conquer the present [adversary].
By "tantra" is meant according to the rules of the scriptures; in the reading "atandreṇa," it means by a person who is free from laziness. || 6 ||
Two human goals, equal and opposing one another like two rams fighting, struggle for mastery;
of these two, that which possesses superior strength prevails.

Now, since the scripture states that "a human is born burdened with three debts," and because it is heard that one owes debts to the gods and others, and furthermore because it is heard that "therefore, this is not dear to them— that humans should know this," any effort made toward the practice of yoga will inevitably be fruitless due to the occurrence of obstacles.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Two. The sense is that as long as defects exist, the gods possess the power to create obstacles;
however, when those defects are overcome by one's own effort, their power to obstruct becomes blunted. || 7 ||
Where misfortune is encountered even through human effort prescribed by the scriptures, one should recognize that there, the agent of misfortune is more powerful than one's own person. (8)

Now, one might ask: "How is it that even for those striving on the path prescribed by the scriptures, misfortune such as disease is sometimes observed? To this he says: "Misfortune... and so forth. The implication is that even such [misfortune] must indeed be overcome. || 8 ||
Resorting to the utmost harshness and grinding teeth against teeth,
one should conquer the inauspicious, previously acquired human effort that is intent upon evil by means of what is auspicious.
"By auspicious exertion of present human effort" means: intent upon the performance of obstacles. || 9 ||
The thought, "This past human effort compels me," must be forcibly set aside;
it is not superior to direct perception.

The fruit of action is the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*). "To be placed underfoot" means to be trodden upon by the foot; that is to say, to be destroyed. In the expression *adhaḥśirasī pade*, there is the substitution of *s* for *ṣ*. 10.
One should strive with great effort and true manliness for as long as one's past negative karma is not pacified of its own accord. (11)

"Supauruṣam" (well-manifested by the self) is an adverbial modifier of the action. "Svayam" (by oneself) is a qualifier intended to ensure its completeness, so that once it has been pacified through another means, there may be no recurrence upon its departure. || 11 ||
A past fault is undoubtedly pacified by present virtues;
for here, the destruction of yesterday’s fault by today’s virtues serves as the illustration. (12)

To the question, "Why might not the previous [cause] alone be powerful? he says: "The defect," etc. [Verse 12]: "By means of qualities" refers to fasting and other such remedies; "of the defect" refers to indigestion and the like from the previous day.
Having cast aside false destiny with a mind that is ever-inflamed by resolve,
one should strive to establish within oneself the crossing over of saṃsāra for the sake of prosperity.
Having cast down and overcome this very evil— namely, past misfortune— with an intellect intensified by present good deeds,

one should strive for prosperity, that is, for the attainment of tranquility, self-control, hearing [the scriptures], and other such perfections, in order to establish within oneself the crossing over of saṃsāra. || 13 ||
One should not walk the path of those who lack exertion—those human donkeys;
rather, one should apply effort according to the scriptures for the sake of accomplishing success in both worlds. 14.
The two worlds are heaven and liberation.
One must emerge from this cavern of saṃsāra by one's own strength,
