relying on human effort, just as Hari [emerged] from the cage of his enemies.
As if from a cage of bondage fashioned by lions, enemies, or men; or as if from a cage of illusion employed by Viṣṇu against the Asuras. || 15 ||
Day after day, one should examine one's own body;
one should discard that which is equal to the bodies of beasts and take refuge in that which is appropriate for the virtuous.

"Equal" means "equality. This is an expression emphasizing the abstract state. One should resort to the company of the virtuous, the study of true scriptures, and so forth, which are appropriate for a noble person. 16.
One should not reduce one's life to ashes by indulging in the tender pleasures of home—such as lovely food and drink—just as a worm does not consume a wound. (17)
*Kalila* means thick, liquid, and slimy. *Vayaḥ* refers to youth, the means for accomplishing all human goals.
*Bhasmasāt* means reduced to ashes; that is to say, rendered useless. || 17 ||

Through auspicious human effort, an auspicious fruit is swiftly attained; through inauspicious [effort], an inauspicious one is always [attained]. That which is called "destiny" (daiva) is nothing at all. 18.
The meaning is that there is nothing whatsoever other than one's prior wholesome and unwholesome [karma]. || 18 ||
He who abandons direct perception and resorts to inference is like one who flees upon seeing two snakes with his own eyes, thinking, "These are two snakes. (19)
Regarding the auspicious and inauspicious unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) of the present day, direct perception and scripture are the means of knowledge;

however, for those that are seen, it is the eye and other senses assisted by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Thus established, one should not abandon the authority of direct perception and scripture—which are equal to the command of a master—and instead pursue the fruits of human effort alone.
Thus ends the section on the ablative case (apādānatā). || 19 ||
"Destiny impels me"—such is the mouthpiece of those whose intellects are consumed by fire, who regard the unseen as supreme;
seeing them, Fortune turns away. (20)
It has not been seen by those who have witnessed the vision of Viśvāmitra and others—those supreme men who attained their human goals through manly effort alone. || 20 ||
Therefore, through human effort, one should first resort to discrimination;
one should thoroughly investigate the scriptures which have the great purpose of self-knowledge. || 21 ||
Discrimination (viveka) refers to the fourfold set of means characterized by the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal, and so forth. || 21 ||
Fie upon the wicked desires of those fools who, while contemplating their own goals in their minds according to the scriptures, fail to accomplish them through their own efforts. 22.

In order to stabilize the inclination toward hearing [the teachings] and so forth, he censures other activities with the words "in the mind" (*citte*). For those who do not contemplate the ultimate reality— the essence of the Self— through their own efforts consisting of activities such as hearing and reflection in accordance with the scriptures, and for that very reason [do not realize] it...
For those fools who do not accomplish the goal of human life, this [human birth] is indeed of endless suffering.

The word "indeed" (eva) is intended to highlight that even when one has obtained a suitable birth, if one does not accomplish that goal, such a birth will be difficult to obtain again. Thus says the Śruti: "If one has realized it here, then there is truth; if one has not realized it here, there is great ruin. (22)
Human effort is not endless, nor is it sought after with excessive exertion;

even with great effort, a jewel cannot be obtained from a stone [nor oil from a stone]. (23) Indeed, because human effort must be performed over such a long period of time, and because of its infinity, one might become weary of it.

That human effort is neither infinite nor limitless, because the arising of direct realization itself serves as its limit. Furthermore, it is not desired nor required even when considering the exertion and toil involved; for the meaning [of this] is based on the Lord’s own words: "The dharma that is directly perceived is very easy to practice and imperishable. Now, one might object to this:

One might suspect that the statement, "By the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one attains all desires," is merely an incitement (prarocanā), since there is a rule that greater effort results in a greater fruit; anticipating this, he states a counter-example (vyabhicāra) with the word "no" (na). It should be understood that even in the case of the *ratnatattva* [and others], there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) [between effort and result]. || 23 ||
Just as a jar is limited, and just as a cloth is limited,
so too is the purpose of man fixed and established within a definite measure.

He confirms what was stated in the first half [of the verse] by means of an illustration— namely, "just as": just as a jar in water is not delimited [by it], whereas a cloth is measured by its length and so forth and determined by means of measurement, in the very same way,
human effort directed toward the goal of man (puruṣārtha) also remains within a definite measure, culminating in the fruit of direct realization.
One who abides in the measure is indeed fixed. || 24 ||

And it is its very nature that it yields its own fruit through good scriptures, the company of the virtuous, and right conduct; otherwise, it does not lead to the accomplishment of one's purpose. (25)
That human effort is accompanied by right conduct; this is the implied meaning. || 25 ||
This is the true nature of human effort; a person who acts in this manner never, at any time, finds their exertion to be fruitless.
"This is the nature of manly effort"—this is the conclusion of what was said. He states the non-deviation from the result for such [effort] with the word "evam" (thus). || 26 ||
Even other supreme men, though afflicted by the suffering of wretchedness and poverty, have attained equality with the Lord of the Gods through human effort alone. (27)

To reinforce what has been said, he shows elsewhere as well that the fruit of this righteous human effort is never-failing—starting with the word "dainya" (misery). Others refers to Nala, Hariścandra, and so forth. || 27 ||

Since one's own true goal is attained through human effort by means of qualities such as the study of scriptures and association with the virtuous, which have been sufficiently practiced since childhood. (28)
Anticipating the objection that "if it does not depend on exertion, then we shall perform it at the end; why do it now?", he says:
"by those acting like tender thorns"—this is the meaning. || 28 ||
Those of evil intellect who think that what is seen, experienced, heard, or done by oneself has arisen from fate or has been taken away by fate, are ruined. (29)
"Seen directly" means it has been perceived by people such as ourselves who are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). "Accomplished" means through the practice of the means (*sādhana*). || 29 ||
If laziness did not exist as a misfortune in this world,
who would not be wealthy or highly learned?
It is because of laziness that this earth, extending to the edge of the oceans, remains so.
It was filled with human cattle and with those who were destitute.

If this is so, then why do not all people strive [toward this]? To this he replies: "Laziness" (*ālasya*). It is called "disaster" (*anartha*) because it is a cause of misfortune and because it obstructs one's goals. "Possessing much wealth" means being most prosperous; the suffix *kap* is applied according to the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā*. "Possessing great learning" means a wise man. "Together with those bounded by the oceans" means together with those whose limits are the seas.

The earth is the ground [for practice]. Therefore, the essential point is that one should cast off laziness and, from childhood onwards, be intent upon the company of the virtuous and similar means; this is the primary position—such is the intended meaning. || 30 ||

When childhood had passed— restless with incessant play— he diligently cultivated his intellect, which was purified in its understanding of words and their meanings through association with the virtuous, beginning from the age adorned by his powerful arms.
A person should perform investigations into their own virtues and faults. || 31 ||

If it is impossible to strive [for this goal] from extreme childhood onwards, then one should strive beginning from youth; thus he says: "In childhood... When childhood has passed—tremulous with incessant and fickle games devised by children—a man, using his two staff-like arms, [should strive] for that which is capable of serving the Teacher and so forth.

One whose intellect is purified regarding words and their meanings, who is skilled in the examination of those words and their referents—that is, in the investigation of reality—is "learned" (vyutpanna); this is the meaning.
Through association with excellent persons, such as one's own teacher, fellow students, and those most renowned for their expertise, one’s own qualities—of the self—are [cultivated].
"Regarding the faults such as tranquility and the objects such as passion, [the sage] deliberated on their benefits and disadvantages.
Vālmīki said:
"When the sage had spoken thus, the day passed away."
For the evening rite, the sun went to its setting;
the assembly, having offered salutations, departed to bathe;
and at the end of the night, it returned together with the rays of the sun.
Śrī Vālmīki said: This is the speech of the divine messenger addressed to Ariṣṭanemi. When the sage Vālmīki had spoken thus to Bharadvāja in the manner described by Vasiṣṭha, the day departed;
the lord, the sun, set, and the assembly of sages, including Bharadvāja, offered salutations to Vālmīki.

She went to bathe for the sake of the evening twilight rites, the *agnihotra*, and other such observances; then, at the end of the dark night, she returned with the morning rays of the sun—that is, together with the sunlight—to the presence of Vālmīki. This same verse applies in exactly this manner throughout the subsequent sections as well.

"It is to be explained [by me], but not by the sage Vasiṣṭha"—thus she spoke. For otherwise, there would be an untimely introduction of extensive descriptions found later on in various places: the description of Daśaratha’s departure from the assembly, the performance of the remaining daily rites, the contemplation of the matters heard by Rāma and the others during the night, and the detailed accounts of the time of dawn, the rising of the sun, and so forth.
Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Establishment of Human Effort," in the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa* of the *Tātparyaprakāśa* commentary on the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.

*** Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Establishment of Human Effort," in the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa* of the *Tātparyaprakāśa* commentary on the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, the great *Rāmāyaṇa* of Vālmīki, belonging to the *Ārṣa* tradition.
The First Day.
Chapter Six.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:

Therefore, since destiny is nothing other than one's own prior human effort, one should cast it far away and forcibly rescue the living soul by means of the company of the virtuous and the true scriptures.
Wherever powerful destiny exists, even there human effort is said to be effective; or rather, it is the powerful destiny of the past, or one's own present human effort, that prevails.
Desiring to establish the very point already stated, Vasiṣṭha said: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Because an independent [cause] is difficult to maintain, there is no destiny (*daiva*) other than prior human effort (*pauruṣa*). Destiny means that one is dependent on it and not independent; this is what is meant by the term "fatalism" (*daiṣṭikatā*). Having cast this far away—that is, having abandoned it—[one should act].
One should cause [them] to cross over; the ellipsis is "from saṃsāra. || 1 ||
"In whatever measure there may be effort, in that same measure shall the fruit quickly arise; thus human exertion alone exists, and destiny is that very same thing. (2)
What is that power? He demonstrates it with the words "just as" (yathā). || 2 ||
Just as in the case of suffering, one says "Alas! What misery! when there is pain, so too "Alas! Fate! is a synonym for the words "Alas! What misery! (hā kaṣṭam). || 3 ||
"Alas, what misery!"—this refers to past karma that has ripened into the form of suffering; the meaning is that this very thing is destiny (daiva). || 3 ||
There exists no such thing as "destiny" (daiva) that has a form other than one's own prior karma;
it can be conquered here by the fool, just as one might conquer a powerful man.
"Of another form" means like a different essential nature. Let it be that past karma alone is destiny; what follows from that? To this he says:
"The child," etc. (Verse 4).
Just as yesterday’s evil conduct quickly attains auspiciousness through beautiful conduct today, so too does prior karma [attain its fruit]. || 5 ||
By means of beautiful conduct, such as expiatory rites and the like, [he attains] auspiciousness, which is the capacity to withstand inauspiciousness. || 5 ||
Those who strive for its conquest, yet are not enslaved by even a fraction of greed,
are wretched, vulgar, and foolish, remaining dependent on fate.
"Lobhas" refers to the fragments of sensual pleasure that incite greed; those who, being addicted to these, do not strive [for liberation], are wretched, vulgar, and base. || 6 ||
Even if an action performed through human effort is destroyed by fate,
one should understand that in such a case, human effort is more powerful than the destroyer.
Even where the predominance of destiny is well-known, he shows that it is actually human effort alone that possesses predominance, with the words "by human effort" (pauruṣeṇa). || 7 ||
Now, when of two fruits on a single stalk one is hollow and empty, effort is exerted toward it for the sake of experiencing its flavor. (8)
"Granted that this may be so in the case of things dependent on human effort; however, in the case of those not dependent on humans, fate alone would be the refuge. To this he replies:

"The remainder [of the verse]: 'Whosoever—whether a human being or an insect—experiences and enjoys that flavor, it is his own previous or present effort that manifests for the sake of obstructing that flavor. (8)
Since even those worldly states that have attained perfection come to destruction, one should recognize that the power exerted by the cause of decay is indeed great. (9)

He demonstrates that the principle stated in one instance applies elsewhere as well, beginning with the words "yat" and so forth. "Yat" means "wherein"; "bhāvāḥ" refers to things or entities well-known in the world. (9)
Two human goals fight each other like two rams;
whichever among them is stronger, that one alone triumphs in an instant. (10)
In this regard, he causes [the reader] to remember what was stated: "Two," [verse 10].
That a king is forcibly reduced to a beggar by a state elephant is due to the great power of the efforts of the ministers, the elephants, and the citizens. (11)

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: it is well known that even if there is an absence of a royal lineage, anyone—even a beggar—may be made king by means of an elephant adorned with auspicious ornaments, released by the citizens and ministers. || 11 ||
Just as food, having been seized by the strength of the hand, is ground by the teeth,
so too is another person, relying on his own prowess, crushed by a hero.

"Annam" means fit for eating, that is to say, suitable for chewing. In the reading "āttam," it refers to that very same thing taken into the mouth. "Ākramya" means having crushed or pressed down. "Anyo" means one who is weak [is overcome] by a powerful hero. || 12 ||
For those who exert effort, even small things become like food for the great;
they may be employed at will in various tasks, just like clods of earth.
For this reason—because they have become food, that is, objects of consumption, and because they are light and of little strength—for that cause, a clod of earth is a dried lump of clay. || 13 ||
Whatever human effort there may be of a capable person, whether visible or invisible,
that is perceived as "fate" by one who is powerless and lacks self-awareness.
In oneself, that is, in one's own self; by the unintelligent, that is, by the foolish. || 14 ||
That which is the most powerful among beings is established as not being destiny;
it is clear that this [power] is the presiding principle even over those [beings], for they exist in mutual dependence upon it. 15.
The syntactical connection is as follows: even among those powerful beings, that which is the most powerful being is their presiding controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*);

this is the restrainer (*niyantṛ*) of those existing living beings (*satām*), clearly and manifestly (*sphuṭam vyaktam*) in relation to one another (*mithaḥ parasparam*), and not some established fate (*daivam*). "By that effort" (*yatnastena*) refers to that.
In the reading, however, it should be explained by breaking down [the compound] as: "For what reason does effort alone persist, and not destiny? || 15 ||

The unreflective, innate intelligence of the teachers, ministers, elephants, and citizens—that is what constitutes the kingdom of the mendicant; it is that which creates and sustains the stability of the subjects.

"Non-conceptual" means having attained unanimity (*aikamatya*). "Innate cognition" (*svabhāvadhī*) refers to that intellect which is spontaneous; it alone is the agent (*kartṛ*) that effects the state of being a king of mendicants, and the sustainer (*dhātrī*) that maintains the stability of the subjects.

In the view that favors grammatical refinement (*pada-saṃskāra*), [the word *buddhi*] is neuter in its general sense as an internal factor (*antaraṅga*) in relation to the external factor (*bahiraṅga*).

It is not sublated by its connection with the qualificand. Thus, in the Mahābhāṣya, in the context of the supplementary discussion on the Vārttika "The restriction of dharma is by means of the scripture," it is stated: "And by this [scripture], even hunger could be stilled by dog-meat and the like; therefore, a restriction is made by the scripture that 'only five types of five-clawed animals are to be eaten.'"
When a beggar or even a king like Maṅgalēbha achieves something at any time, it is either due to past human effort (puruṣakāra) or else that past effort is the powerful cause therein. (17)

Fearing the over-extension [of the principle] that one person might enjoy the fruit of another's effort, he states an alternative position, beginning with the word "bhikṣuka" (the beggar). In that context, the connection is that either past karma or powerful present effort is the cause. || 17 ||
The present destroys the past, and the past forcibly destroys the present;
in this regard, the person who always acts with composure is the victor.
"Puruṣaspanda" is the effort that causes the person to vibrate; "anudvega" means one who has desisted from agitation; likewise is the state [of being free from agitation]. || 18 ||
Between these two, the superiority of the present day would be evident from direct perception;
for it is possible through efforts to conquer fate, just as a youth can defeat an old man. (19)
He states that very point clearly: "Of the two," etc. (Verse 19).
Just as the harvest acquired over a year is carried away by a cloud, so too is this human effort of the cloud; he who exerts greater effort triumphs.
One might object: "Is it not observed that the opposite occurs when the fruits of agriculture are destroyed by the falling of hailstones and the like?
Anticipating this, he states, "By the cloud," showing that even this is an example that establishes our desired point.
The meaning is that [the fruit] is led away, removed, or destroyed by the cloud.

The meaning is that just as this is the human effort (puruṣārtha) of the person who identifies with the cloud, so it should be understood in other cases as well. This has been stated as a concession; however, in reality, even there, the cause is one's own prior human effort alone, operating through the medium of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa). || 20 ||
Even when wealth acquired through gradual effort is lost, one should not feel distressed;
where my strength was not effective, what cause for lamentation is there? (21)
Or, even if human effort should sometimes prove fruitless, nevertheless, despondency is not appropriate; rather, renewed exertion alone is fitting.
Thus he says with the four verses beginning with "In due order" (krameṇa). 21.
If I suffer for the sake of that which I cannot avoid,
then it is fitting for me— who am not yet dead— to weep every single day.
All these states of the world manifest themselves through the power of place, time, action, and substance; may he who exerts the greatest effort be victorious! 23.

He teaches this as follows: thus, having abandoned that place or time where one's own effort proved fruitless, one must certainly strive again in another place, at another time, by means of another action, or with another substance. The point is that even the asceticism of Viśvāmitra, though obstructed in the eastern and other directions, was seen to achieve success in the northern direction. || 23 ||

Therefore, relying upon human effort, and having brought one's wisdom to purity through the study of authentic scriptures and association with the virtuous, one should cross the ocean of saṃsāra. (24)
These two fruits of human effort—the former and the present—arise like fruit-bearing trees in the forest of humanity; of these two, the latter triumphs. (25)

Those two trees, capable of producing fruit and being of such a nature, became fruit-bearing trees in the forest of men. Here, by the cutting of the root of one, there is withering; for the other, there is sprouting—this is victory. (25)
The ignorant creature who does not destroy his insignificant past karma through auspicious endeavors is not the master of his own happiness and suffering. (26)

Showing the undesirable consequence that would follow if the stated meaning were not accepted, he refutes the doctrine of dependence on a Lord (Īśvara) with the verse beginning "karma" and so forth. The meaning is: if a living being who does not destroy [his own karma] were powerless and not independent—being impelled by a Lord—he would go to heaven or even to hell even without [the influence of] merit and demerit. || 26 ||
Impelled by God, he may go to heaven or even to hell;
he is always dependent on another, a mere beast—of this there is no doubt. (27)
And thus, there would follow the consequence of no liberation; so he says: "He" (sa). || 27 ||
But he who possesses noble wonder and dwells in virtuous conduct emerges from the delusion of the world, like a lion from its cage. (28)
But he says that this fault does not apply to his own position: "As for that which... Herein, the marvel consists in the skill of effort.
"He is impelling me in this way"— in such a useless and false imagination,
whoever remains while abandoning what is seen for what is unseen, that lowest of men should be shunned from afar. (29)

He concludes the refutation of God’s absolute autonomy with the words "some [say]": "But surely, [it is said in scripture: 'It is He indeed who causes him to perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds; He who, dwelling within the self, controls the self from within;
the Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, O Arjuna,' and so forth. Thus, [the opponent argues,] based on such scriptural and traditional (smṛti) passages...

As one acts and as one behaves, so one becomes; the doer of good becomes good, the doer of evil becomes evil. One should sacrifice, offer oblations, and give gifts, for the agent exists because the meaning of the scriptures is otherwise rendered purposeless. This [doctrine] regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) contradicts numerous scriptural texts, aphorisms, traditional law codes, and direct experience, such as: "The Lord does not create agency nor actions for the world."

Dependence on another is what is meant [by dependence]. For the individual soul (*jīva*), being not independent, cannot be an agent; this is because it would contradict the authoritative teaching that "the agent is one who is independent. Nor could this person—who is dependent upon the more powerful Lord—be held guilty of an offense such as the killing of a Brahmin, even if incited by a hundred injunctions or prohibitions. Or how could he himself act toward those things that are inherently unequal?

If the Lord were to cause some of them to turn away [from the path], thereby making them partakers of hell and other such states, the faults of partiality and cruelty would not attach to Him. Or how [could this be reconciled] with the supplementary statement in the Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa: "There is no other seer than He; there is no other hearer than He; there is no other [perceiver] than He"?

Through the passage beginning with "The thinker" (*mantā*) and so forth, the refutation of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the establishment of the absolute sovereignty of the Lord alone becomes consistent. However, if one were to rely on the view of a purely ignorant person and maintain the doctrine of the soul's autonomy based on the engagement in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), then [the aforementioned argument serves] to bring about the weakening of that [doctrine].
Relying upon the discriminative vision directed toward realizing the single selfhood (*aikātmya*) in all beings, one should contemplate the Lord:

"This very Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without interior, and without exterior; this Self is Brahman, the experiencer of all. The Lord does not create the agency or the actions of the world."

Such are the declarations of the Śruti and Smṛti. For example, when a wooden elephant running is seen through the perception of an elephant—as in a dream or a mirror—it is the elephant that runs, not the wood. But when seen through the perception of wood, it is only the wood that runs, not the elephant. From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, there is neither the elephant nor the wood, nor indeed anything at all.
If you say there is no contradiction because [the world] runs on while remaining unmodified, existing as the very nature of the Puruṣa like a mirror or other such objects,

then the refutation of the Lord’s sovereignty in this context is indeed appropriate, since even the words of Vasiṣṭha— who propounded the means to liberation— refer only to the ignorant (ajña). And thus says the commentary of the venerable Pāda:

Taking as its very foundation this mutual superimposition of the Self and the non-Self, which is called ignorance (*avidyā*), all worldly transactions involving means of knowledge and objects of knowledge proceed, as do all scriptures concerned with injunctions,
prohibitions, and liberation. And thus, the independence of the individual soul (*jīva*) established from the perspective of the ignorant—
The intended meaning is that there is also the consequence of [the Lord being subject to] partiality, cruelty, and so forth. || 29 ||
Thousands of legal disputes come and go;
one should conduct oneself among them according to the scriptures, having abandoned both pleasure and pain.

They approach through the fruit of gain and so forth, and they depart through its obstruction. The meaning is that, having abandoned attachment and aversion toward what is pleasant or unpleasant among them, one should conduct oneself exactly according to the scriptures. || 30 ||
For one who does not abandon his own boundaries and remains unbroken according to the scriptures,
all treasures attend him, just as they do in the ocean.
The word "all" refers to all desired things; this is the remainder [of the sense]. || 31 ||

The wise have designated by the term "human effort" (pauruṣa) that single-minded dedication to the exertion required for accomplishing one's own purpose; when constrained by the scriptures, it leads to success.

He states the meaning of the word *pauruṣa* (human effort): "svārtha... and so forth. *Svārtha* means happiness and the cessation of suffering; it refers to being solely intent on the effort directed toward those necessary means that bring about those [ends]. That [effort] is for the sake of accomplishment, that is, for the sake of the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*). || 32 ||

The capacity of action, which is by nature characterized by movement, to accomplish its own purpose is itself sharpened by the intellect through the contact with the virtuous and the study of authentic scriptures. (33)

The meaning is that "vibration" (spanda)— the movement of the body and so forth— is the means for accomplishing one's own goal by means of service consisting of a succession of those [movements], as well as through activities such as hearing [the teachings], association with the virtuous, and true scriptures, which remove doubts and misconceptions regarding the nature of that substratum. || 33 ||
The wise know the ultimate truth to be infinite and equal bliss;
those scriptures and virtuous ones from whom it is eternally obtained should be served. (34)
He states the definition of the virtuous person and the true scripture: "Infinite," etc. Equanimity (*samatā*) is the cessation of the inequality produced by ignorance. || 34 ||
Having come here from the world of the gods, it shall bring benefit to both worlds; that former human effort is indeed what is designated by the term "fate" (daiva). (35)

The meaning is that whatever human effort (pauruṣa) may be beneficial for both worlds, that alone—remaining as a residue after being experienced in the world of the gods—is designated by the term "fate" (daiva) for one who has come from the world of the gods and is established here. || 35 ||
This is appropriate; we do not deny that this exists.
Those who believe in destiny as it is imagined by fools have come to ruin. (36)
The remainder of the sense is: "This is proper; there is no doubt regarding this. We do not censure it, nor do we condemn it.
What, then, is being censured? He says: "by the deluded" (mūḍhaiḥ). The remainder of the sense is: "we censure them [who say] that 'they have gone to destruction'. || 36 ||
Benefit for both worlds arises eternally from one's own self alone, just as yesterday’s misdeed attains splendor through a virtuous deed. (37)
Now, one might ask: "Could not even the prior attainment of the world of the gods have occurred solely through destiny? To this he replies with the word "nityam" (eternally).
He concludes by summarizing what has been established through its result, beginning with the words "hyastanī" (yesterday's) and so forth. || 37 ||
Therefore, one who possesses a task should exert effort this very day;
for that fruit is seen to arise from human effort alone, as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand.
The deluded man, having abandoned direct perception, sinks into the delusion of fate. || 38 ||

Thus, "today" (in some versions it is not found as *adya*) connects with the preceding phrase: "the former splendor is surpassed by that of today. Now, one might ask: let there be victory in the past, but how is the attainment of the goals of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*) achieved therein?
To this he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The connection is as follows: for one who possesses the task (*kāryavat*), its fruit is seen as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand.
Indeed, disregarding that unreal destiny— which is devoid of all causes and effects and is merely constructed by the power of one's own conceptualization—
Now, [consider] your own manly effort and your virtuous intention. || 39 ||

Therefore, O one of virtuous intent, for that reason, one's own conceptualization—that is, the mental activity which is essentially empty—is, by its very nature, fashioned under the influence of that [conceptualization] and is therefore insubstantial (*asanmaya*). The suffix *mayaṭ* is used here in the sense of identity with the object itself. The reason for this is that it is devoid of all causes, effects, and purposes. Such is it.
Disregarding destiny, take recourse in and embrace human effort. || 39 ||
When that fruit, which was conceived by the scriptures and the local customs manifested through the conduct of the virtuous and has been deeply rooted for a very long time,
flashes forth in the heart, the mind undergoes a transformation.
Following that, they say this is the sequence of auspiciousness and human effort. || 40 ||

What is that human effort which is called "fame"? To this he says: "By the scriptures," and so forth. By the scriptures such as the Vedas and the Smṛtis; "sadācara" means the conduct of the virtuous (*satām ācaraṇam*). The suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the *ghan* suffix according to the rule "ghañ-arthe kavidhānam.
By that [conduct], and by those "deśadharmas"—meaning the customs restricted to various regions—which have "expanded" (*vijṛmbhitāḥ*), i.e., become widespread—that mind... [is purified].

When that which is well-established and renowned [in the world] flashes forth in that heart and intellect, and when there is a desire for it, the mind—through the wish to practice the means for its attainment—undergoes *cupana*, which is vibration. The root *cup* signifies slow movement; the suffix *lyuṭ* forms the noun. It "attains" (*eti*) [this state], meaning it reaches it; accordingly, the series of limbs—the senses, hands, feet, and so forth—also undergoes *cupana*.
The meaning is that the learned say that one who conducts oneself through hearing and so forth—this alone is "manly" (pauruṣa). || 40 ||
Having realized that this state of being human is the fruit of personal effort,
one must always remain devoted to self-exertion;
for it is through this alone that such excellence can be brought to its ultimate fulfillment.
By serving true scriptures, virtuous people, and learned scholars. || 41 ||

Having understood that this state of being a human— attained through birth as an eligible person— is the fruit of human effort and is fruitful only upon the accomplishment of the goals of human life (puruṣārtha) and not otherwise, one must always remain devoted to personal exertion. Now, that devotion to exertion is achieved through service to authentic scriptures and virtuous people, and through inquiry following them, which has the knowledge of the Self as its fruit.
The second [verse] || 41 ||
This human effort has been practiced by those who, being skilled in discerning between fate and human exertion,
were constantly convinced that "this alone ever triumphs."
The task at hand is the exertion of serving noble persons. || 42 ||

The meaning is that one who knows reality should always exert effort through the cultivation of hearing and other means, understanding that when human effort is constantly practiced alongside the divine, it surely triumphs; thus, one should discern the relative strength of fate and human exertion. || 42 ||

Having understood that this living soul consists of a succession of births and is afflicted by disease, let it bring peace through the unfailing supreme medicine— namely, innate human effort alone— for the sake of spiritual perfection in this world.
By serving other wise men who are satisfied with refined [learning]. || 43 ||

May this individual soul (jīva), having understood that the innate merit being accomplished here in this present life as an eligible person for the sake of attaining the supreme goal of human existence—as taught by the scriptures—lead to peace; and may it lead to peace that which consists of, or abounds in, the succession of births of the supreme beings who are ever-contented with everything. (The verb is used in the sense of a benediction.)
The meaning is: since the means are so easily accessible, for what reason does one despair? || 43 ||

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Refutation of Fate," in the section on the Conduct of Those Seeking Liberation within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Sages (*Ārṣa*).
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Refutation of Fate," in the *Tātparyaprakāśa* (The Elucidation of the Essential Meaning) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*.
The Seventh Canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having obtained a body free from disease and with diminished physical suffering,
One should thus concentrate upon the Self so that one is not born again. || 1 ||
The preeminence of human effort alone is established here through extensive examples, counter-examples, and logical arguments. (1)

Having already established the primacy of human effort (*puruṣārtha*) by refuting the power of fate (*daiva*), and now wishing to reinforce this through examples and counter-examples, the author introduces the subject of human endeavor for the benefit of the qualified student with logical arguments for the instruction: "Having obtained... [and] "a small amount of additional marriage-portion" (*ādhivedanā*).
In that [state] where one experiences mental suffering, one should apply oneself—that is, strive—for the stabilization of the mind. || 1 ||
He who desires to turn back destiny through human effort shall have all his wishes fulfilled in this world and the next.
To show that effort cannot exist for one who lacks desire, he states the necessity of desire there with the words "By destiny" (daivam).
The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "one becomes one whose desires are completely fulfilled. || 2 ||
Those who, having abandoned exertion, remain dependent on fate, destroy their own dharma, wealth, and pleasure; they are enemies of themselves.

He supports the point already stated by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as well, beginning with the words "Those who..."—those who hate the Self are enemies of their own selves. (3)
The vibration of consciousness, the vibration of the mind, and the vibration of the senses—these are the forms of the human goal; from these, the arising of the fruit occurs.

Desiring to refute destiny (*daiva*) as being contrary to perceptible human effort (*pauruṣa*), he states the perceptually established nature of human effort with the words beginning "the vibration of consciousness" (*saṃvitspanda*).

The vibration of consciousness is the manifestation of the goal of man and its means; by that [manifestation], there arises the desire for those means and effort, which is the vibration of the mind (*manaḥ-spanda*). By that [vibration of the mind]...

The activity of the organs of action for the purpose of moving the limbs is the vibration of the senses (*aindriyaspanda*). By the two particles *eva* and *ca*, the vibration of the body and external instruments prompted by those [senses] is also included. These are the successive manifestations of the human form of the Puruṣa’s purpose. From these, which function uninterruptedly—
The emergence of the fruit is the accomplishment of the desired object; this is the meaning of "well-known. || 4 ||
Just as the mind is according to its perception, so too does it undergo that vibration (as the reading *caittatathā* suggests).
In that very same way the body moves, and in that very same way there is the state of being the enjoyer of the fruit. || 5 ||

He explains the aforementioned point with the words "yathā" (just as). Just as there is a manifestation of the object in the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) prior to its perception, the mind subsequently undergoes a corresponding vibration;
in that very same way, the body moves through the vibration of the organs of action (*karmendriya*). The meaning is that the attainment of the fruit follows the activity. || 5 ||
This is established even among children, wherever and however it may be:
fate is never seen anywhere; therefore, in this world, human effort alone prevails.

In whatever fruit—whether worldly or Vedic—and in whatever manner human effort is employed, mental action alone is primary in meditation and the like, while physical posture and silence are its subordinate members; or in praise and the like, vocal action alone is primary, while one-pointedness and facing [the deity] are its subordinate members; but in travel and the like, physical action alone is primary.

The restraint of speech and mind are its limbs. In some cases, however, there is predominance of two [limbs], and in others, of all three; thus, in each respective instance, that human effort—extending even to children—is well-established and perceptually proven.
But divine [agency] is never seen anywhere, and therefore it is non-existent; this is the meaning. || 6 ||
By means of human effort, Bṛhaspati alone became the preceptor of the gods,
and Śukra attained the status of being the preceptor of the lords of the Daityas through human effort.
He clarifies the stated meaning through examples with the four verses beginning with "puruṣārthena" (by means of the purpose of the Person). || 7 ||
O virtuous one, even those best of men who were afflicted by the suffering of wretchedness and poverty have attained a status equal to that of the Lord of the Gods through human effort alone.
Great beings, who were the refuge of various wonders through the enjoyment of their vast power,
have become guests of hell solely due to the fault of their own human pride.
Nahuṣa and others were the supports for various manifestations of wondrous forms bearing diverse names. (9)
Through the power of their own human effort alone, the various classes of beings have ceased [their suffering] amidst thousands of existences and non-existences and diverse conditions.
Existence, non-existence, absence, and calamities—thousands of these have ceased and passed away for them. 10.
Success is achieved through three means: from the scriptures, from the teacher, and from oneself;
in all matters, it is the human effort that prevails, never fate alone.

Worldly matters such as sacrifices and the like are established through two means: by oneself and through scripture; however, knowledge is established through three means: by oneself, through scripture, and from a teacher—thus there are three types of accomplishment (*trisiddhi*). Now, regarding the printed text reading "But if fate is not accomplished, what loss is there?": for those who maintain that fate is inactive and difficult to grasp, there are these three accomplishments of fate.

If one relies on this view, there follows the undesirable consequence of the abolition of all injunctions; for sacrifices such as those enjoined by the sentence "One should sacrifice with Soma" are produced by an activity (vyāpāra), and since bhāvanās are the cause of a person's engagement (pravṛtti), and engagement consists of physical motion (parispanda). || 11 ||
One should diligently cause the mind, when it has entered into unwholesome states, to descend into wholesome ones alone; this is the summary of the meaning of all the scriptures.
Among those [topics], he shows the essence relevant to the present subject: "In regard to the unwholesome," etc. (12).
"O son, practice with diligence that which is supreme, that which is not trivial, and that which is free from misfortune"—thus stand the teachers. (13)
The "excellent" is that which is supreme; the "non-trivial" is the ultimate truth; it is eternal and free from the lower realms.
Whatever fruit is of such a nature, practice that very thing. 13.
"In whatever measure my effort is directed toward the fruit, in that same measure the fruit comes quickly;
thus, I am the enjoyer of the fruit through human exertion alone, and not through destiny. (14)
"It becomes swift and rapid"—this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Having thus resolved. || 14 ||
Success is seen to arise from human effort; through human effort comes the progress of the wise. Destiny is merely a consolation for those whose intellects are weak in the face of suffering. (15)
This is the practice of gradual progression: for those of tender intellect who weep in suffering, it is merely a consolation, equivalent to wiping away their tears. || 15 ||
In this world, the sequence of human action—such as traveling to other lands and so forth—is constantly seen to bear fruit through means of valid cognition headed by direct perception. (16)
Going to another country is "gama" (going). || 16 ||
The enjoyer is satisfied, not the non-enjoyer; the goer goes, not the non-goer;
the speaker speaks, not the non-speaker; thus, human effort bears fruit for men. (17)
Thus, it is seen to be fruitful; this is the remainder [of the sentence]. || 17 ||
Through human effort, those of sound intellect cross over insurmountable perils without exertion, but not through this futile course.
By this "fate," which is characterized by futility and a state of inactivity— [the reading is *rūpatayā*]— 18.
Whoever exerts effort in whatever manner, that very person alone partakes of the corresponding fruit;
indeed, no fruit is obtained here by anyone who remains silent. 19.
Sharing one [portion], it is certainly a vessel. || 19 ||
Through auspicious human effort, an auspicious fruit is attained;
through inauspicious, an inauspicious one, O Rāma—do as you wish.

The attainment of the fruit from human effort here, occurring either after a long time or quickly according to the influence of place and time— that which is thus attained is traditionally known as destiny (daiva).

If there is great devotion to destiny (daiva), then one should rely on human effort (puruṣārtha) itself under the notion that it is destiny, and not some other baseless imagination; with this intention, he says "from human effort," etc. "Attainment of the fruit" means the perfection of the result. || 21 ||
Fate is not seen with the physical eye, nor does it exist in another world;
what is called "fate" is simply the fruit of one's own action in the heavenly realm.

Now, one might object: "Surely the divine being residing in worlds such as heaven cannot be denied here on earth simply because it is not perceived. To this he says: "No," [meaning] in the world of heaven (svarloka). || 22 ||
A person is born in this world, grows, and then decays;
yet fate is not seen therein, as it is in childhood, youth, and old age. (23)
In that person. || 23 ||
The wise have designated as the term *pauruṣa* (human effort) the state of being solely intent on the exertion required to achieve a goal; by means of this, everything is attained.
He states the distinction between the real and unreal human efforts with the words beginning "artha" (object), etc. || 24 ||
The movement from one place to another, the grasping of objects by the hand, and likewise the functioning of the limbs, are due to human effort and not through destiny. (25)

The reaching of another place by the two feet occurs through human effort; likewise, the activity of the other limbs is seen to be through human effort alone, and not by fate—this is the meaning. || 25 ||

But that which is characterized by a single effort directed toward an action that results in the attainment of what is useless is called "the behavior of a madman," for nothing at all is attained by it. (26)

"Because of the attainment of what is harmful" (*anarthasya prāptiḥ*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with non-co-referential members (*vyadhikaraṇapada*). Alternatively, it is a co-referential compound (*samānādhikaraṇapada*) with the suffix *ktin* used in the sense of the object (*karman*). The ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*) is "nothing auspicious. However, by its very nature as that which possesses the quality of motion (*spandadharmiṇī*), action (*kriyā*) necessarily brings about what is inauspicious while accomplishing its own purpose.
It is raised up by the intellect, sharpened by the company of the virtuous and the study of authentic scriptures. || 27 ||
He states once more what was already said with the intention of further elaboration, beginning with the words "by action" (*kriyayā*).
The reading ending in the instrumental case, *kriyayā*, has been explained previously. However, in some places there is the reading *kriyāyāḥ spandadharmiṇyāḥ*;
in that case, since it is well known that action accomplishes its own purpose, [the reference is] to the cognition which is the fruit thereof.
It is raised up by itself; that is to say, it is lifted up. || 27 ||
The wise know the ultimate reality to be their own infinite, equal bliss;
those scriptures and virtuous teachers from whom that is attained through effort are to be served. (28)

Equanimity (*samatā*) is the cessation of the inequality caused by ignorance; those who know the bliss characterized by that [equanimity], and those from whom that bliss is obtained, are the "good" ones (*savya*), who are to be won over through prostration, inquiry, service, and so forth, as well as through repeated practice. || 28 ||
The excellence of good scriptures and the like increases through the intellect, and the intellect increases through the excellence of good scriptures and the like;
they both grow by mutual practice, like two lotuses over time.
He states what was said with a specific intention, even though it might appear redundant, beginning with the words "sacchāstra" (good scripture).

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the company of the virtuous (*sādhu-saṅga*) is included. Among these, the quality resulting from the practice of associating with the virtuous is the attainment of a character identical to theirs; the quality resulting from the practice of scripture is the knowledge of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the scripture.

*Matih* is the awakening to reality. To the extent that one becomes devoted to serving the teacher and practicing the scriptures, to that same extent one's awakening increases. And to the extent that awakening increases, to that same extent there is an increase in confidence in the teacher and the scriptures, through the increase of their qualities.
Through the increase of pleasure and so forth, one ascends to progressively higher stages; in terms of time, this occurs over a long duration and specifically during the rainy season.
Through qualities such as the study of scriptures and association with the virtuous, practiced sufficiently from childhood, one’s own beneficial purpose is accomplished by human effort. (30)
To state that one must likewise exert effort for a long time for its increase, he says again what has already been said: "From childhood... (30).
The Daityas were conquered through human effort, the activities of the world were established,
and the worlds here were fashioned by Viṣṇu, and not by fate.
O Raghunātha, exert yourself for a long time in this world where human effort is the cause; otherwise,
you shall go by the names of trees and reptiles.
O fortunate one, so that we may behold you without any doubt. || 32 ||
Human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is human exertion; it is the very cause for achieving the goals of man in such a world.
The address "O Raghunātha" is used to illuminate his preeminence within the chosen lineage. "Sarīsṛpa" means a serpent.
Thus it is stated in the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* by Vālmīki, in the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa*, according to the archaic usage.
[2] The Seventh Chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Primacy of Human Effort."

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Establishment of the Primacy of Human Effort," in the section on the Conduct of Those Seeking Liberation within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Eighth Canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
There is no form, nor actions, nor movement, nor prowess.
What is that which is called "fate" (daiva), which has become firmly established like that false knowledge? (1)
The falsity of fate has been described through extensive examples and is further supported by arguments such as its contradiction with the means of subsistence.

Thus, having rejected destiny, even when human effort and autonomy are established, one becomes bewildered due to a lack of confidence— [according to another reading: "established by the unity of autonomy"]— and here, in this very twenty-fifth canto on dispassion (*vairāgya*), his wicked deeds are described.

In this world, another [principle] is called the crest-jewel (cūḍāmaṇi), which is known as destiny (daiva) and time (kāla). By it, this entire succession of beings, as fragile as a garland of frost, has been brought to a state of extreme distress, as if by heat.
"O Sage, for Kṛtānta (Death), who is as if intensely impassioned as he dances, there is constant and supreme desire for his beloved Niyati (Destiny). Thus has it been described at length by himself,
and in numerous Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas [the reading "Purāṇetihāseṣu" is found].

Perceiving Śrī Rāma— who believes that destiny (*daiva*), renowned for its supreme independence, is undeniable— to be one who will not place his trust until a contradiction with the very basis of that destiny’s independence (or, according to another reading, the identity with independence) has been demonstrated, [the Lord] addressed him.
Desiring to demonstrate this, Śrī Vasiṣṭha said, beginning with the words "Not form" (nākṛtiḥ):

"Form" (ākṛti) refers to genus and the pervasive configuration [of a thing]. The distinction among actions, movements, and powers arises through the presentation of mental and physical results, or by way of the relationship between the general, the particular, and its further subdivisions.

The meaning is that because people cannot determine in reality what the nature of that "destiny" (daiva) is for one who lacks these [causes], it is difficult to describe; therefore, it is merely established as being like false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). Even in the reading *mitho'jñānavat*, "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) refers to erroneous cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*), and it is just like that in mutual worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
The meaning is "established. || 1 ||
Those utterances which state that "this has come to pass in such a way as the result of one's own karma" have attained widespread renown under the name of "destiny. (2)

If it is asked, "Upon what basis does delusion rest? the author clarifies this mutual worldly discourse by stating, "one's own karma" (*svakarma*). Those verbal expressions—the linguistic usages such as "this action was performed in this manner according to this sequence" or "it is endowed with such a result"—are, by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), directed toward that [karma].
This is the meaning. || 2 ||
In that very matter, those of deluded intellect have reached the certainty that "fate exists," grasped through their lack of understanding just as one might seize a snake in a rope. (3)
Therein, among those [beings], it is "taken" (ātta), meaning grasped, through delusion that is difficult to comprehend. || 3 ||
Just as yesterday’s misconduct attains beauty through good conduct today, so too does today’s [conduct] depend on that of the past; therefore, one should strive with effort to perform virtuous deeds.
And thus, he says "hyastanī" (yesterday's) to show that what I have stated is indeed proven. || 4 ||
That fool of wicked mind for whom destiny is established by fallacious inference— by him it must be accepted that there is no burning from fire, even though the burning occurs due to destiny.
Desiring to state the contradiction with the authoritative means of knowledge that must be relied upon, he first states the contradiction with one's own perceptible activity:
"If fate alone is the agent here in this world, what is the use of human effort?"
He alone shall perform the bathing, giving of gifts, sitting, and evacuation for the sake of the gods.
The utterances refer to the recitations of the mantras and so forth belonging to the limbs of giving and the other [perfections]. || 6 ||
Or what is the use of the instruction of the scriptures? This person is indeed mute; he is merely moved by destiny—what can be taught here to whom?

And thus, there would be a contradiction with the authority of the Vedas and other scriptures; so he says: "What [is the fault]?"—a mute person is one who is not independent even in the activity of speech. || 7 ||
Moreover, no lack of movement is observed here in the world except in the case of a corpse;
since the attainment of results follows from movement, destiny is therefore useless.
He states that there is also a contradiction with what is perceived: "And not," [verse 8].
Nor is any cooperation between the formless destiny and the embodied person ever observed; therefore, destiny is useless.

One might object: "Is it not the case that in the inference—'the movement of the body and so forth has a composite agent other than [the physical body] as its agent, because it is an action, like the carrying of a palanquin'—since a corporeal other agent is sublated by perception, an immaterial auxiliary agent will be established; and that very thing is what we call 'fate' (daiva)? Anticipating this, he says: "And not... (na ca).

And thus, the meaning is that "having a creator who is a composite of material things" and "having a creator who is a composite of perceptible things" are the limiting conditions (*upādhi*). Consequently, since the absence of the limiting condition exists in the subject (*pakṣa*), the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) is established;
this he states with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). || 9 ||
When the various limbs come together mutually, each one acts as an agent for the other;
thus, when the hands and other members are struck down, it is not at all the work of destiny.

In some cases, such as during writing or shaving, when two [instruments] come together by encountering each other's parts—such as a pen and a razor—it is observed that between the two, there is the rejection of the second and the agency of each one; this is to be supplied [to the context]. In other cases, however, [agency] is observed in a book or in a man; this is the meaning of the phrase "is observed."

It is further recited: by this, the hypothesis of fate as an instrument—like that of the hands, feet, mind, intellect, and so forth—is also refuted; thus he says, "of the hands, etc. In that regard, since the hand and other such organs, when present, establish the causal efficacy [of action] through them and thus render fate superfluous (*anyathāsiddhi*), it is impossible for them to function as instruments [if they were merely fate]; therefore, it is stated "when [the hand] has been struck or destroyed by wind-disease (*bātaroga*) and the like."
The particle *ha* is used in the sense of *kila*.

Moreover, this destiny is not experienced here as one experiences mental cognition; even down to the cowherds, it is not perceived by those of cultivated wisdom. Therefore, destiny is always non-existent.
If cognition is distinct from the object, then that [cognition] itself would be the other; if they are identical, how can there be any difference between them?
If you claim that conceptual construction is the means of valid cognition, why is human agency not likewise postulated? (12)
Furthermore, regarding the establishment of fate (*daiva*), the proof must be either the very notion of causal factors such as the agent, or a notion of something distinct from them.

In the second case, one would be postulating a meaningless entity, namely that "fate" is something entirely different and useless for the action. In the first case, it would mean that the well-known agent and so forth are simply being designated by the word "fate. To this he says: "distinct," etc. But [an objection may be raised]: [The text continues: "But..."

If it is argued that among those who study while desiring the same fruit, such as equal proficiency, only some are endowed with that fruit and not all, one must necessarily postulate a cause for this disparity, since the inference of a cause is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for explaining a discrepancy in effects—then [the author] says: "In the case of a postulation," and so on. Even there...

The meaning is that only a previous human effort of a similar kind is postulated, not an unestablished "fate" (daiva). (12) There is no contact between that [fate] and one who possesses a body, just as there is none with the formless sky;
yet a corporeal object is seen to be joined [to another]. Therefore, fate does not exist. (13)
He states that the postulation of such [an agent] is also not logical because it would be incapable of cooperating with other causal factors—beginning with "no.
"By that" means by another causal factor. "Contact" (saṅga) means conjunction. "Of one possessing a body" refers to ourselves and others. The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis.
Since only that which possesses form is seen to be attached—that is, mutually conjoined—therefore [the agent cannot be formless]. || 13 ||
Even if there were anything else in the three worlds superior to the destruction of beings,
the hosts of beings would lie [subdued], for destiny will accomplish everything.
"They lie down" (śerate) means "they should lie down" (śayīran). The present indicative (laṭ) is used here by way of transposition (vyatyaya) in the sense of the optative (liṅ). || 14 ||
"Driven by fate, I do what has come to pass;
this is merely a word of consolation, for in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as fate. (15)
"Abhiyuktaḥ" means impelled; "sthitam" means established as accomplished by divine will. || 15 ||
Fate is imagined by the foolish, and those devoted to it have gone to ruin;
the wise, however, through human effort, have attained the highest state.
Tell me, what indeed is the use of those who are brave, those who are valiant, those who are wise, and those who are learned in this world? One must wait for destiny. (17)
"What?"—this interrogative particle (*kāku*) expresses a censure under the guise of a question. || 17 ||
If he whose extremely long life has been determined by those who know the times should live even with his head severed, then that indeed is the supreme destiny.
An objection is raised: "But do not astrologers declare that the planets themselves are destiny?

Anticipating this, the author states—beginning with the words "by those who know time"—that their purpose is merely to indicate human effort and its results through the distinction between bodily marks, omens, and conduct, rather than to be the actual cause. || 18 ||
O Raghava, if one who has not been taught at all is recognized as a scholar by those who know the proper time, then that is surely the supreme power of destiny.
The supreme and most excellent cause shall succeed; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 19 ||
O Rāma, by the sage Viśvāmitra, having cast fate far aside,
brahminhood was attained through human effort alone and not otherwise.
O Rāma, by us and other men who have attained the state of sages,
this long-lasting ability to travel through the sky has been acquired solely through human effort.
To strengthen his confidence, he cites the fruit of human effort among those who preceded him: "By Viśvāmitra," and so forth.
Having destroyed the hosts of gods within the belly of the three worlds,
the lords of the Dānavas established their empire through human effort alone.
As for that which is well-known as the divinity of Indra and others, he says "having destroyed" (utsādya) to show that even that is known to have been defeated by human effort. || 22 ||
By their very manly effort, the lords of the gods forcibly crushed and shattered the expansive world of the Dānavas.

He states that even his victory was due solely to human effort and not of its own accord, with the words "ālūna": "In such a manner as the vast (*ābhogi*) and extensive world, and the enemy host, were *ālūna*—meaning cut down, shattered, and worn away—in that act of battle and so forth, they seized [the victory] and brought it back. And thus, even of fate...
The sense is that fate is nothing other than human effort itself. || 23 ||
O Rāma, it is by human effort and skill that this beautiful water is held for a long time within a casket; fate is not the cause in that matter. (24)
By this well-known human artifice, consisting of anointing with lac, beeswax, and so forth;
in a *karaṇḍaka*, that is, a bamboo casket. || 24 ||
O Rāma, efficacy is seen in the grounds of supporting, seizing, exertion, agitation, and fatigue, but not in destiny, just as it is not seen in a medicine [when the patient's karma is exhausted]. 25.

Supporting refers to the nourishment of one's own kin; seizing refers to taking by force from another kingdom and so forth; agitation refers to the suppression of others through anger; and distractions refer to the indulgences of pleasure. Furthermore, regarding other spheres of exertion—human endeavors that are difficult to accomplish—the efficacy of destiny is not observed therein. [This includes] the gathering of medicinal herbs.
The mention of gems, mantras, and so forth is merely illustrative of that very [power]. || 25 ||
91) Devoid of all causes and effects, it is fashioned by the power of one's own conceptual construction.
Therefore, O noble-minded one, disregarding fate which is composed of unreality, take refuge in the highest human effort.

O noble-minded one, disregard fate—which is like something fabricated from your own innate and personal conceptualization and delusion, consisting of nothingness and being mostly trivial—and instead take refuge in human effort. 26.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Refutation of Fate," in the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* tradition.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Refutation of Destiny," in the section on the Conduct of the Seeker of Liberation within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Ninth Canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, that which has reached the state of stainless stability—tell me, O Brahmā, what is called "divinity" (daiva) in this world? || 1 ||
In order to establish the denial of destiny (daiva), it is asserted that [the world] consists of mind alone;
yet this does not mean that action, along with its fruit, or the mind itself, possesses the nature of pure consciousness (cidātmatā). || 1 ||
In order to establish the independence of human effort (*puruṣa-svātantrya*), in some instances fate (*daiva*)—being non-existent—is denied by being asserted as "it does not exist at all.

In other instances, however, it is stated that fate is merely the result of past exertion, or that human effort itself is fate. Regarding these, in the first alternative, [the opponent argues] that if fate were non-existent, the very firm worldly and Vedic consensus would become baseless; yet this is untenable when [fate] is weak.
[The reading is *durbale tatsāpekṣaḥ*. Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the statement that human effort is powerful when dependent on that [fate],

and in the second case, there is the inconsistency of the proposition that "fate is non-existent," because even contemporary activities arise in accordance with prior karma as its fruit, and thus lack any opposition to it.

With the hidden intention of raising an objection regarding the contradiction in the statement that [the Self] is conquered by those [powers], and of challenging the impairment of the person's autonomy even while they are dependent upon them, Śrī Rāma, desiring to know in which alternative (kalpa) the Guru’s conviction lay, said: "O Blessed One," [referring to] that which has attained extreme renown and established status.
The meaning is: is that destiny which has been attained non-existent, or is it indeed existent? || 1 ||
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
O Raghava, human effort is the agent of all actions and nothing else;
it is the enjoyer of the fruit everywhere, and destiny is not the cause therein.

Thus questioned, the venerable Vasiṣṭha—having understood Rāma’s intention and desiring to make him realize the non-dual reality of the Self through the negation of the world by means of the very logic used to negate the gods—held a hidden purpose: that there is, in effect, no difference between the two alternatives. Adopting the first alternative alone, he spoke as follows: "The human [effort]," and so on.

In reality, because the Self is indifferent, it possesses neither agency nor enjoyership; therefore, even when the action is performed by the person (the body), the designation of that agency is attributed to the Self. || 2 ||
Fate does nothing, it does not enjoy, nor does it exist;
it is neither seen nor heeded—it is merely such a mental construction.
It is not respected by those possessed of discernment; the meaning is that it is a delusion firmly established through conceptual construction among worldly people. || 3 ||
In this world, for one who possesses the fruit resulting from human effort,
the attainment of auspicious or inauspicious objects is designated by the term "destiny" (daiva).
He refutes the impossibility of [fate] being without a basis: "of that which is established.

The meaning is this: that very auspicious or inauspicious result which is obtained by a wife, a rival wife, or others, from a man who possesses a fruit—that is, one who necessarily has a fruit—such as a husband, a body, and so forth, is what is conventionally designated as "fate" (daiva) by taking that very thing as its basis. || 4 ||
The constant acquisition of desired or undesired objects brought about by human effort—whether that acquisition be desirable or undesirable—is designated by the term "fate" (daiva). || 5 ||

Sometimes the attainment of the undesirable follows after the desired, and sometimes the attainment of the desired follows after the undesirable; it is for this reason that such a statement is made. The word "by people" (lokaḥ) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 5 ||
That future goal which arises from human effort and is accomplished solely through human exertion is what is designated by the term "destiny" (daiva) in this world. (6)
He states the view of the Lokāyatikas with the word "bhāvi" (it will be). Here, "human purpose" refers to experience. || 6 ||
Indeed, O Raghava, for some person in this world, destiny—which is like the nature of space—both acts and does not act. (7)

He states the established conclusion (siddhānta) with the words "nanu" and so forth: To someone, by virtue of a deluded vision, a certain thing—namely destiny (daiva)—appears as something like space, resembling a void or the blueness of the sky; it does not appear so to one who possesses discernment. || 7 ||
When the human effort has been accomplished, that expression regarding the arising of auspicious or inauspicious results—
namely, "this is situated thus"— is called destiny (daiva).
This fruit exists in this very way, having previously existed in the form of its seed. (8)
"In this way my thought arose; indeed, in this way my conviction was formed"—such a statement regarding the attainment of the fruits of action is called destiny (daiva). || 9 ||
That which expresses the attainment of desired or undesired results as "this is [it]," being a mere word of consolation, is called "fate" (daiva). || 10 ||
When the attainment of desired or undesired fruits occurs, the notion that "this prior karma was of such and such a kind" is included within human effort alone among all such conceptualizations. (10)
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, that which was accumulated through previous karma is called destiny (daiva).
How was that which is called "fate" refuted by you? (11)

Not understanding the intention expressed by the non-difference of the two alternatives, and perceiving a contradiction between beginning with the first alternative and concluding with the second, Śrī Rāma, revealing his own underlying thought, said: "O Blessed One," and so forth. That which was previously called *karma* is indeed repeatedly referred to as *daiva*.
"If that which has been stated truly exists, then how is it that you have brushed it aside and denied it?
What is the intention behind such a denial? This is the meaning. || 11 || Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"Excellent, O Rāghava! You understand; listen, for I shall tell you everything by which your intellect will become firm in the conviction that there is no destiny. (12)

Revealing his own intention, the venerable Vasiṣṭha said, "Excellent! The sense is: you understand the contradiction and the faults in both alternatives; thus, your conviction is firm and unassailed by doubts regarding those faults. 12.
That mental impression which formerly existed indeed in great abundance,
that very same thing has undergone transformation for human beings into the form of karma. (13)

The meaning is that [it exists] as action, in the form of bodily and vocal action; for the intention is that according to the Vedic revelation and likewise through experience, "whatever one meditates upon with the mind, that one speaks with speech, and that one performs with action. (13)
O Rāma, whatever is a living being's latent impression (*vāsanā*), that it becomes its doer (*kartṛ*) and its deed (*karman*) in an instant;
for it to have one deed and another nature is simply not possible. (14)
He establishes that very point by demonstrating positive and negative concomitance: "The living being... (verse 14).
One who intends to go to a village reaches the village, and one who desires a city reaches the city;
whoever has whatever latent impression (vāsanā), that person always strives for that very thing.
He states that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established in the general case through the observation of concomitance in specific instances: "One going to a village" (*grāmaga*).
One going to a village is one whose latent impression (*vāsanā*) has arisen from the sphere of activity consisting in going to a village. (15)
Whatever action was performed firmly in the past out of intense spiritual urgency (saṃvega), that alone is here referred to by the synonymous term "fate" (daiva). || 16 ||
That which is performed with intense urgency, due to an excellence of longing for the fruit, and through the force of diligent application toward the action. || 16 ||

Thus, actions reside in action; one's own latent impressions (vāsanā) are matured by action. Latent impression is nothing other than the mind, for the mind is traditionally held to be the person (puruṣa). || 17 ||

Those who abide in actions are "karmasthas," meaning the agents; for them, all actions occur precisely in the manner described above. And action is nothing other than one's own matured and accumulated latent impression (*vāsanā*). Furthermore, this *vāsanā* is not distinct from its cause, the mind, according to the principle stated in the Śruti: "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name" (*vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyam*). Even though...

Although action is also observed in speech and body, nevertheless, with regard to those two as well, this was stated with the intention of explaining—as will be said later—that they are merely mental impressions (*vāsanā*) when subjected to inquiry. Furthermore, the mind is the Person (*puruṣa*), the complete Self itself, and is not distinct from it; for the Śruti says, "He made that mind [thinking], 'May I have a self,'" and so forth. Thus, regarding the mind...
The meaning is that it is because [the world] is a transformation of the Puruṣa. || 17 ||
That which is called fate is those very actions; O virtuous one, action is indeed the mind.
Since the person is the mind, the certainty is that there is no such thing as fate.

And since, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the person (puruṣa) consists solely of changeless consciousness, it follows that when the mind is non-existent, action is non-existent, and consequently, destiny—which is of the nature of that action—is non-existent. He states this in the verse beginning with "yat": || 18 ||
Whatever beneficial thing this very mind-born being strives for, that very thing he obtains by himself indeed through destiny. 19.
According to the Śruti, "Breathing, it becomes what is called breath; speaking, speech; seeing, the eye; hearing, the ear;

thinking, the mind"—since the Self alone exists in the form of the mind and so forth through superimposition, it also exists in the form of action and its results. If it is therefore argued that the Self itself is "destiny" (daiva), let it be so; however, [that does not resolve the issue].
With the intention that this constitutes a violation of human autonomy, he says: "This very [Self]..."—that is, having attained the state of the mind and so forth. || 19 ||
"O Rāma, the wise have declared that *manas*, *citta*, *vāsanā*, *karman*, *daiva*, and *niścaya* are synonyms for *durniścaya* (evil resolve). (20)
If the mind (*manas*) were absolutely non-existent, how could worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) be established by it, since such is not seen in the case of the son of a barren woman and the like?
Anticipating this objection, [the text] demonstrates its indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*) from the perspective of what is illogical (*ayauktika*), stating:
"This very heart, this mind, this perception (*saṃjñāna*), this cognition (*ājñāna*), this discernment (*vijñāna*), this wisdom (*prajñāna*)."
In accordance with such scriptural passages as these, he states that the various designations such as "divine" and so forth belong to the mind alone—namely, "the mind.

This refers to the person who has assumed the nature of that mind, which is difficult to ascertain—that is, which cannot be determined in its true essence through distinctions such as existence or non-existence, consciousness or insentience, difference or non-difference—and which is therefore illusory. || 20 ||
O Rāma, for a person of such a name who exerts himself constantly with firm resolve, he obtains the fruit accordingly and in abundance.
And thus, he states that human autonomy is established: "Having such names. This means one whose names are of the kinds previously described. || 21 ||
Thus, O scion of Raghu, everything is obtained here through human effort and by no other means; therefore, may that human effort be a source of auspiciousness for you. (22)
Śrī Rāma said:
O Sage, just as the web of past latent impressions compels me, so do I remain; being wretched, what can I do? (23)

Even so, Rāma raises a doubt—that for one who remains under the sway of past latent impressions (*vāsanā*), independence is not established at present—by saying "the past" (*prāktanam*). "Miserable" (*kṛpaṇaḥ*) means wretched; that is to say, one who is dependent on others. || 23 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For this very reason, O Rāma, you shall attain eternal welfare through human effort alone, brought forth by your own exertion, and not otherwise.

Granted that there may be a lack of independence regarding the fruit at present, there certainly is independence regarding the effort conducive to the subsequent fruit; for even in a birth governed by that [effort], the prior latent impression— which is inferred from the birth of one endowed with the knowledge of reality and its resulting true exertion— acts solely as an obstruction to its own contrary fruit.
