Intending to show that if there were no independence in the activity of those [beings], it would follow that the scriptures concerning karma and the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) would be rendered useless, the venerable Vasiṣṭha said: "For this very reason," and so forth.
"For this very reason" means precisely because of the conformity with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that cause birth for those who are qualified [for action].

The meaning is that [this is known] through inference based on the specific excellence of birth, discrimination, and attainment, which correspond to one's latent impressions (*vāsanā*). "You attain" (*prāpnoṣi*) means "you will attain"; this is an expression in the present tense used because of its proximity to the present time. || 24 ||
O Rāma, there exists for you a twofold accumulation of latent impressions (vāsanā)—both auspicious and inauspicious—from the past; or perhaps only one of the two.
In order to support the very point already stated, he asks by dividing *vāsanā* [into two types]: "It is twofold" (verse 25).
If you are led there today by a pure flood of latent impressions, then,
through that very auspicious sequence, you shall attain the eternal state.
Regarding that, he first says with reference to the first [case]: "by the flood of latent impressions" (vāsanaugheṇa) || 26 ||
Moreover, if an impure disposition binds you to a crisis,
then that former habit must be conquered by you with effort and force.
Regarding the second point as well, he says: "Now" (*atha*). The awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) does not occur independently;

rather, it occurs in accordance with their awakener (*udbodhaka*). If, by chance, through association with the wicked or similar causes, a single impure latent impression should arise, even that [is overcome] by the company of the virtuous and the study of sacred scriptures, which are its opposites.
The meaning is that, having brought forth or produced a contrary latent impression (vāsanā), it should be instantly set aside. || 27 ||

You are the wise one, consisting of pure consciousness; you are not the body, which is inert by nature. Since you are perceived by another consciousness, how indeed could that state of being an object of perception belong to you? (28)

Now, one might object: "Is it not heard in scripture that there is another, the conscious Self (prājñātman), who is the impeller of the mind—'He who dwells in the mind and is within the mind, whom the mind does not know'? Since the arising of mental impressions (vāsanā) is dependent upon Him, how can I possess the independence to give rise to virtuous impressions? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The conscious [Self]..."

That which is heard of as the *prājña*—consisting of pure consciousness (*cetana-mātra*) and having the nature of pure awareness (*cin-mātra-svabhāva*)—that alone are you; you are not the insentient self, nor the subtle or gross body by which you might be thought to be other [than that]. This is because of such scriptural texts as, "There is no seer other than this," and "That thou art. Therefore, for you whose essential nature is thus pure awareness, [there can be no need] for another mind or conscious agent.

Where could there be the state of being an object of consciousness (*cetyatva*) or the state of being manifest (*bhāsyatva*)? If the Wise One (*prājña*) were other than you, then—since consciousness cannot be manifested without another consciousness—he would not be omniscient, as he would not perceive you; therefore, the identity established through mutual exchange (*vyatihāra*) is that you alone are He. This is the intended meaning. (Regarding the variant reading: *anyena*)... [variant reading]... [end of fragment].

"If you are perceived by another, where indeed does your nature as consciousness exist? This means that if you are perceived—that is, manifested—by something else, then where is your status as consciousness (cetastva) found? For it would be unavoidable that what is manifested by consciousness would itself become insentient (jaḍa). || 28 ||
If another makes you conscious, who else makes that other conscious? Who would make this one conscious? Therefore, an infinite regress is not real. (29)
If consciousness were knowable by another consciousness within it, then that too would be knowable by yet another, leading to an infinite regress; thus he says: "by another.

Who could make this conscious subject known? If there were yet another for that one as well, there would be an infinite regress, and such a regress is not real, as it cannot establish the reality of the thing.
Therefore, the sense is that your sovereignty in exerting effort to awaken the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the Real is unimpeded. || 29 ||
The river of latent impressions, flowing along both auspicious and inauspicious paths, should be directed onto the auspicious path through human effort. (30)
He states the fruit of establishing the independence of the person (puruṣasvātantrya) with the words: "By the auspicious and the inauspicious," [verse 30].
O best among the strong, by means of human effort and power, draw your own mind away from what is unwholesome and establish it only in what is wholesome. (31)

The mind of a living being, having moved away from the unwholesome, goes toward the wholesome, and from that [wholesome state] it moves again to the other; therefore, one should restrain it by force, as if it were a child. (32)

The river of the mind flows in two directions—toward merit and toward evil—and when one stream is obstructed, it flows doubly in the other; following this teaching from the *Yogaśāstra*, he says: "From the inauspicious... [The mind] is moved, that is, diverted. From that auspicious state, even the other—the inauspicious—is moved. The ellipsis is: "one should move [the mind] away from the inauspicious."
One should quickly pacify with equanimity— not abruptly, but gradually—
and protect the child of the mind through human effort alone.

Thus, according to the sequence described, one should quickly— that is, very swiftly— bring the child-like mind to a state of faultlessness by means of consoling it in its natural equanimity through the abandonment of imbalances such as passion; then, one should gradually protect it within the nature of the Self by means of human effort characterized by restraint, and not otherwise.

One should restrain [the mind] immediately and by force, lest there be a lapse in concentration due to agitation. Thus says the Lord: "One should gradually withdraw by means of the intellect held with fortitude," and so forth. || 33 ||
The flood of latent impressions (vāsanā), whether auspicious or inauspicious, was previously made dense by you through practice; today, make the auspicious one dense.
Whether you have accumulated merit or demerit, let it be so; nevertheless, today accumulate only merit.
The sense is that this is necessary: for in the first case, it is for the sake of the swiftness of the fruit, while in the second, it is for the sake of dispelling obstacles. || 34 ||
O crusher of enemies, know that when, by the power of prior practice, those [thoughts] of yours give rise to latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then the practice has borne fruit. (35)

Nor should one suspect that the practice of mental impressions (*vāsanā*) is fruitless, because the production of results from the practice of prior impressions is directly perceived; thus he says: "Previously," etc. "Arising" (*udayam*) means emergence or the process of becoming solidified. || 35 ||
O sinless one, even now your latent impressions (vāsanā) are becoming dense due to the power of habit; therefore, apply yourself to virtuous practice.
"Even now" means: the sense is that it is exactly like that. || 36 ||
If your latent impression (*vāsanā*) did not reach the state of wealth in the past due to a lack of practice, it will certainly increase now; therefore, my dear, be happy even at this moment.

To one who doubts even when the density of past latent impressions (*vāsanā*) has been thinned, he says: "Previously," and so forth. The sense is that since one should accordingly engage in worldly affairs with ease, it is not appropriate for you to feel despondency due to the apprehension of misfortune caused by the increase of evil tendencies (*durvāsanā*). || 37 ||
Even when there is doubt, cultivate only that which is exceedingly auspicious;
for in this increase of latent impressions, no fault whatsoever arises from what is auspicious.
If so, why do you urge me toward the cultivation of auspicious latent impressions (*vāsanā*)? To this he replies:

"Even when it is doubtful. *Samāhara* means "accumulate" or "build up. There is no fault whatsoever in the increase of these auspicious impressions through the practice of virtuous conduct; for even when the commencement of the fruits of good or evil is uncertain, [the effort toward the good remains blameless].
The meaning is that it follows the maxim: "One should perform what is auspicious; for if it were not so, what would happen? If it were so, the nihilist would be destroyed. || 38 ||
"Whatever one practices in this world, one becomes absorbed in that very thing"—this has been observed among the wise, even down to children, and is free from doubt. (39)

In reality, however, there is no possibility of doubt; for it is established elsewhere as well that practice is the cause of strengthening that which is being practiced. Thus he says: "Whatever [is practiced]... and so forth.
Therefore, endowed with auspicious latent impressions, take recourse here to supreme human effort and, having conquered the five senses, strive for your own welfare.
As long as your mind is unrefined and you have not realized that supreme state, practice that which has been determined by the authority of the Guru and the scriptures. (41)
In that case, for how long should pure mental impressions (*śubhavāsanā*) be practiced? To this he says: "Until [the mind] is fully developed" (*avyutpanna*).
This means until the attainment of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) include reasoning, personal experience, and so forth. || 41 ||
Therefore, since your afflictions have been ripened and you have surely realized the true nature of reality,
you, being free from all suffering, must certainly abandon even this stream of pure latent impressions.

By one whose impurities of the latent tendencies of passion and the like have been loosened—like the portions of dirt clinging to cloth and the like by the process of boiling with alkaline salt—and who has subsequently realized the reality of the Self; for thus says the Smṛti: "When the impurity has been ripened by actions, then knowledge arises. For this very reason, he is free from all mental anguish.
"By the full [moon] which is free from the suffering of waning," so it means. || 42 ||
Following that which is exceedingly beautiful and practiced by the noble ones, with a mind perceiving it as a delightful state,
attain the state that is forever free from sorrow.
Thereafter, having cast even that aside, remain well.
Summarizing the very point already stated, he indicates the auspicious conduct that should be practiced with the words "yad" (that which):

"By means of an intellect endowed with those delightful states—that is, auspicious latent impressions (*śubhavāsanā*)—attain the goal, the ultimate reality; realize it directly. Furthermore, having even relinquished the pursuit of those auspicious latent impressions, abide in the form of the Sage (*sādhu*)."
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Examination of Karma," in the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "An Inquiry into Karma," in the Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Tenth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The reality of Brahman as it truly exists is called the fixed nature of existence.
That is the teacher’s quality as a teacher; that is the disciple’s quality as one to be trained. || 1 ||
The manifestation of his own nature here for the sake of liberating all beings is declared to be "his own teaching"; such is the sequence of the descent of knowledge. (1)
Granted that what is called "fate" (daiva) is indeed nothing but past human effort (pauruṣa), and thus it can be overcome by present virtuous conduct;

yet "necessity" (niyati) is truly invincible. For that which is described in the section on dispassion as the beloved of Kṛtānta—that necessity characterized by the inevitability of future events—[is indeed difficult to overcome].
The learned say that destiny, which is synonymous with inevitability, is irremediable:

"If there were a remedy for things that must inevitably happen, then Nala, Rāma, and Yudhiṣṭhira would not have been afflicted by sufferings. And thus, even though the person is subject to it, [there is no fault].
Desiring to dispel the doubt that [the world] might be independent, Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "As it truly is.

The reality of Brahman (brahmatattva) exists as it truly is—as the self-luminous nature of being, consciousness, and bliss—abiding everywhere with equanimity and in conformity with all things; the very existence (satta) of all objects is related to that [Brahman].

*Niyati* (destiny), known as *bhavitavyatā* (the state of being destined to be), is that which is designated by its connection with the future time. And *sattā* (existence) is the reality of Brahman as it truly is in all places; for that very reality exists in the form of the regulator and the regulated within both cause and effect. When the cause exists, [the effect] necessarily...

The necessity that there must be an effect when there is an effect, and that there must necessarily be a cause when there is an effect, is *niyati* (destiny) or *niyama* (law). Furthermore, with respect to the guide (*vinetṛ*) or controller—such as the cause—the state of being a guide is the quality of regulating the effect and so forth. With respect to the guided (*vineya*) or regulated—such as the effect—the state of being guided is the quality of being regulated. This refers to the causality consisting in existence at a time strictly prior [to the effect].

The meaning is that "the state of being an effect whose existence is necessarily posterior" consists merely of existence as qualified by specific place and time; the intention is that the previously mentioned *niyati* (fate/limitation) is also the power of Time (*kāla-śakti*), which is the very existence of Brahman, the cause of all. || 1 ||
Therefore, for the sake of your ultimate welfare, rely upon that which is harsh yet eternally your kinsman;
fix your mind one-pointedly upon it and listen to these words of mine. (2)

Therefore, since it is of the nature of the existence of Brahman which is favorable to all, destiny (niyati) is indeed favorable even when human effort (pauruṣa) is successful, and not adverse; thus, the statement to be spoken—which teaches the means for achieving one-pointedness—is first uttered: "Human effort," and so forth. (2)
Quickly restraining the senses— which fall into intermediate objects and mount upon the chariot of one's desires— bring them to a state of equanimity through human effort.

The senses, having mounted upon the mental desire— the longing for sense objects— are prone to causing one to fall midway, that is, into the pleasures of this world or heaven prior to liberation (the reading *nipatana* is preferred). Therefore, by means of human effort, one should restrain the mind through self-control so that it does not mount upon such desires, and instead abide in equanimity.
The meaning is "not so. || 3 ||

For the sake of attaining success in this world and the next, I shall proclaim this compendium, fashioned from the very essence [of knowledge], which bestows the fruits of human endeavor and consists of the means to liberation.

He states what the subsequent task is with the words beginning "here" (*iha*), etc. "Here" means liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*); "there" means liberation after death (*videhamukti*). Alternatively, it means for the sake of the attainment of knowledge by those qualified [for it] in this world of humans (*manuṣyaloka*) and in those worlds such as heaven (*svarga*) and so forth. It consists of the means to liberation—that is, it abounds in instructions on the methods for achieving liberation.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "Accept that Saṃhitā which I shall speak. || 4 ||
Having abandoned within themselves the latent tendencies of worldly existence so as never to grasp it again,
they have attained perfect tranquility and contentment through their noble intellect.
Even for one who has become slightly dispassionate upon hearing that [teaching], there is no qualification; this is indicated by the fact that [the word] "again" (*punar*) is not used [in the verse].
Tranquility (*śama*) and contentment (*saṃtoṣa*) are, like peace (*śānti*), states of happiness characterized by the absence of craving.
Having made the mind— which has been drawn away by the investigation of the meanings of preceding and succeeding sentences— equipoised within the Self through continuous contemplation.

The scriptural passages concerning the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) are the preceding statements; the scriptural passages devoted to meditative worship (*upāsanā*) are the subsequent statements.

The investigation of their meaning constitutes the means for attaining knowledge. The analysis of the meaning of these preceding and subsequent statements, combined with that which is not contradicted by their subject matter—this is the grammatical analysis (*vigraha*). It is that which, within the Self, is accompanied by continuous reflection and is of a single, uniform flavor (*samarasa*).
That is to say, it involves the attainment of the identity between one's own experience and the method taught by the Guru and the scriptures.
(6) O Rāma, listen to this means of liberation which I shall describe; it brings about the destruction of pleasure and pain and is the sole cause of great bliss. (7)
Having heard this discourse on liberation together with all those who possess discernment,
you shall go to the supreme state free from suffering, where no destruction exists.
This statement was made by all the discerning ones in order to prevent even the entrance of the undiscerning into the hall of sacred hearing. || 8 ||
This was spoken in a former age by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord:
it brings about the destruction of all suffering and is the supreme consolation for the intellect.

Having thus introduced the study (*śravaṇa*) along with its constituent parts, the author—desiring to explain the manner of its introduction for the sake of establishing the scripture (*śāstra*) and other elements that are to be heard (or, according to another reading, "for the sake of establishing the scripture and so forth")—says: "This," etc. "In a former aeon" (*purākalpe*) means at the beginning of the aeon (*kalpādau*). || 9 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, by what cause was this spoken formerly by the Self-born One?
And how was it obtained by you? Tell me this, O Lord. (10)
Desiring to know Vasiṣṭha’s intention, Śrī Rāma said: "By what... (10).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: There exists the sky of consciousness, whose nature is infinite manifestation, all-pervading, the refuge of all, imperishable in essence, and the lamp within all living beings. 11.

Therein, first, in order to speak of the birth of Parameṣṭhin, he states its fundamental cause: "He exists" (asti). The Self exists as the substratum of infinite illusory manifestations (*māyika-vilāsa*). It is described as "all-pervading," "within all," "the refuge of all," and "the support of all" in order to indicate His transcendence over *māyā* and its effects.

The phrase "a lamp for all beings" is intended to convey its state of being eternally manifest through the nature of immediate consciousness (or, according to another reading, through immediacy itself). || 11 ||
From that [state] which possesses the nature of both vibration and non-vibration, Viṣṇu was born,
like a wave from the ocean filled with flowing essence.

The meaning is: from that which is changeless, whose single form and nature are the same whether in the vibration (*spanda*) or the non-vibration (*aspanda*) of *māyā* and its effects; [from] Viṣṇu, whose nature is to pervade all effects, the cosmic Virāṭ self of the universe, who was born through the sequence of creation of the subtle elements; [from] the flowing sap, that is, water.

Just as a wave arises from the ocean—which, despite its states of movement and stillness due to the influx [of water], never deviates from its single nature of being water—by this it is implied that the origin of the world from the Changeless is of the nature of an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) alone, and not a transformation (*pariṇāma*). || 12 ||
From that heart-lotus, which had Mount Sumeru as its pericarp, the quarters as its petals,
and the stars as its filaments, the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) was born. (13)
From that heart-lotus of Virāj— which has Mount Sumeru as its pericarp, the quarters of the sky as its petals, and is possessed of such filaments as the intermediate directions— [the worlds emerged].
Adorned by a circle of divine sages who were knowers of the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas,
he created the entire multitude of conceptual constructs, just as the mind does.
By means of the circles or assemblies of gods and sages, [he created] the creation, the collection of living beings. || 14 ||
In this corner of Jambūdvīpa, in the region named Bhārata,
he indeed created a flood of human beings overwhelmed by mental and physical ailments.
In this creation of all living beings— the reading being *sarvabhūtānām*— the limbs of creatures are despondent due to existence and non-existence, they are intent upon arising and destruction,
and it is crowded with various calamities. (16)
O friend, one whose body and mind are dejected by existence and non-existence, by gain and loss;

for whom birth is a calamity and death is its immediate destruction; who possesses but a short life—such is the state of people in this creation of elemental beings, which is crowded with various kinds of attachments to the enjoyment of sense-objects.
"Having seen suffering"—this is to be connected with what follows. || 16 ||
Seeing that suffering of these people, the Lord, the creator of all worlds, was moved by compassion, just as a father is at the suffering of his son. (17)
The Lord is capable of warding off that suffering. || 17 ||
"Who can bring an end to the suffering of these whose hopes are destroyed and whose lives are forfeit? Thus he reflected with one-pointed concentration for a moment for their welfare.
"He brings to an end; he destroys"—thus [the word] *anta* [is derived]. He reflected, "What means might there be? || 18 ||
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One, the Lord himself, created austerity, righteousness, charity, truth, and indeed the sacred fords. (19)
First, he states the creation that is the means for purification: "Thus," etc. (19).
Having created this, the divine creator of beings reflected once more:
"By this alone, there shall be no end to the suffering of men," he thought himself.
"Of those connected with creation," that is to say, of the persons created by himself; "end" means their cessation from the very root. || 20 ||
Nirvana is called the supreme bliss, by means of which one is neither born nor dies; it is obtained solely through that knowledge. (21)
The person, the living soul, is neither born again nor does it die; that is Nirvana. || 21 ||
For a living being, knowledge alone is the means for crossing over saṃsāra;
austerity, charity, and likewise pilgrimage sites are proclaimed to be non-means. (22)

"Those which are without means are proclaimed as non-instruments; for neither by ritual action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth—these forms of sacrifice are but frail rafts," and so on, in such scriptural passages. || 22 ||
Therefore, for the sake of liberating these wretched people from suffering— [according to another reading, "for the sake of this great-souled one"]—
I shall quickly reveal a fresh means of crossing over. (23)
"Fresh" means new; that is to say, firm. || 23 ||
Having reflected thus, the Blessed Lord Brahmā, seated upon a lotus,
formed a mental resolve and brought me, this one, into existence.
But me, standing here before you. || 24 ||
O sinless one, having arisen from somewhere, I quickly appeared before him, just as one wave swiftly rises from another wave. (25)
Having arisen through the production of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) solely by the power of inexplicable māyā from some source, he quickly arrived at his father's father; that is the meaning. || 25 ||
The Lord, bearing a water-pot, was saluted and greeted by me, who also bore a water-pot; he, possessing a rosary, was likewise saluted by me, who possessed a rosary. || 26 ||
Having bowed down so as to have his rosary visible, and having become humble, he was saluted—that is, paid homage. || 26 ||
Having said to me, "Come, my son," he joined me with his hand upon the northern petal of his own lotus, like the cool-rayed moon being placed within a white cloud.
"Yojayāmāsa" means he joined together; that is to say, he caused him to sit down. || 27 ||
Clad in a deer-skin, with a deer-skin as his own garment,
my father Brahmā spoke to me, like a noble swan addressing a crane.
"O son, for a mere moment your mind, fickle as a monkey, has been entered by ignorance, just as the hare [mark] enters the moon. (29)

Let ignorance—the cause of fickleness—enter and take possession of your mind as its agent, making it as restless as the species of monkeys; let the hare-marked spot [of the moon] enter as well. || 29 ||
Thus, having been cursed by him immediately after my deliberation, I indeed forgot my entire stainless true nature. (30)
The reflection belongs to the Supreme Lord; immediately following that is His volition. Everything is complete. (The particle) *kila* expresses wonder.
Then I fell into a state of wretchedness, remaining with an unawakened intellect, tormented by suffering and grief, like a person who has become destitute. (31)
He felt wretchedness and miserliness, like one whose wealth has been stolen. || 31 ||
"Alas! How has this defect called 'saṃsāra' come to be here?
Having thought thus within himself, he remained silent.
He remained silent and inactive. || 32 ||
Then my father said to me, "Son, why are you sorrowful? Ask me about the destruction of suffering, and you shall be forever happy. (33)
"Upaghāta" means that which destroys suffering; it refers to the means [for such destruction]. The suffix *aṇ* is applied here according to Pāṇini's rule on verbal derivatives (*karmaṇyaṇ*). 33.
Then, seated upon the petal of a golden lotus, I questioned that Blessed One, the creator of all worlds, regarding the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra.
"How has this saṃsāra, consisting of great suffering, come to be?
And how is it exhausted for a living being?"—thus was I questioned by him. (35)
The connection [of this] is with the subsequent phrase, "it was told by him to me. || 35 ||
That knowledge has been declared to be most abundant, knowing which it is the supreme purifier;
indeed, I have remained as if exceeding my father's intention. (36)
The father’s intention—superior to all, most excellent, stainless like the realization of reality, and of a perfectly complete nature—remained fixed; "kila" (it is said) expresses wonder. || 36 ||
Then the Creator of the world, the Speaker, and the Cause of all things spoke to me, who had realized what is to be known and was established in my own true nature. (37)
That speaker, the instructor, my father, spoke to me. || 37 ||
Having reduced you to a state of ignorance by means of a curse, I have made you my questioner, O son, for the sake of the spiritual attainment of all people through this essence of knowledge. (38)
For the sake of attaining knowledge for all eligible persons. || 38 ||
p.
96) Now, with your curse pacified, you have attained supreme awakening;
you abide as one with the single Self, just as I do, like gold [is not distinct] from the gold-ore. (39)

Just as gold, having long been associated with impurities and thus seemingly fallen into a state that is not gold, returns through purification to its original state of pure gold, so it is in this case. 39.
O virtuous one, go now upon the surface of the earth to Bharata-varṣa, situated within Jambūdvīpa, for the sake of bestowing grace upon the world. 40.

The fruit as well, having previously ascended into the intellect—[the reading is "the cause of the established action"]—is called "by means of the cause" because it is the cause of the action. || 40 ||

In that regard, O son of great intelligence, those devoted to the section on ritual action (kriyākāṇḍa) should be instructed by you, following the sequence of the ritual section in its proper order. (41)
Regarding the word "therein": the sense is that it is according to the principle, "One should not cause a disturbance of the intellect in the ignorant who are attached to action."
O virtuous one, those whose minds are dispassionate, who possess great wisdom, and who are discerning, should be instructed by you with knowledge that bestows bliss. (42)
They are possessed of great wisdom, skillful in grasping subtle meanings, investigative, and inclined toward critical examination. || 42 ||
Thus commissioned by my father, the lotus-born Brahmā, I remain here, O Rāghava, for as long as the succession of living beings endures. (43)
The lineage of beings, the succession of those who hold office, shall endure for as long as it persists. || 43 ||
Indeed, there is nothing at all that must be done by me here;
with the thought "I shall simply remain," I am established upon this earth with a mind perpetually asleep through a state of utter tranquility.
I perform action, yet I do nothing at all.

The purpose of action is what ought to be done. One who has transcended the mind is "beyond-mind" (atimāna), that is, one who is without mental activity (nirmanaska). Therefore, by means of that state (*vṛtti*) in which the intellect is perpetually as if asleep and free from ego-inflation, I perform my duty—the following of whatever comes to pass. Alternatively, established in a perfectly tranquil state, I act through the intellect of those who are perpetually asleep in ignorance.
The meaning is that one performs an action by means of one's own intellect, yet [in reality] one does nothing at all. || 44 ||
Thus ends the tenth canto, titled "The Descent of Knowledge," in the Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the tenth canto, titled "The Descent of Knowledge," in the Mumukṣuvyavahāra section of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Eleventh Chapter. 11.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
All this has been told to you regarding the descent of knowledge upon earth,
as well as my own purpose and the deeds of the Lotus-born One.
The descent and expansion of knowledge, the praise of detachment, and the characteristics of the speaker and the questioner are described here primarily. (1)
Furthermore, intending to describe in detail the manner of entering into knowledge (*jñānāvatāra*) as well as the characteristics of the speaker and the questioner,

he concludes what was stated for the purpose of that introduction with the words "this" (*etad*): "This much is my own intended effort (*īhita*)— my personal activity such as birth and so forth— for the sake of causing others to enter into knowledge, just as it was for the Lotus-born One (*kamalodbhava*)."
And the conduct of my father has indeed been told to you; such is the grammatical connection. || 1 ||
O sinless one, my heart has become intensely eager today to hear this supreme knowledge from you, owing to the ripening of my great merit. (2)
From the arising of well-performed deeds, that is, from the ripening of merit. || 2 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, how did the intellect of you, the Supreme Lord, proceed toward the descent of knowledge in this world immediately after the creation?

Desiring to know by what kind of characteristics the arising of such merit is to be recognized, and what the manner of instruction regarding the objects indicated by those characteristics is like, Śrī Rāma spoke—asking "How?"—desiring to hear the detailed account of the previous narrative through the medium of inquiry: "How? In what manner? Explain that manner in detail."
The meaning is "describe. || 3 ||
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
In the supreme Brahman, Brahmā himself was born by the power of his own nature,
eternally consisting of vibration, like a wave in the ocean.

One's own state (*svabhāva*) is the accumulation of the impressions (*vāsanā*) of past knowledge and actions; by virtue of that, the self (*ātman*) itself arises as an adjunct (*upādhi*) corresponding to it. It consists of vibration (*spandamaya*), being abundant in the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). Having thus constantly and repeatedly seen this afflicted creation and the entire course of creation—
The Supreme Lord beheld her existing in the past, the present, and the future.

And he, having seen that very creation— the multitude of beings in the world— distressed and suffering due to its own ignorance through the modes of birth, old age, death, hell, and so forth immediately after the initial creation,
[perceived] by that very example the entire [nature] of creation existing throughout the past, present, and future times.
He beheld her course. || 5 ||
When the destruction of the Kṛta and other ages— the time of active worldly processes— had arrived, the Lord, perceiving the delusion of the worlds, was moved by compassion.

And specifically, having observed the impending delusion of the world when the Kṛta Yuga and other ages—times suitable for the performance of the means to heaven and liberation—had come to an end. || 6 ||
Then the Lord, having created me and repeatedly endowed me with knowledge,
dispatched me to the surface of the earth for the sake of pacifying the ignorance of the world.
Having repeatedly joined [the disciple] with knowledge through repeated instruction. || 7 ||
Just as I have been sent by him, so too have many other great sages,
headed by Sanatkumāra and including Nārada and others, in great numbers.
Through the sequence of ritual action and merit, as well as through the sequence of knowledge,
these [teachings] have been proclaimed to uplift the world which is bound by the disease of mental delusion.

*Kriyā* refers to ritual action according to the sequence of its instruction; *ca* implies [also] according to the sequence of the instruction on meditation (*upāsanā*). *Manaḥ* (mind), *mohaḥ* (delusion), and *ajñānam* (ignorance)—these two, or the disease (*āmaya*) consisting of them, is the sickness of *saṃsāra*;
by that it is "bound" (*unnaddham*), meaning fettered or brought under control. They have been "impelled" (*īritāḥ*), i.e., driven forth. || 9 ||
Then, in ancient times, when the Kṛta Yuga had waned and the pure sequence of ritual acts had gradually diminished upon the earth, those various great ṛṣis [acted].
The connection with the following verse is that "kings were appointed by the great seers. "Pure" means Vedic, or untainted by passion, greed, and so forth. || 10 ||
For the purpose of establishing the sequence of ritual actions and for the regulation of boundaries, kings were appointed according to the division of separate territories. (11)
For the purpose of establishing and for the purpose of setting in motion. || 11 ||
(97) Many treatises on Smṛti and treatises on sacrifice have been composed on this earth, being appropriate for the attainment of dharma, pleasure, and wealth. 12.
Then, immediately after the arrangement of kingship, the legal treatises (smṛti-śāstra) were composed, which are appropriate for regulating the respective duties of both kings and subjects. || 12 ||
While this Wheel of Time flows, and that sequence has thus dissolved, people are daily intent on eating and devoted to the acquisition of rice. (13)
The mention of "food" is an illustration for all objects of enjoyment, and the mention of "rice" is an illustration for all sensory objects.
(13) The pairs of opposites have arisen among kings for the sake of sense-objects;
consequently, living beings on earth have come to be subjected to punishment in great numbers. (14)

"Dualities" refers, by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), to the enmities residing therein; these are for the sake of objects, for the sake of territory, or for the sake of things to be enjoyed.

Alternatively, "dualities" refers to cold, heat, and so forth; they are for the sake of objects, meaning for the sake of procuring the objects that serve as means to avoid them. And from that, it follows:

Because wealth is the impurity resulting from the attainment of sense objects, living beings belonging to those who worship other deities have come to deserve punishment—that is, they are liable to be punished—for the sake of that wealth. || 14 ||
Consequently, the kings were unable to protect the earth without war;
at that time, they fell into a state of wretchedness along with their subjects.

Those who were previously patient and capable, immediately thereafter, being no longer capable, became wretched—having fallen into a state of dejection—due to the notion of the body being the self; that is to say, because of the fear of the destruction of the self upon the destruction of the body in battle and the like. || 15 ||
For the sake of removing their dejection and for the sake of the gradual attainment of right view, great perspectives on knowledge have therefore been proclaimed by us and others. (16)
Right view is the knowledge of the reality of the self; its *krama* is its progression, its circulation in the world—for that purpose. || 16 ||
This science of the self was first described among kings;
subsequently, as it spread throughout the world, it was designated as the "royal science" (rājavidyā). || 17 ||
For the reason stated by him, it has been proclaimed as "the royal science" by Vyāsa and others. || 17 ||
This is the royal science, the royal secret, the supreme knowledge of the inner self;
having known this, O Raghava, kings have attained the highest state beyond suffering. (18)
Now, O Rāma, after many kings of stainless fame have passed away,
you have been born today here on this earth from Daśaratha.
O crusher of enemies, this beautiful dispassion, which is purifying and without apparent cause, has arisen in your mind toward him who is so exceedingly serene. (20)
"Extremely serene" means utterly pure. "Without signs" (nirnimitta) means devoid of the visible signs to be mentioned later, such as cemeteries, calamities, and wretchedness. || 20 ||
For indeed, O Rāma, in every single person—even in the virtuous and the discerning—a passion-based detachment arises preceded by some specific cause. (21)
Or rather, it belongs to all objects, to all the multitude of people—

including even those virtuous ones renowned for their excellence— standing in the midst of every discerning host of persons (or, according to a variant reading, "the purpose of the person"). Precisely for this reason, it is caused by the experience of suffering seen as the effect of the quality of *rajas*.
[This is] characterized by passion (rājasam). || 21 ||

But this unprecedented state that has arisen in you, which causes wonder among the wise— this dispassion of yours, free from external cause, born of your own discernment and characterized by purity— is truly marvelous.
Because of the Smṛti passage beginning with "From sattva arise happiness and knowledge," it is sāttvika because it arises solely from discriminative knowledge. || 22 ||
Who indeed would not become dispassionate upon seeing a loathsome object? For the supreme detachment of the virtuous arises solely from discernment. (23)
He clarifies what has already been stated: "The loathsome," etc. (23).
Indeed, those great ones of supreme wisdom whose dispassion arises even without a [specific] sign possess a truly stainless mind. (24)
Indeed, by means of an intellect detached through the contemplation of the wonder of its own discernment,
a living being shines like a youth with a garland of bridegrooms.
By the very power of one's own discernment, that reflective awareness of wonder which is directed toward reality leads to detachment from other objects. || 25 ||
Those who, having discerned this structure of worldly existence through discrimination, attain dispassion—they alone are the supreme among men. (26)
By the power of one's own discrimination alone, having investigated this again and again, one must forcibly abandon this magical illusion, both its external and internal aspects. (27)
This entire collection of visible phenomena is like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), meaning it is illusory (*māyika*). It is not merely external;
rather, it includes both the external and the internal, extending as far as the body, senses, vital breath, mind, intellect, and ignorance. || 27 ||
Who would not become dispassionate upon seeing a cemetery, calamity, and wretchedness? That dispassion which arises spontaneously is the supreme good. (28)
Having attained a state of great, natural dispassion, you are fit for the essence of knowledge, just as soft soil is for a seed. (29)
He has attained that which is not reached by others. The essence of all forms of knowledge and sciences is the science of the Self; [this he has attained].
(29) By the grace of the Supreme Lord, the Protector, the Supreme Self, a virtuous intellect such as yours pursues discernment. (30)

Through the power of austerity and by the grace of the gods; for those men who possess supreme devotion to the God, the latent impression of non-duality arises solely through the favor of the Lord—namely, through the grace of Rudra together with Bhavānī.
Knowledge concerning the inner self arises through many births.
Following such scriptural and traditional texts (śruti-smṛti), he says: "By grace" (prasādāt). || 30 ||
Through a great sequence of ritual actions, through austerity, through observance of rules, through charity, through pilgrimages, and through discernment practiced over a long period of time; (31)

Following such scriptural passages as, "Brahmins seek to know Him through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting," he says: "by the sequence of ritual acts. And the sequence of ritual acts consists of conception (*garbhādhāna*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the birth ceremony (*jātakarman*), the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*caula*), and initiation (*upanayana*).

The vehicle, the four Vedic vows, the ceremonial bath, union with a wife who practices the dharma together, the performance of the five sacrifices, the Aṣṭakās, the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha, and the seven seasonal rites—namely, the Śrāvaṇī, Āgrayaṇī, Caitrī, and Āśvayujī. (Note: The reading "of these, as well as of gods, humans, spirits, and Brahman" is also found.)

The seven forms of the *pākayajña* are: the establishment of the sacred fires (*āgnādhāna*), the fire-oblation (*agnihotra*), the new- and full-moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), the *āgrayaṇa* offering, the independent animal sacrifice (*nirūḍhapaśubandha*), and the *sautrāmaṇī*.
The seven forms of the *haviryajña* are: the *agniṣṭoma*, the *atyagniṣṭoma*, the *ukthya*, the *ṣoḍaśin*, the *vājapeya*, the *atirātra*, and the *aptoryāma*.
The Āptoryāma—these are the seven forms of the Soma sacrifice; thus, these are the forty sacraments.

There are also eight qualities of the self: compassion toward all beings, patience, freedom from envy, purity, lack of fatigue, auspiciousness, generosity, and lack of possessiveness. He who possesses these forty sacraments...

"He attains union with Brahman through the eight qualities of the self," as shown in the Gautama-smṛti; [this is achieved] by means of restraint, that is, the restraint of the senses, the vital breaths, and the mind. || 31 ||
When evil deeds have come to an end and one engages in the investigation of the ultimate truth,
the intellect of a living being proceeds by way of a chance occurrence.

"Like the arrival of crows [and] like the falling of palmyra fruits"—this refers to the occurrence through the yoga that has been accomplished, namely, the gathering together of the collection of means (*sādhana*).

Furthermore, by the rule "after a compound whose object is that [same thing], the suffix *cha* is added to another word denoting a standard of comparison" (*samāsācca tadviṣayāt* Pāṇini 5.3.106), the suffix *cha* is applied to another word denoting a standard of comparison following a compound whose object is that same thing.
Thus, the meaning is that the very arising of the inquiry which motivates the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is itself difficult to attain. || 32 ||
(98) Those who are intent on ritual action are fully occupied with the whirlpools of worldly existence; people wander here as long as they do not behold the supreme state. (33)

Why is that? Because as long as they do not perceive the supreme state, they cause the wheel to revolve—that is, they cause the person to spin—being shrouded by the tendencies of passion and so forth.
Thus, all of them, being solely intent on activities that serve as means for enjoyment in this world and the next, wander here in saṃsāra.

The meaning is that this is according to such scriptural passages as: "Existing in the midst of ignorance, though wise themselves, they consider themselves learned; wandering about, the deluded go astray like blind men led by one who is himself blind. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.5) || 33 ||
Having seen this saṃsāra as it truly is, and having abandoned the mind absorbed in it, they go to the Supreme, like elephants freed from their tethering posts. (34)

The meaning is: "as it truly is" (yathābhūtam) means existing as it is, being the ultimate reality (paramārthabhūta). This is the supreme Brahman-tattva, which is eternally immediate (nityāparokṣa). Alternatively, the meaning is: having seen this entire collection of visible objects as they truly are—ultimately unreal, essence-less, and consisting of suffering—by means of the intellect of discrimination (vivekabuddhi); [this is] the supreme.
They go to Brahman; that is, they attain it through knowledge. They have emerged from the *ālāna*, which is the tethering post.
34 O Rāma, this course of worldly existence here is difficult and endless.
A great being endowed with a body does not perceive it without knowledge. 35
Due to the superimposition of identity with the body, he is joined as if he were one with it; for this very reason, even a great being is like a mere worm or insect. (35)
O descendant of Raghu, by means of the boat of knowledge and reasoning alone, those of great intellect have crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra, so difficult to traverse, in the blink of an eye.
Those of great intelligence are discerning. || 36 ||
Listen with an attentive mind and constant vigilance to this method of knowledge, which carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra. (37)

By means of that well-known intellect, which is constantly attentive and devoted to the practice of inquiry, and which is perfected through discernment, dispassion, and so forth; being attentive, that is, one-pointed. || 37 ||
For these worldly fears of suffering, with their endless turmoil,
burn within for a long time unless one possesses blameless skillful means.

*Saṃrambha* is the force of agitation. It is well known as the impulse of speech, the impulse of the mind, the impulse of anger, the impulse of the tongue, the impulse of the stomach, the impulse of the genitals, and so forth. (38)
O Raghava, by what means can the dualities of suffering—such as cold, wind, and heat—be endured by the virtuous, except through the power of knowledge? (39)
Afflicting thoughts fall upon the foolish man at every step and at their appointed time, burning him just as a flame of fire consumes straw. (40)
Mental agonies do not burn the wise man who has understood what is to be known and possesses right vision, just as flames of fire do not consume a forest drenched by rain.

One by whom the inner scriptures (*adhyātma-śāstra*)—which are to be known, have been known, and are fit to be understood through deliberation—have [been mastered]; for that very reason, one who possesses right vision (*samyag-darśana*), which is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the reality of Brahman; [and] mental afflictions (*ādhi*), which are sufferings of the mind.
Even when the desert wind of saṃsāra, which revolves with mental and physical afflictions,
is turbulent, the knower of reality is not shattered, like the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).

In this desert-like whirlwind of saṃsāra, where mental and physical afflictions are the supreme and most powerful eddies, even when the wind is agitated and turbulent, [the world] is broken, crushed, and oppressed— this is the meaning. || 42 ||
Therefore, a wise person who desires to know reality must, with effort and full of devotion, question one who is truly wise, authoritative, and awakened in soul. (43)
Through diligent effort, such as approaching [the teacher], prostrating, and serving; a "prāmāṇika" is one who is skilled in the means of valid knowledge, such as the Vedas. || 43 ||
The speech of an authoritative person who has been questioned, who possesses a noble mind,
should be received with effort, just as saffron is taken up by a fine cloth.

Just as saffron is grasped by a cloth that has been immersed in a saffron solution, being retained without departing due to its being colored by that very state—so too is the object of perception to be understood. 44.
O best among those skilled in speech, there is no one more foolish than that man who questions a person whose words are not to be accepted because he does not know the truth. (45)

Desiring to state the characteristics of the speaker and the questioner for that purpose, he censures the non-investigator as "one who does not know reality" (*atattvajña*). This means one whose speech is not to be accepted—that is, not to be taken up. || 45 ||
There is no person more base than he who, when questioned with effort by an authoritative speaker who knows that [truth], does not carry out his word. (46)
Having first ascertained through the effect whether the speaker was ignorant or possessed of knowledge of that matter, the man who then poses a question is a highly intelligent inquirer. (47)
From its effect, that is, from the mark of conventional usage. || 47 ||
The child who asks a question without having first determined the speaker is an inferior inquirer; he is not a fit vessel for the great meaning.
Without having determined through investigation who is the superior speaker, the fool remains ignorant. || 48 ||

When one possesses an irreproachable intellect capable of reconciling what precedes and what follows, a wise person should answer what is asked; not, however, in the case of a base person who follows the nature of a beast.

One whose intellect is capable—that is, competent—to discern and determine the resolution of what has been stated and what has not been stated regarding the preceding and the subsequent [sections]. || 49 ||
The wise call that man the most foolish who speaks here without first considering whether the questioner is capable of grasping the authoritative meaning. (50)
Thus, without examining the speaker, he also censures him, saying: "He is authoritative," and so forth. || 50 ||
O descendant of Raghu, you are exceedingly fond of praising virtues and are an inquirer;
I too know how to speak—this union of ours is well-suited. (51)
He demonstrates the relevance of the description of the characteristics of the speaker and the questioner to the subject at hand with the word "you" (tvam). || 51 ||
O you who are skilled in words and their meanings, whatever I say, you should determine with effort to be this very matter and carry it out in your heart without fail. (52)
O great sage, you are dispassionate and a knower of reality regarding the condition of living beings;
what you say takes root within [us] like saffron water on a cloth.
He was great by virtue of his lineage, his qualities, his virtuous conduct, and so forth.
Devoted to focused attention and discerning the ultimate truth, your wisdom enters into its object like the rays of the sun entering into water. (54)

The possession of intelligence and eloquence is obtained through these two qualifying attributes. "Arkabhāḥ" means the splendor of the sun. 54–55. Whatever I say should be accepted and diligently applied to the heart;
otherwise, I am to be questioned by you, but not here in vain.
To strengthen this sense of reverence, he says: "Whatever... [and so forth]. "With effort" means through the exertion of long-term practice and the like.
"For the mind, O Rāma, is fickle—a monkey in the forest of saṃsāra.
Having purified it with effort within the heart, one should listen to the song of the supreme truth. (56)
He states another method of effort as well: "The mind," [verse 56].
Having kept for a long time at a very great distance those who lack discernment, the ignorant, and people who take pleasure in the wicked, one should indeed honor the virtuous. (57)

Regarding that, he states the first point to be taught: "one who lacks discrimination. This refers to one in whom knowledge arising from the scriptures does not exist. "At a very great distance" means extremely far away. || 57 ||
Through constant association with the virtuous, discernment arises;
it is taught that enjoyment and liberation are the two fruits of the very tree of discernment. (58)
He states the fruit of that [practice] with the words "constantly" (nityam). || 58 ||
Four gatekeepers are proclaimed at the door of liberation:
tranquility, inquiry, contentment, and fourthly, association with the virtuous. (59)
These four, or two, or three, should be served with effort;
they open the door to the royal palace of liberation. (60)
If [the former] is unable, three; if those too are unable, two. || 60 ||
Or else, one should resort to even a single person by exerting all effort, even at the cost of one's life;
for when one is brought under control, all four likewise come under control.
"Having abandoned their lives" is an expression of the extreme degree of their venerability. || 61 ||
For one who possesses discernment is the vessel for the scripture, knowledge, austerity, and sacred learning; he is like the sun, the form of whose ornaments is the very nature of its radiance.

A person endowed with discernment (*viveka*) is a fit vessel for the scripture, for hearing (*śruta*), for austerity (*tapas*), and for the contemplation of its meaning; he is worthy of honor as the foremost ornament, like a crest-jewel among ornaments. He is like the sun (*bhāskara*) in the midst of luminaries.
...as it were. || 62 ||
For the dullness of wisdom in those lacking consciousness reaches a state of density;
through its rigidity, it becomes like the immobility of water turning into the hardness of stone.

Dullness of wisdom is ignorance (*maurkhya*). Solidity (*ghanatām*) means impenetrability; it refers to immobility (*sthāvaratām*), lack of fluidity (*adravatām*), and hardness (*kāṭhinyam*). This is due to numbness (*jāḍyāt*), that is, an excess of cold; for this is well known in the case of snow, hail, and the like. || 63 ||
But you, O Rāghava, with your inner heart blossomed by kindness, virtuous qualities, and insight into the meaning of the scriptures, stand like a lotus at sunrise.
To turn [the mind] toward him, he praises Rāma once more with the words "But you... (64).
O noble-minded one, you ought to raise your ears to hear and understand these words of wisdom, just as a living being raises its ears for the sound of a lute. (65)
To understand means to comprehend. One whose ears are "upraised" (uddhata)—that is, erect—is such a creature as a deer or similar animal. || 65 ||
O Rāma, through the yoga of the practice of dispassion, strive to acquire the wealth of equanimity and goodness—[the wealth of tranquility and kindness]—in which no destruction is found. 66.
The dharma of virtuous people consists of goodness, humility, and so forth; it is the very nature of such excellences.

At the outset, for the sake of liberation from saṃsāra, one should increase wisdom itself through the study of the scriptures, association with the virtuous, and the practice of austerity and self-restraint. (67)
Wisdom (prajñā) is the intellect (buddhi) that is more capable than others in discerning, grasping, and retaining [the truth]. || 67 ||
Know this alone to be the supreme destroyer of his ignorance: that he studies some scripture with a refined intellect. (68)
Intending to show that even for the increase of that [knowledge], the means is precisely the repeated study of this very text, he says: "This... (verse 68).
This poisonous tree of saṃsāra is the sole abode of calamities;
it constantly deludes the ignorant, so one should destroy this folly with diligent effort. (69)
"Āspada" means a foundation. The ellipsis to be supplied is "because it would cause delusion from that [foundation]. "Maurkhya" means ignorance. 69–70.
By means of ignorance, which moves like a serpent of evil desires and leaps within the heart, the mind undergoes contraction, just as a piece of leather placed over a fire does.

Because it possesses a crooked gait like that of a serpent due to its evil intent, the mind—whether understood as the intellect (*buddhi*) or the conscious self (*cidātman*)—is agitated by the "serpentine movement" within the heart; that is, it moves as the inner-facing reality (*pratīcī*), dancing with a nature consisting of thousands of mental distractions. It thus undergoes contraction, a lack of clarity like that of a closed lotus.
That is to say, it means "impurity. || 70 ||
In one who possesses wisdom, this vision of reality becomes clarified, just as the sight [is clear] when the moon’s entire stainless orb is visible in a cloudless sky. (71)

Where, then, does it find favor? He says: "In the wise one" (*prājñe*). This "vision of reality" (*vastudṛṣṭi*)—previously mentioned—is that subtle intellect by which the object in its ultimate form is perceived. As the Śruti states: "But it is seen by the foremost intellect, by the subtle intellect, by those who perceive the subtle. It is that which has become the true nature of things.

Or rather, the vision that has attained identity with the reality as it truly is—that is, the vision whose nature is consciousness—becomes clear when there is a wise teacher; having cast off the impurity of ignorance, it shines forth. || 71 ||
He whose mind possesses the beautiful skill of investigating what precedes and what follows, and which is accompanied by discernment—he is called a man in this world. (72)
Describing the characteristic of the expansion of the intellect (*mati*), he praises one who possesses it with the words "pūrva... and so forth.

The meaning is that the intellect, which is capable of grasping the most subtle objects through the investigation of what precedes and what follows, and which shines with cleverness (*cāturya*), is said to be "expanded" (*savikāsā*). Such a person [is praised] for accomplishing the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).
The meaning is that his human birth has been rendered purposeful. || 72 ||
You shine with a heart that is blossomed, white, dispelling darkness, cool-rayed through its excellent discernment, and endowed with virtue.
You are like the sky with the stainless moon. || 73 ||
Then, consoling Rāma who was doubting whether his own mind was expanded or not, [the Lord] said:

"By the expanded... You shine forth with a heart that has cast off the darkness of ignorance (*tamas*), and is therefore white, clear, and virtuous—endowed with qualities such as tranquility—and with the aforementioned intellect. || 73 ||

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Speaker and the Questioner," in the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* tradition.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Speaker and the Questioner," in the Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa.
The Twelfth Chapter. 12.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
O Raghava, you are one whose mind is fulfilled, worthy of honor, and you know how to inquire; you also understand what has been said, and for that reason I have proceeded to speak with reverence.
The futility of worldly existence, the supreme majesty of knowledge,
and the abundance of qualities in Rāma as an inquirer are described here.

Desiring to explain to others as well the harmful nature of worldly existence for the sake of strengthening their discernment and dispassion, and the greatness of knowledge, he praises [Arjuna] by saying that not only is his intellect fully expanded,
but he also possesses many other virtues and all the characteristics of a true questioner, in order to encourage him.
Encouraging Rāma, the venerable Vasiṣṭha said: "One whose mind is completely full" (paripūrṇamanāḥ).

This refers to one whose mind is filled with the qualities already mentioned and those yet to be described. And it has been said: "You understand even what is indicated by a general statement, and you discern it in its specific detail. (1)
Having established your mind within the Self— free from passion and darkness and following pure goodness— be steady in order to hear this knowledge. (2)

Through *rajas* there is restlessness of the mind, while through *tamas* there is obscuration; therefore, having established the mind within the Self—which is free from those [qualities] and thus follows the *sattva* quality of the Supreme Self—one should remain steady and diligent. || 2 ||
The entire array of qualities of an inquirer exists within you, as well as the qualities of a speaker;
and my own array of qualities is in me, like the jewel-glory in the ocean. (3)
The splendor of jewels is their excellence; "Śrī" refers both to that excellence accompanied by jewels and to the goddess Lakṣmī. || 3 ||
"O son, you have attained detachment born from discernment and non-attachment, just as a moonstone becomes moist when struck by the rays of the moon. (4)

The address "O son" is used according to the maxim that one should regard disciples as one's own children. "Moistness" means the state of being wet. "Lagna" refers to that which possesses the rays (utkara) of the moon's beams. || 4 ||
From childhood onwards, you have long practiced pure virtues; as one who is naturally pure, these virtues are like the long, continuous filaments of a lotus.

"Practice" (abhyāsa) means cultivation; that is to say, "connection. Of you, who are pure. With "long" [threads], meaning those extended in all directions; with "continuous," meaning uninterrupted. In the case of the lotus, [it refers] to the threads or fibers, and also to qualities such as fragrance. || 5 ||
Therefore, listen; I shall tell you a story, for you alone are its worthy recipient.
Indeed, without the moon, the night-lily does not bloom in its pure splendor.

The vessel is the support for awakening to the fruit of hearing [the teaching]. It is pure and bright; it is blooming, being the support for awakening produced by the moon. Or, the meaning is that just as the night-lily (*kumudvatī*) blooms only when the moon is present, so too does this discourse bloom only within you. (6)
Whatever undertakings there may be and whatever views there may be,
they all indeed attain complete cessation when that state is perceived.
If it is asked, "What is the limit for this undertaking of listening to the narrative?
the answer is: it is rest in the vision of the supreme state. With this in mind, he says: "Whosoever...
All those undertakings, all those perspectives on the means of knowledge and their objects—[the text continues: "Is there not here a man, a woman..."
If it is argued that there ought to be an *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member) [of the compound], since unlike a *dvandva*, an *ekaśeṣa* is not optional—this is true;

nevertheless, there is no fault, because we observe the use of a sentence expressing its own constituent analysis (*svapadavigraha*) for the application of *ekaśeṣa* in the usage of experts such as the *Mahābhāṣya*. || 7 ||
If the mind of a fortunate person were not to find rest in consciousness, then who in this cycle of existence could endure the profound dullness of such anxiety? (8)
He prevents the lack of confidence regarding the aforementioned state of rest with the words "yadi" (if). What discerning person would tolerate that?
The sense is that because of the inability to tolerate it, one would quickly become intent on abandoning the body—this being the reading "tvamiha dehe. || 8 ||
Upon reaching the Supreme, all mental fluctuations dissolve,
like the rocks of the principal mountains through contact with the multitude of suns at the end of an aeon.

Not only do external views dissolve, but mental ones as well; thus he says, "the supreme. And so says the Śruti: "The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut away, and his karmas are exhausted—when That is seen."
Regarding the phrase "parāvare" (in the high and the low): in the case of the illustrative example, it refers to the end of the lifespan of Hiraṇyagarbha. || 9 ||
O Rāma, this unbearable cholera-like affliction caused by the onset of the poison of saṃsāra is pacified by the purifying Gāruḍa mantra of yoga.
In the world, cholera is well known even from contact with poison. Yoga is the realization of the oneness of the individual soul (jīva) with Brahman;
that itself is the Gāruḍa mantra. By means of that purifying [mantra], there is the cleansing of the poison. || 10 ||
And that yoga is surely obtained through the investigation of the scriptures with virtuous people; it is indeed the mantra for the knowledge of the ultimate truth. (11)
"With a virtuous person" means with a teacher, a fellow student, or the like; and because of the word "ca" (and), it also bears fruit [in other ways]. || 11 ||

For it must be understood that when inquiry is certainly conducted here, there occurs the complete exhaustion of all suffering; therefore, those who possess the vision of inquiry should not be viewed with disregard. || 12 ||
He elaborates upon the meaning stated in verse by means of prose, beginning with "avaśyam" (inevitably) and so forth.
The syntactical connection here is: "In this birth of the qualified person, it inevitably occurs. They are not to be viewed with *avahelā*, that is, with disregard. || 12 ||
By a person possessed of discernment—[according to another reading:

by virtue of discernment]—having cast off this entire cage of sovereignty [according to another reading: the cage of illusion], like a snake shedding its fully ripened skin, he becomes free from fever with a cooled inner heart.
To one who possesses right vision, the entire world is perceived like a magical illusion for the sake of diversion;
indeed, for one who lacks right vision, this very world is supreme suffering.

By a person possessing discernment (*vicāra*), possessing right vision (*samyagdarśana*), and for that very reason possessing a tranquil inner heart; or, if the reading is *vaśataḥ*, it means from the power of discernment, which is immediate awakening (*aparokṣabodha*). Having completely cast off this entire cage of mental afflictions (*ādhipañjara*) like a snake shedding its fully ripened, worn-out skin, one views this whole world as a mere curiosity, like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*).
It is perceived as having the nature of happiness. The word "param" is a particle used for emphasis; or, it may mean that [the other] is the supreme suffering. || 13 ||
For the passion for saṃsāra is exceedingly treacherous;

like a serpent it bites, like a sword it cuts, like a spear it pierces, like a rope it entangles, like fire it burns, and like night it blinds. Like a stone falling unexpectedly upon men, it renders them helpless.
Craving carries away wisdom, destroys stability, and causes one to fall into the blind well of delusion;
it wears one down, and there is no suffering in cyclic existence that a person does not encounter through it. (14)

He elaborates upon the very inequality that was asserted by means of examples, beginning with "Like a serpent" and ending with "in the blind well of delusion. In all these instances, the agency belongs to the passion for *saṃsāra* (or, according to another reading, to the disease itself). In all instances ending with "renders helpless," the phrase "men who have fallen unexpectedly" is to be understood as the object.

The connection is through the sense of being an object (*karmatayānvaya*). Its meaning is: "men who have fallen into sense-objects through delusion, without even suspecting or anticipating harm. Like a stone fallen upon the head, it renders one helpless and causes one to faint. It causes one to fall from wisdom—the faculty of discernment—and from stability—the sense of moral restraint (*maryādā*).

The word "men" (*puruṣān*) is supplied from the previous verse. In the well of darkness characterized by delusion—where "darkness-well" (*andhakūpa*) may also refer to a specific hell—it causes men to decay, making them as frail as *soma* through pressing; it simply makes them weak.
Why say more? He says this in a single statement: "There is nothing that... (verse 14).

(101) This chronic cholera of the sense-objects, it is said, if not treated, leads to the production of various results that result in a succession of many cities of hell; such indeed does it do. (15)

The bodies are like cities of the hells filled with filth, urine, and so forth; their "mass" (*nikara*)—the collection of one's own kinsmen, dependents, and the like—binds a person through attachment to them. [This interpretation of the commentary should be examined in accordance with the root text. That which has such a nature is characterized by sense objects (*viṣaya*).
If cholera is not treated, then it indeed brings about thousands of the aforementioned miserable states of hell. || 15 ||
Where the fall of a sword sharpened on stone is like the striking of a pebble; where fire is like a cooling bath of snow; where the cutting of limbs is like anointing with sandalwood paste;
where forests are like the workings of woodworms; where a halo is like the dusting of one's limbs; and where the unceasing movement of flames is like the activity of warriors in battle.

The arrival of the rainy season is the dispelling of the summer heat, the raining down of spray from a shower-house, the beheading that renders pleasant sleep mute, the binding of the seal upon the face, and a great accumulation [of merit]. || 16 ||

Where "shila-shita" means being ground by stones; "asibhiḥ śātaḥ" means being cut into pieces with swords; "pātaḥ" means being cast down from mountain peaks; "upalaghanaiḥ" means being beaten with heavy stones; "agninā dāhaḥ" means being burned by fire; "himena avasekaḥ" means constant drenching with snow, resulting in perpetual dampness; and "aṅgānām akartanam" means the cutting off of limbs with axes, knives, and other such tools.

It is like the rubbing and grinding of sandalwood wood upon stone slabs; it is like running through forests of sword-leaf trees; it is like the experience of wood-boring insects being crushed within a wooden machine in every limb; and it is like being encircled by glowing iron rings and chains.

"Enveloping on all sides" means the wiping away of the limbs with brushes of thorns— that is, the removal of their skin. "The continuous falling, like a stream, of battle-arrows"— meaning arrows discharged in combat— refers to those from which flames of fire issue incessantly due to their constant contact with the fire, such that they resemble a torrential downpour.

[This is] an introductory phrase (*nipāta*). "The diversion" means the passing of time during the heat of the summer season; the ellipsis [to be supplied] is "without shade or water. Likewise, in the cold season, there is the sprinkling of droplets in shower-houses (*dhārāgṛha*), and the repeated cutting of hair that has grown back after being shaved. Regarding the matter of pleasant sleep, however—

"Rendered mute" means that there is not even a whisper; "sealing of the face" means causing it to be breathless by closing it; "rigidity" refers to the uneven state of the limbs—meaning their incapacity for activity due to being distorted; and "great accumulation" is like that of a mountain.

The meaning is: "of each individual limb of the body. Alternatively, [the practice consists of] where the fourfold [treatment], beginning with being sharpened on stone, must be endured like the application of snow; the cutting off of limbs like the anointing with sandalwood paste;
and the triad beginning with the trees and forest, like the cleansing of the limbs—that is, like the refinement of the body.
The falling of a shower of exceptional arrows is like the sprinkling of spray from a fountain-house for the purpose of cooling the summer heat;

death inflicted by the severing of the head is like a pleasant sleep; and the forceful silencing by covering the mouth is, by its very nature, like the sealing of a face with a kiss, as well as [the experience of] bitterness.
The meaning is that it must necessarily be endured, like the accumulation of great wealth. || 16 ||

Therefore, O Rāghava, one must not treat with indifference this machine of saṃsāra, which is so terrible with its thousands of such painful exertions; rather, it must certainly be reflected upon and understood in this way, for indeed, the highest good arises from the investigation of the scriptures. || 17 ||
Having shown that this is merely an illustration of the directions because the sources of suffering are infinite, he concludes by stating its relevance to the present subject: "Thus, in this way...
The "constraint" (yantraṇa) of the unstable and perishable bodies consists of confinement (yantra), limitation (saṃkoca), circumscription (pariccheda), and dependence on others (pāravaśya).
In that very [context], in the manner about to be described; he states that very [point] with the words "yathā" (just as). || 17 ||
Furthermore, O moon of the Raghu dynasty, if these great sages, great seers, brahmins,

and kings have their bodies shrouded by the armor of knowledge, how is it that they— though incapable of enduring suffering— yet experience those various worldly afflictions preceded by the pursuit of livelihood?
They remain with minds constantly joyful. || 18 ||

One might raise the objection: "How can it be certain that spiritual welfare (*śreyaḥ*) results from the investigation of the scriptures, given that even for those such as Māṇḍavya who were devoted to them, we observe thousands of misfortunes? Dispelling this doubt, [the author] demonstrates that knowledge has visible results by saying, "Moreover..."—those whose bodies are enveloped in the armor of wisdom (*jñāna-kavaca*). Thus:

If you think that even these aforementioned sages and others, though unworthy of suffering, remain experiencing various forms of worldly misery—which cause pain and are preceded by mental activity—just like ignorant people, then how is it that they remain with minds constantly full of joy? Such is the logical connection (*anvaya*). [The word] *munayaḥ*...

The sages were devoted to meditation; the seers were devoted to the recitation of mantras; the brahmins were devoted to ritual action; and the kings, such as Janaka and others, [were devoted to their respective duties]. || 18 ||
For here, Hari, Hara, Padmaja, and the others remain as they are— free from curiosity and devoid of the disturbances of conceptual construction.
The supreme among men, who have attained the lamp of the self and possess pure intellects, remain thus established in the world. || 19 ||

The phrase "iha hi" (for here) connects with both the preceding and the following verses, according to the maxim of the lamp on the threshold (*dehalīdīpanyāya*). If so, what is their state? He describes it as "free from curiosity" (*vikautukāḥ*). Curiosity (*kautuka*) is the zeal for seeing and enjoying unprecedented objects; they are devoid of that. They are also "free from the confusion of conceptual constructions" (*vikalpa-viplava*); confusion (*vikṣepa*) is the distraction caused by such constructions, and they are free from that. || 19 ||
When delusion is utterly exhausted, when the dense cloud of ignorance has dissolved— this being the reading "dissolved dense"— when reality is fully known and the infinite Self is attained;
then, having deliberated with the Noble Ones, one who possesses a moving body perceives it as truly such.
When reality is perceived through wisdom, this worldly existence becomes a wandering for the sake of delight. || 20 ||

If these [enlightened ones] are like the gods beginning with Brahmā, possessing all their desires fulfilled, then how is it that they are seen wandering through the realms of saṃsāra? Dispelling this doubt,
he shows that inquiry and the like have as their fruit the wandering of one liberated while living (jīvanmukti), by means of the verse beginning with "parikṣīṇe."

First, for that qualified seeker who— having deliberated together with noble teachers and others in the purification of categories— has discarded the physical bodies, such as the gross body and so forth, by means of the realization of their non-self-nature through their deviation from self-similarity due to the false superimposition of identity based on superficial resemblance; for him, first...
When the reality [of the Self] has been fully known from the scriptural statement, and when the Self— having transcended [all limitations] and being undivided—

has been realized through reflection (*manana*) by means of the complete removal of misconceptions; and when, through the intellect (*dhi*), which possesses the state of that [reality]— namely, the state of Brahman— in which contrary notions have been dispelled by meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*), it is seen, that is, directly perceived.

When delusion is utterly exhausted and the dense cloud of erroneous cognition—which is its effect—has dissolved, this wandering through the world, this roaming, this delighting, and this sporting is indeed not a source of affliction; such is the meaning. || 20 ||
Furthermore, O Rāghava:
when the nature of consciousness is serene, and the Supreme, which arises from tranquility, dances within the heart;

When all perceptions of mental constructions have become the very embodiment of tranquility before one, and when the activity of the internal organ tastes the flavor of equanimity, this worldly wandering becomes a sport for the intellect once the Reality has been perceived. 21.
