He establishes the very nature of delight as follows: "When the pure," and so forth. When the *cit-tattva*—the ultimate reality whose intrinsic nature is pure consciousness—is serene; when the supreme, most excellent state of peace has emerged and is attained;
and when all perceptions of mental constructs (*akhilakalanādṛṣṭi*) have become the full enjoyment of tranquility within all fluctuations of the intellect (*samastabuddhivṛtti*).

When there exist perceptions whose nature is the tasting of the flavor of peace (śānti-rasa)—[the reading is "perceptions" (pratītiṣu)]—one’s internal organ reaches a state of equilibrium, devoid of inequality, such that it becomes as if it has tasted the essence of Brahman (brahma-rasa). Therefore, the state of being delightful (ramaṇatva) is appropriate; this is the meaning. || 21 ||
And furthermore:
The body is the chariot, the sense-faculties are the horses, and their movement is the driver; the vital breath is the wind, and the objects of pleasure are the bliss derived from riding.
When the reality is perceived through a stainless intellect that [realizes], "I am either the supreme atom or the embodied soul wandering in the world," then this worldly wandering becomes a delight.
He states that pleasure is possible through the metaphorical perspective of the chariot, beginning with the passage: "Know the self as the rider, and the body as the chariot.
He says: "The chariot. The body is a chariot, insentient like a felled tree-stump;
the skillful movement of the senses toward their objects is the arrangement and course of the horses on all sides.

Vibration (*spanda*) is movement; that by which it occurs is the *pragraha* wind. The mind, dominated by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), is—by implication—possessed of objects consisting of bliss through being conveyed or brought [to them] by means of the chariot and so forth.
Such an embodied self (*dehī*) is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) itself during meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and likewise during the time of worldly activity.

Due to the limitation imposed by the adjunct of the intellect (*buddhy-upādhi*), he is atomic or subtle; the word "charioteer" is to be supplied. The meaning is that even with the thought, "Being such as this, I move about in the world," his delight is indeed [in the Self alone]. || 22 ||
Thus ends the twelfth canto, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Reality," in the Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, a work of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the twelfth canto, titled "Description of the Majesty of Reality," in the Mumukṣuvyavahāra section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Thirteenth Canto. 13.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having firmly grasped this vision, those of noble intellect who have realized the Self move about here in this world like great beings who have risen [to spiritual eminence]. (1)

In this work, the arising of qualities such as dispassion has been described extensively; moreover, tranquility (śama), which is crowned by the fruit of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), is treated in particular detail. || 1 ||

Intending to describe the means such as dispassion and tranquility, he describes the very state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) which is under discussion—beginning with the words "etām" (this).
"Abhyuditāḥ" means those who have attained a state of exaltation, as if having reached the prosperity of a universal empire. || 1 ||
They do not grieve, nor do they desire, nor do they beg for good or evil;
they perform everything, yet here they do nothing at all.
Since they do not desire to acquire or abandon what is auspicious or inauspicious, for that very reason they do not beg for the means to achieve them. || 2 ||
They abide in purity alone; indeed, they proceed by making themselves pure.
Free from the dualistic notions of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, they remain established in their own self.
Through the vision of the unattached Self, they act in accordance with the scriptures—pure and untainted—and they proceed upon the true worldly path. || 3 ||
They come and yet do not come; they go forth and yet do not go.
They act and yet do not act; they speak and yet do not speak.

They come and go as seen by others, but not so by one's own vision; for the Śruti declares, "He who has eyes is as if sightless, he who has ears is as if deaf, he who has a mind is as if mindless," and so forth—this is the intended meaning. || 4 ||
Whatever undertakings there may be and whatever views there may be— all those cease, in terms of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, once the state [of liberation] has been attained.

The meaning is that they perish due to the destruction of the motivating hatred and attachment—or, according to another reading, the motivating defects and qualities—and due to the destruction of the cognition of reality regarding their objects. || 5 ||
Having abandoned all worldly attachment and possessing a mind of sweet composure,
one attains happiness from every side, like the orb of the moon standing aloof.
Striving, desire, exertion, a sweet disposition, tranquility, and the form of Brahman—these constitute happiness;

the agent is the mind, and the action is [the state of] being situated within the lunar orb. Or rather, it is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā): the mind, as the agent, is as if situated within the lunar orb like a celestial being. || 6 ||
Even the undertaking of a divine emanation, in which every curiosity is perfectly ordered,
does not find room within oneself, just as an elixir does not fit within the moon.

Since the curiosity of contemplating sense objects is itself the cause of distraction, it follows that in its absence there is undistracted bliss; the meaning is that the mind has attained the nature of bliss. It does not measure, that is, it is not delimited.
"In the moon" refers to the full moon. "Elixir" means nectar. || 7 ||
He performs no magical illusions, nor does he pursue latent impressions;
having cast off the fickleness of a child, he shines forth from the very beginning.

Having cast aside the magical nets of illusory distractions, their cause—the latent impressions (vāsanā)—and the restlessness attached to delusion as if one were a child, the primordial bliss of the Self, established from time immemorial, shines forth. || 8 ||
For such states of being are obtained from the vision of the reality of the Self, and not otherwise.
He concludes, once again in prose, the utility of the detailed exposition of the purpose with the word "evam" (thus):
the *vṛttis* are the *sthitayas*. 9.
Therefore, through inquiry, the Self alone is to be sought, meditated upon, and known by a person throughout his life, and nothing else. || 10 ||
Seeking consists of the practice of hearing and reflection; worship is profound meditation (nididhyāsana). || 10 ||
Through the continuous practice of that which brings into harmony one's own experience, the scriptures, and the teacher,
the Self is beheld.
Unity of statement is the state of being grounded in a single meaning; it is the certainty [attained] by a qualified practitioner through the practice of hearing and so forth.
One who disregards the meaning of the scriptures and treats great men with contempt should not, even when fallen into painful adversity, become equal to the foolish. (12)
By whom the scriptures and their meanings have been treated with contempt; by whom the great, venerable persons who know reality have been disregarded and neglected. (12)
Neither disease, nor poison, nor calamity, nor likewise mental anguish on this earth causes such distress to men as the single state of folly residing within their own bodies. (13)
For those whose intellects possess some degree of refinement in Sanskrit, there is no other treatise whatsoever that removes ignorance as effectively as this scripture has been heard. (14)
Since the scriptures are difficult to master, he says "something" (kiñcit) to address how the cessation of ignorance might occur even for those with only slight proficiency. || 14 ||

This scripture, which is pleasant to hear, brings happiness, and is beautiful through its illustrations, is entirely free from contradiction by virtue of its connection with the meaning of the words. 15.

By means of appropriate illustrations, the meaning of the statement is as follows: by one for whom the Supreme Self—the most beloved kinsman—is necessarily desired to be attained, [this teaching] must be heard; it is something that must certainly be listened to. || 15 ||
Those calamities which are difficult to overcome, and those miserable, base births—
all these are produced from folly, just as thorns grow from the khadira tree.
They are empty and base. || 16 ||
O Rāma, it is better to wander for alms with a bowl in hand through the streets of the outcaste dwellings than to lead a life destroyed by folly. 17.
He says in two verses that, in comparison with all causes of misfortune, even each single misfortune is better. 17.
It is better to be a blind worm in solitude within terrible dark pits or even in the hollows of trees than to possess a foolishness that brings extreme suffering.
Or even in hollows. || 18 ||
Having attained this light which consists of the means to liberation,
no person shall ever again fall into blindness, even within the darkness of delusion.
Delusion is the gateway to fainting and death; even in darkness possessing that characteristic, one does not become blind—what then to say of other [forms of darkness]? This is the meaning. || 19 ||
Indeed, craving causes the lotus of man to contract as long as the stainless radiance of the sun of discernment has not arisen. (20)
"Indeed, we do not see a means for the abandonment of craving. To this, he says: "tāvat" (first), etc.
The "lotus" (*ambuja*) is the lotus flower (*padma*). || 20 ||
For the sake of liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra, together with kinsmen such as myself,
one should realize the true nature of the self through the authority of the Guru and the scriptures. (21)
"Having known [this], one should dwell"—this is the connection with what follows. || 21 ||
O Rāghava, conduct yourself here just as Hari, Hara, and others, as well as other Brahman-sages, move about as those liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
In this world, sufferings are infinite while happiness is like a mere blade of grass;
therefore, one should not fix one's gaze upon pleasures that are followed by suffering. (23)
Adopting this view. || 23 ||
That state which is infinite and effortless must be attained with diligent effort by a person who possesses discernment, for the sake of achieving the essential goal.

That knowledge by which that reality of the Self (ātmatattva) is reached or attained—that is the "state" (pada); it must be cultivated as a means for the accomplishment of the supreme human goal. || 24 ||
These very persons are the supreme among men and the vessels for the goal of human life,
whose minds— free from all feverish distress— rest upon the unsurpassed state.
There exists no other state or entity that is more supreme or most excellent than that;
yet those of wicked mind who, by merely partaking of the enjoyment of food, find satisfaction in pleasures such as sovereignty and the like—know them to be blind frogs. (26)

The frogs are the *dardura* and *bheka* species. For he, staying in that well, does not see what is outside; and if he were even blind therein, it would be all the more so—this is the intended meaning. || 26 ||

Those who are devoted to the deceitful, the malevolent, those characterized by the undertaking of evil deeds, to enemies in the guise of friends, and to those who indulge in sensual enjoyments; || 27 ||

"Among the deceitful, the fraudulent, the difficult to endure, and the difficult to sever"—that is to say, among those who are powerful. "Those who are devoted and attached [to them] go [to hell]"—this is the connection with what follows. || 27 ||
Those fools, whose intellects are dulled by delusion, go from the difficult to the more difficult, from suffering to suffering, from fear to fear, and from one hell to another hell. (28)
From that difficult and perilous situation; those of sluggish intellect are those of dull understanding. || 28 ||

O Rāma, because they are said to destroy one another, one should never remain fixed in the pursuit of worldly welfare within the states of pleasure and pain, which are as fragile as a flash of lightning. (29)

"Suffering follows immediately after happiness, and happiness follows immediately after suffering; revolving without rest like a water-wheel, one goes round and round again and again. Through such statements, since it is said that the states of happiness and suffering mutually destroy one another, this person never abides in the highest good (*śreyas*); thus, he is "one who stands in the highest good" only in name, lacking true repose.
It is so. Furthermore, their transience is well-known even through direct perception; thus he says: "Pleasure and pain," etc. (29).
Know those great-souled men like you, who are dispassionate and perfectly detached, to be worthy of worship— the sole vessels for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
They are well-secluded and truly discerning. || 30 ||
Relying firmly upon discernment through the yoga of dispassion and practice,
one shall cross over this terrible river of worldly existence, which is a source of calamity.
This calamity, which has the form of the river of saṃsāra. || 31 ||
A discerning person who understands this world should not sleep within the illusions of saṃsāra, for they bestow the stupor and delusion of being poisoned. 32.
In those illusions called saṃsāra—which are false means of deception and which have the nature of inducing a swoon and a state of delusion and distress like poison—[he remained]. || 32 ||
He who, having encountered this saṃsāra, remains with indifference, lies upon a bed of straw in a house that is fiercely ablaze. || 33 ||
The genitive case in "tārṇasya" (of the grass-made) is used through a conceptualization of distinction based on its substrate, as in the expression "the head of Rāhu. || 33 ||
That state, reaching which they do not return and attaining which one does not grieve—that state is indeed attainable through wisdom; there is no doubt in this matter. (34)

One might object: "Since there is indeed nothing other than *saṃsāra*, relying on what could one act within *saṃsāra*? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "That which... [is] certainly obtainable through *śemuṣī*—that is, capable of being attained by mere knowledge. It is not non-existent; for if it were non-existent, it would follow that the world is blind, and it is impossible to deny the Self (*ātman*).
This is the state of being. Thus it has been said in the Purāṇas:
"If this Lord of the Mountain were not present, this world would become blind, like the world deprived of light due to the absence of the sun. And there is a Śruti passage:
"He indeed becomes non-existent if he knows Brahman to be non-existent; if he knows that Brahman exists, then they know him as existing. (34)
If that [self] does not exist, what fault would there be for you through such investigation?
If it does exist, then you shall have crossed over the ocean of existence.

"Even when the next world is doubted, it is better to take refuge in the path of the scriptures; for if it did not exist, what would happen to the wretched nihilist?"—according to this maxim, he says "If it does not exist" even to one who is still doubting. The underlying sense is that even in the face of doubt, that which yields great fruit is not fit to be neglected. (35)
When a person's inclination here is toward investigating the means to liberation,
he is said to be one who partakes in liberation. (36)

If one asks, "In that case, why do not all engage [in spiritual practice]?"—anticipating this doubt, [the author] states: "As long as the grace of the Supreme Lord does not arise directly, no one finds a true guru or even a true scripture.

According to this statement, engagement in the means to liberation belongs only to those who possess the qualification for attaining liberation through the grace of the Lord; it does not belong to others.

He says "of all" and explains it as "activity. The meaning is that the fruit of activity—namely, the state of being a partaker in liberation—is to be inferred from the inferential mark (liṅga). || 36 ||
A state of well-being that is unfailing, free from fear, and devoid of delusion does not exist within the three worlds without the attainment of absolute liberation (kevalībhāva). 37.

One might object: "What is the use of this scripture as a cause for attaining the state of absolute isolation (*kevalībhāva*), which is devoid of body, senses, and objects, when even while the body and so forth still exist, happiness such as that of heaven can be achieved through other means? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Infallible" (*anapāyī*). [Heaven and the like] are indeed seized by the instability of the fear of falling back into ruin; therefore, only the state of absolute isolation is [the goal].
The sense is that it is for the sake of the human goal (puruṣārtha). || 37 ||
Upon attaining that, upon attaining the supreme, no affliction arises;
neither riches, nor friends, nor kinsmen are of any help. (38)

The word "tat" (that) refers back to the commencement of the investigation [on the Self], as it is appropriate [to do so]. When that [investigation] is attained—that is, when the attainment of the supreme *kaivalya* (isolation) occurs—no further affliction arises. Now, one might object: "Let the state of isolation (*kevalībhāva*) be achieved through wealth and other such means;
what is the use of investigation? To this, he says: "No" (verse 38).
There is no moving of hands or feet, no traveling to other lands, no exhaustion from bodily mortification, and no resorting to sacred fords or shrines. (39)
The movement of hands and feet occurs in acts such as physical prostration; meeting in another land occurs in journeys and the like;

and through bodily exertion in fasts and similar practices, there is a depletion of strength, enthusiasm, sleep, and so forth. Sacred fords (tīrtha) and shrines (āyatana) are holy sites (kṣetra), and [the term refers to] residing therein. 39.

That state is attained solely through the conquest of that mind alone—a conquest achieved by human effort as the sole means, with the action of subduing the latent impressions as its singular purpose. (40)

By what means, then, is that attained? To this he says: "by the human effort" (*puruṣārtha*). Human effort consists of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption; it is by that which is accomplished solely through such effort. It is by a single object—that is, by a mental impression (*vāsanā*) having the same objective domain—namely, a firm impression in the form of Brahman that is opposed to the latent tendencies toward duality.

The meaning is: by means of the realization that is to be accomplished through action; that is, by means of the victory characterized by the uprooting of duality which consists of the mind alone. As they have said: "Thus, the mental impression (*vāsanā*) 'I am indeed Brahman,' when cultivated without interruption, removes the distractions of ignorance just as an elixir (*rasāyana*) removes diseases. (40)
By abandoning the nets of suffering, this [state] is attained by a man who achieves it through solitude alone and reaches certainty through exclusive inquiry. (41)

Discrimination (*viveka*) is the separation of the Self from the body, senses, and so forth; and inquiry (*vicāra*) is the removal of doubts and misconceptions through hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*). These two enable one to ascertain [the truth] and to renounce the nets of suffering that are the sense objects. (41)
By one seated on a comfortable seat, reflecting upon that for oneself, no grief is felt once that state is attained; indeed, such a person is not born again.
He has attained his station. || 42 ||
The virtuous know that to be the ultimate limit of the essence of all happiness; they call that unsurpassed, motionless state the supreme elixir.

The ultimate limit and supreme culmination of the existence and manifestation of all other insubstantial pleasures—those which are renowned as the essence within *saṃsāra*—or rather, the boundary and cloud-like source of pleasure; for it is said:
"Other beings subsist on only a fraction of this very bliss; that is the pinnacle, that is the supreme goal."
The intention is that this is because of such scriptural passages as these; for from Him arises the unsurpassed, motionless essence of bliss for those who meditate. 43.

Because all states of existence are subject to decay, there is no happiness at all in either heaven or the human realm; it is like water in the case of two people who are already dead and yet still thirsty.
Therefore, the conquest of the mind should be contemplated as the means for achieving tranquility and contentment;
from that, infinite and equal union is attained, and through it, bliss is obtained. (45)
In the infinite, union is equanimity, characterized by a state of uniform harmony. || 45 ||
Whether standing or walking, falling or wandering,
[this applies] to a Rakshasa, a Danava, a Deva, or a human being.
He states that there is neither physical exertion nor the restriction of eligibility to human beings by saying "tiṣṭhata" and so forth.
That supreme bliss which is to be attained arises from the pacification of the mind; it is the fruit of the lofty tree of discernment, which has tranquility as its blossoming flower. (47)
The blossoming tranquility is the flower of that lofty and excellent tree, the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), whose fruit is supreme bliss. || 47 ||
Even while intent on worldly affairs and encountering a multitude of tasks,
he neither abandons nor desires them, remaining like the sun situated in the sky.

Lest it be objected that even what has been attained might be lost again through the recurrence of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*), he says: "Worldly activity... It is not abandoned nor relinquished because, being complete, it is not something to be discarded; for this very reason, it is not even sought after.
The mind is profoundly tranquil, exceedingly clear, resting in peace, and free from delusion.
Free from striving and devoid of longing, he neither desires nor rejects anything. || 49 ||
To the question, "When the mind exists, how could there not be desire?", he says: "The mind... (verse 49).
Listen now to these gatekeepers at the door of liberation in their proper order;
by devotion to even one of them, one enters the door of liberation. (50)

Listen now to the detailed description of those who were previously mentioned [in the eleventh canto, in the passage beginning "The gatekeepers at the door of liberation"], as they are being described in full. 50.
The vast desert expanse of saṃsāra, which bestows both pleasure and suffering and is long-lasting,
becomes cool for a living being through the light equal to that of the moon.

Therein, until the end of the chapter, he begins to introduce tranquility (*śama*) with the words "sukha" and so forth. By the word "sukha," its longing (*āśā*) is indicated. That very longing is like the state of suffering from thirst and heat for a traveler; it is a state of fault that is long-lasting and difficult to overcome.
[The phrase] "it attains coolness through tranquility" is to be supplied. "Equal in radiance" means possessing a brilliance equal to that of the sun.
The transposition of word order is Vedic (chāndasa). It is just as the moon has its own radiance;
this is explicit in the reading "śītaraśmisamaprabhā" (having a luster equal to the cool-rayed one). || 51 ||
Through tranquility, the highest good is attained, for tranquility is the supreme state;
tranquility is auspiciousness, tranquility is peace, and tranquility is the warding off of delusion.

Indeed, because the highest good (*śreya*) is attained through tranquility (*śama*), therefore— by way of metaphorical identification (*amedopacāra*), as in the expression "clarified butter is life" (*āyur ghṛtam*)— that very tranquility is "the supreme state," that is, the "supreme state of Viṣṇu" well-known from the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). Thus, it is not non-existent.

The meaning is that Śiva alone, who is established in the scripture as "Śiva is indeed the non-dual," is tranquility (śama) itself; likewise, the cessation of all suffering, which is established by such scriptural passages as "He who knows the Self crosses over sorrow," is also nothing but tranquility. || 52 ||
For a man who is satisfied by tranquility, whose self is cool and clear,
and whose mind is adorned with peace, even an enemy becomes a friend.
He whose self—the conscious self—is cool because it is not tormented by passion, hatred, and the like, and is exceedingly clear because it is free from delusion. || 53 ||
For those whose inner disposition is adorned by the moon of tranquility,
their supreme purity arises like that of the oceans of milk. (54)

The disposition is the mind. The innate purity attained through knowledge increases, as it were, by doubling itself through tranquility; the meaning is that it is like the whiteness of the milk-ocean at the rising of the moon. || 54 ||
Those virtuous ones in whose hearts the lotus of tranquility has blossomed within the sheath of the heart-lotus are indeed like Hari, possessing two lotus-hearts. 55.

*Kuśeśaya* means a lotus. They are equal to Hari, like Hari himself; the sense is that they have become twofold by serving as the lotuses of Brahma’s seat outside the very heart-lotus of Hari. || 55 ||
Those for whom the beauty of tranquility shines upon their stainless moon-like faces are noble moons, worthy of homage, having conquered their senses through their loveliness. (56)

Those of noble birth are from good families; they alone are "moons" because they are the cause of illuminating their own and others' lineages and of pacifying evil. This is clear in the reading *vijitendavaḥ*. In the alternative reading, however, it means those by whom the eyes, minds, and other senses of others have been conquered—that is, won over—by their beauty and virtues. 56.

The splendors of sovereignty, even those resembling the wealth of universal empire, do not bring such joy to one dwelling within the belly of the three worlds as do the manifestations of tranquility found in the stages of spiritual life (āśramas). 57.
The meaning is that their form alone resembles the glory of universal sovereignty, but not in other qualities.

Whatever sufferings, whatever insatiable cravings, and whatever unbearable anxieties there may be—all of these perish within those whose minds are peaceful, just as darkness vanishes before the sun. (58)

The word "tatsarvam" (all that) is neuter because of the rule *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccāsyānyatarasyām*, which prescribes a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) with a singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*). || 58 ||
For the minds of all beings attain tranquility [the reading *manugacchati* is also found] when [he is present],
not as they do at the sight of the moon, which merely arouses curiosity in peaceful people. (59)
"From the moon," meaning from the moon as the instrumental cause (*nimitta*); the ablative case is used here because the object is intended to be expressed as the cause.
"In which [the mind] has generated curiosity"—that is, in which there is the wonder of experiencing its own nature; the connection is that it attains serenity (*prasāda*) in such a manner. || 59 ||
In a virtuous person who possesses tranquility and friendliness toward all living beings, the supreme reality manifests of its own accord. (60)
"By oneself alone" is a statement regarding the absence of effort. || 60 ||
Just as toward a mother, all beings here place their utmost trust in one who is endowed with tranquility, regardless of whether they are harsh or gentle. (61)
"Uneven" refers to those with cruel and crooked intentions; "soft" refers to those whose dispositions are the opposite of that. || 61 ||
One does not attain such happiness through the drinking of elixirs nor through the embrace of Fortune as one attains when the mind is pacified within.
In the station of Indra, by drinking the elixir of the nectar of immortality; in the station of Viṣṇu, by the embrace of Lakṣmī. || 62 ||
O Rāghava, comfort with the sprinkling of the nectar of tranquility this mind, which is shaken by all manner of mental and physical afflictions and overcome by the threefold wheel of craving.
"Calitaṃ" means shaken by the terrifying [wind]. "Ākrāntam" means pulled here and there by a leather rope (*carma-rajjvā*) consisting of the three excellent qualities;
that is to say, it is exhausted. || 63 ||
Whatever you do and whatever you eat with a mind cooled by tranquility, that alone tastes sweet and delicious, O dear one; nothing else does so in the mind. (64)
Just as it is sweet and delicious, so too does that [object] taste exceedingly sweet and please the mind there. (64)
O Raghava, I believe that even those limbs which have been severed will grow back again by means of that peace and bliss which the mind attains when covered by the nectar-like essence of tranquility.
"Nirvṛti" means happiness. By that nirvṛti, they "grow," meaning they manifest again. "I think" (*manye*) expresses a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*). || 65 ||
Neither piśācas, nor rākṣasas, nor daityas, nor enemies, nor tigers, nor serpents harbor hatred toward one who abides in tranquility. (66)
Arrows do not pierce one whose every limb is well-armored with the nectar-like armor of tranquility, just as they cannot penetrate a diamond-stone.

One whose every limb is well-armored and perfectly protected—[they] pierce and afflict him with armor and mail that take the form of nectar; [they are] sufferings and the causes of suffering. || 67 ||
A king does not shine so much even when staying within his inner apartments as he does with a mind that is equanimous, clear, and characterized by tranquility.
The word "as a person" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 68 ||
A person does not attain such satisfaction upon seeing something dearer than their own life as they do upon beholding one whose disposition is peaceful and who has attained tranquility. (69)
The meaning is that people do not attain such satisfaction; [he refers to one] whose intention (āśaya) is endowed with tranquility (śama). || 69 ||
He who conducts himself well with a conduct that is disciplined, tranquil, and approved by the world, truly lives here; no one else does.
He who lives thus has a life that is fruitful. || 70 ||
Whatever action a virtuous person performs with an undisturbed mind and in tranquility,
all these beings rejoice in it.

He whose mind is neither agitated nor overbearing is virtuous—[the reading "sādhusaṃmataḥ" (esteemed as virtuous) is also found]—and is peaceful, such that even through negligence he commits no offense. || 71 ||
He who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, smelled, or bathed— whether it be auspicious or inauspicious— neither rejoices nor desponds, is called "peaceful. (72)

Now, in order to examine the hypocritical person who possesses the quality of goodness (sāttvika), he describes the characteristics of tranquility, beginning with the words "Having heard" and so forth:
"the auspicious and inauspicious, the pleasant and unpleasant. (72)
He who is equal toward all beings, who desires what is to come and does not abandon it, and who has conquered his senses through effort—he is called "peaceful. (73)
He does not long for future happiness and the like, nor does he reject what is brought about by his past karma (prārabdha). || 73 ||
Having touched upon all things with a pure intellect, wherein actions are seen exactly as they are both internally and externally— he is called "the peaceful one" (śānta).

He states that straightforwardness (*ārjava*) is also a characteristic of that [right conduct], saying "having touched," etc. The ellipsis is "even having touched—that is, having known—the crookedness and other such traits of others. These are actions to be performed as means for liberation (*mokṣa*). || 74 ||
He whose mind is undisturbed, shining like the orb of the moon, is said to be "peaceful" even in the midst of death, festivals, or battle. (75)

In battles that are like festivals of death, he remains undisturbed by fear, passion, or anger, and thus untormented; for this very reason, he possesses a splendor resembling the orb of the moon, the maker of frost.
Even when standing, he is as if not standing; he neither rejoices nor becomes angry.
He who is established in his own nature, like one in deep sleep, is said to be "peaceful. (76)
Even though situated in a place characterized by the causes of joy and anger. || 76 ||
He whose gaze, lovely with the flow of nectar, extends toward all people with affection, is called "peaceful. (77)
Like a stream of nectar, a flow of immortality, she is auspicious and a bestower of happiness. || 77 ||
He who has attained inner coolness, who does not sink into worldly objects, and who engages in worldly affairs without being deluded— he is called "peaceful. (78)
Even while engaged in worldly activity among existing things and sense-objects, he does not sink, nor does he become attached. || 78 ||
Even amidst endless calamities or even at the great dissolution of the eons, he whose mind does not dwell upon the trivial is said to be "peaceful. (79)
[The mind] is not fixed upon the great, long-lasting [objects], nor upon the trivial, false, and perishable things such as the body and so forth, for whom there is no thought of "I. || 79 ||
That man engaged in worldly affairs whose mind incurs no stain, being like the sky, is said to be "peaceful. (80)
She is of one flavor (*samarasā*) with the Supreme Space (*paramākāśa*), which is Brahman; she is immutable like the well-known ether (*prasiddhākāśa*).
"Stain" (*kalaṅka*) refers to the taint of passion (*rāga*) and the like. || 80 ||
Among ascetics, the learned, sacrificial priests, and kings—among those who are powerful and rich in virtues—it is only the man of tranquility who truly shines. (81)
He says, "Among ascetics... (verse 81), because in the world as well, tranquility is renowned for its preeminence among all virtues.
For the great ones who possess virtuous qualities and whose minds are absorbed in tranquility,
bliss arises from the heart like moonlight from the white-rayed moon.
The boundary of all multitudes of virtues,
the exclusive ornament of manliness—
tranquility shines forth with splendor in times of distress and in places of fear. (83)

The limit—the boundary or end—of multitudes, that is, collections, of virtues; the sole ornament, the primary adornment; the illustrious one, possessed of the perfection of all virtues: tranquility shines forth. (83)
Having relied upon that supreme state— tranquil, immortal, unassailable, and guarded by the Noble Ones— those of great majesty have departed for the highest goal, just like the sons of Raghu.
Maintain that very sequence for the sake of accomplishment. || 84 ||

"Unassailable," meaning incapable of being taken away by others; "guarded by the noble ones," meaning protected with vigilance; having relied upon this supreme and most excellent means, the high-souled ones have reached the highest state in such a manner—maintain that very sequence, meaning you should rely upon it and preserve it. (84)

Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "The Description of Tranquility," in the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* tradition. 13.
Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "The Description of Tranquility," in the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Fourteenth Canto.
14. Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: With a mind that is supremely pure and stainless through the understanding of the scriptures, [one attains this state].
One who knows the causes should constantly engage in self-examination. || 1 ||
In this context, inquiry—strengthened by association with the virtuous, the study of authentic scriptures, and purity of disposition—is praised as the cause of tranquility and contentment. (1)

Having thus described the first gatekeeper of liberation named Peace (Śama), Vasiṣṭha, wishing to describe the second, Discernment (Vicāra), said: "The scripture," and so forth. Therein [are included] the investigation into what is beneficial and what is harmful, the investigation into the essential and the non-essential, the investigation into what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, the investigation into the authority and intent of the texts, and the examination of the true nature of the Self.

And thus, reflection (*vicāra*) is fivefold. Among these, the first consists of an investigation through methods such as positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), [determining] that natural inclinations and sense-objects are connected with harm, whereas scriptural inclinations and dispassion (*vairāgya*) and so forth are connected with the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).

The first consists of the investigation into the impurity and inauspiciousness— such as feces, urine, and so forth— of one's wife, children, and one's own body, based on their inherent nature (*svataḥ*), their seed-cause (*bījataḥ*), and their transformation (*pariṇāmataḥ*);
and the second consists of the investigation into the impermanence and the fact that pleasures up to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) are permeated by suffering.

These two—detachment and the desire for liberation—are the causes [of inquiry]. Furthermore, regarding whether the means to liberation subsequent to the desire for liberation is ritual action (*karman*) or indeed meditation (*upāsana*), and whether those two are to be combined (*samuccita*), or combined with knowledge (*jñāna*), or whether it is knowledge alone:
this is the third [section], consisting of an investigation. Even when it is knowledge alone, what then is that?

The fourth [section] consists of an investigation into whether that which is accepted by the Sāṃkhyas, Vaiśeṣikas, and others— being based on the authority of their respective scriptures taught by Kapila and Gautama, or being indeed Vedic— even when it is Vedic, has its purport in duality or non-duality, in the qualified or the unqualified Self, or in the non-Self. And that [investigation is as follows]:

This is called "hearing" (śravaṇa). Even when one has ascertained through means of valid knowledge such as scripture that the non-dual Self— which is Being, Consciousness, and Bliss— is Brahman, one must still investigate, according to the analogy of testing a gem, whether or not that state actually exists within one's own self in reality, by consulting with a teacher and fellow students who are established in direct experience.

And the fifth [limb], consisting of critical examination (*parīkṣā*), is that which continues until the final ascertainment through the purification of the principles of the individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśvara*), and the world (*jagat*). Among these, the fruit of the first three is the attainment of the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*);
whereas for the last two, it is respectively the removal of doubt regarding the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*). Now, although the first [of these]...

Although these may arise by themselves through the power of fortune, they must nevertheless be performed again, preceded by the Guru and the scriptures, in order to strengthen one's own conviction. As for the last two, however, they arise only through the Guru and the scriptures;
thus it is said that [the practice] is to be done with an intellect purified by the understanding of the scriptures, which is common to all. This is stated by one who knows the cause.

Alternatively, the meaning is: "together with a teacher who possesses knowledge of the distinctions between the subject matter (*viṣaya*), the doubt (*saṃśaya* or *viśaya*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), and the purpose (*prayojana*), and who is skilled in the means for demonstrating the reality of the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of cognition (*prameya*). In this context, he demonstrates the utility of even mental purity (*cittaśuddhi*) by saying: "by one who is supremely pure. || 1 ||
Having attained sharpness through reflection, the intellect perceives the supreme state;
for reflection is indeed the great medicine for the long-standing disease of saṃsāra. (2)
Sharpness, which is skill in penetrating subtle reality. || 2 ||
The forest of calamities, whose form is made to sprout by endless striving,
does not grow again once it has been cut down by the saw of discernment.

The forest is so called because it is difficult to cross due to its calamities. Its form and configuration have grown through passion and other afflictions, as if overspread on all sides by endless strivings and activities. A *krakaca* is a saw for splitting wood. || 3 ||
O one of great wisdom, everything is pervaded by delusion during the loss of kinsmen, in times of distress, and in states of confusion; for indeed, discernment is the refuge of the virtuous.

In situations of suffering such as the loss of kinsmen, whatever is appropriate to be done and by whatever means there may be the overcoming of suffering and the stabilization of the mind—all that is pervaded by delusion and mental distraction, and thus does not manifest; the meaning is that in such cases, inquiry alone is the path and the cause for reconnecting with that [proper course]. || 4 ||
(107) For the wise, there is no means other than inquiry.
By means of inquiry, the minds of the virtuous abandon the inauspicious and attain the auspicious. (5)
He says that very thing: "No," [verse 5].
Strength, intellect, vigor, discernment, and the fruit of action—
all these bear fruit for the wise solely through investigation.

*Tejas* is power (*sāmarthya*). *Pratipatti* is the manifestation appropriate to each respective occasion. *Kriyā* is the performance of that [manifestation] and its fruit. They "bear fruit" (*phalanti*), meaning they are accomplished or become fruitful.
Relying on expansive inquiry, which is a great lamp for what is appropriate and inappropriate and an achiever of one's desires, one may cross the ocean of saṃsāra.
What is logical and appropriate is to be adopted; what is illogical and inappropriate is to be rejected. This [work] is a great lamp for illuminating those two—vast and not meager.
The lion known as inquiry, being a pure self, tears apart the great elephants of delusion whose lotus-hearts have been mangled.
Those by whom the lotuses of discernment situated in the heart have been torn up—those whose pure self is free from defects such as verbal quibbles, fallacies, and futile rejoinders. (8)
That even the deluded, by the power of time, have reached the supreme state in this world is the unsurpassed manifestation of the lamp of inquiry. (9)
The deluded are those who are utterly confused regarding the path and the means of crossing;
such a manifestation is the fruit of illuminating that very path.
Kingdoms, vast prosperity, enjoyment, and eternal liberation— O Rāghava, these are the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree of inquiry.
Those thoughts of the great ones here which expand through solitude do not sink in adversity, like gourds upon the water. (11)
In this context, "discernment" (viveka) means inquiry; those intellects which expand by means of it do not sink, nor do they despair. "Gourd-bowls" refers to dried bottle-gourds. || 11 ||
Those who conduct themselves with an intellect that brings about the arising of discernment indeed become the recipients of most exalted fruits. (12)
Those who conduct themselves with an intellect possessed of discernment, which brings about the arising of discrimination—[they are] among the noble and the excellent.
The clusters of blossoms upon the karañja trees of non-investigation—those which dwell in the forest of the fool’s heart and which first obstruct hope—are the very ways of suffering. (13)

The very heart-mind of fools is their forest; for those dwelling therein, whose nature it is to obstruct the hope for the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*) and the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*), they first block them. [This refers to] *karañja* trees, which are *kuberākṣa* creepers. In that context, "hope" (*āśā*) means the directions (*diś*). For these [creepers], by way of forming a fence, indeed block the directions.

The flower-clusters and the clusters of fruit-caskets are merely the ostentation of the conventional usage of "suffering," for they are well known to be thorny and to contain bitter fruits within. || 13 ||
O Rāghava, may that sleep—stained like powdered collyrium, possessing the nature of intoxication from wine, and consisting of a lack of discernment—come to an end for you. 14.
Like dust or powder, it is soiled; like the nature of intoxication from wine, it possesses such things as delusion and stumbling.
The ellipsis is that "it should go to destruction through discernment. 14.
A man devoted to right reflection does not sink into delusions, even when they are as vast as the great ocean; he is like a mass of light amidst darkness.
In those delusions—which are both great calamities and exceedingly long-lasting—[there is] the mass of splendor, the sun. || 15 ||
He in whose clear mental lake the multitude of lotuses that are reflection has surely blossomed shines like the Himalaya. (16)
The mind itself is the lake; it is the very same Mānasa lake renowned in the interior of the Himalayas, for it is like the Himalaya in its qualities such as coolness, loftiness, and stability. (16)
For one whose intellect has become dull due to a lack of discernment, a thunderbolt arises from the moon like a phantom Yakṣa appearing before a child. (17)

Sluggishness is stupidity. When the mind—which is presided over by the deity Candra and is thus fit for the illumination of discernment like the moon—is capable of manifesting knowledge and happiness similar to moonlight, it is only fitting that such a state arise;
therefore, for that fool in whom sorrow, suffering, and the like emerge, even a thunderbolt or lightning bolt issues forth from the moon itself, as is the case with a young child.
In the same way, from ignorance and so forth, the yakṣa—the previously mentioned vetāla—arises.
O Rāma, that lowest of men who lacks discernment must be abandoned from afar; he is a fragment of suffering, unsubstantial, and a springtime for the creepers of ruined fortune. 18.

The man devoid of discernment is the lowest of men, fashioned like a pit of earth for the incessant sowing of the seeds of suffering; for there exists no such thing as "gross" [in comparison to him], meaning he is exceedingly gross.
He is the springtime for the sweet creepers of the distorted perceptions (*viparyāsa*), meaning he is the cause of their blossoming. (18)
Whatever undertakings are ill-conceived, whatever conducts are wicked, and whatever anxieties are base—they all appear without scrutiny like ghosts in the darkness. (19)
"Bad undertakings" are actions conducive to the suffering of oneself and others; "bad conduct" refers to the performance of prohibited acts; these "shine forth," that is, they manifest. || 19 ||
O scion of the Raghus, keep far away from him who lacks discernment, who is like a solitary tree in the forest, and who is incapable of performing virtuous deeds.

Entirely and invariably possessing qualities identical to those of forest trees; or, existing in a secluded place frequented by humans, sharing the same nature as a forest tree. For this very reason, [he is] among the virtuous—those who provide shelter in the shade and perform other such services for travelers—and in matters conducive to the human goals (puruṣārtha).
Or "vākṣama" means incapable or incompetent. || 20 ||
For when the mind of a living being is secluded and freed from the helplessness of desire,
it attains supreme bliss within itself, like the full moon.
It is secluded and accompanied by reflection; it is free from the helplessness and subjection to others caused by desire; it is blissful tranquility and the happiness of rest. || 21 ||
Discernment, once arisen within the body, thoroughly cools everything and adorns it exceedingly,
just as moonlight does the world.
It is like moonlight, the lunar radiance; just as that cools all people afflicted by heat and fully satisfies those afflicted by thirst, so too does it [cool and satisfy]. || 22 ||
For a living being, discernment shines like the moon in the night—the white fly-whisk of the intellect that bears the banner of ultimate truth. (23)
For a person who possesses a birth of authority,

the investigation of the relationship with pure intellect (*śuddhabuddhi*)— which indicates the attainment of the state of a king characterized by the supreme human goal (*paramārtha*)— is like a unique white chowrie (*dhavalacāmara*), serving as a banner (*patākā*).

The royal insignia shines. The decorated banners and yak-tail whisks are compared to the night and the moon; therein, the night functions as the object of comparison through grammatical coordination with a different locus [vaiyadhikaraṇya]. || 23 ||
Living beings who move with the grace of discernment, illuminating the ten directions like the sun, truly shine forth as further removers of the fear of worldly existence. (24)

Through inquiry alone, living beings gradually become disciplined and, having attained the state of being liberated while living, they shine like the sun, dispelling the darkness characterized by the fear of worldly existence for the majority of creatures by means of the light of their inquiry. (24)
The life-taking vetāla, imagined by the delusion of a fool’s own mind in the night sky, dissolves through investigation. (25)
"Is it not observed that fear ceases through inquiry? To this he replies: 'Of the child...
Thus, just as a Vetāla imagined for the purpose of preventing a child from going outside at night dissolves, so too does the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) dissolve. || 25 ||
All worldly phenomena are beautiful only so long as they are not investigated;
their true existence is non-existent, for they fall apart under scrutiny. (26)

Granted that this may be so there [in that example], one might ask: how is fear removed in the present case? Anticipating this, he says "all indeed" (*sarva eva*), because the world—the cause of fear—is determined to be false through investigation. "Charming" (*cāravaḥ*) means beautiful like the truth;
"fragile" (*viśarāravaḥ*) means having the nature of crumbling away like a clod of earth dashed against a stone; and "insubstantial" (*asārāḥ*) means being unreal (*mithyā*).
Up to [verse] 26.
The long-standing vampire of saṃsāra, imagined by a man’s own deluded mind and bestowing manifold suffering, dissolves through inquiry. (27)
He clarifies what has already been stated with the words "of the person" (puṃsaḥ) || 27 ||
Know this state of absolute perfection (kevalībhāva) to be equanimous happiness— free from affliction, infinite, and independent— the fruit of the tree of higher discernment. (28)

It is not merely the cessation of fear, but the attainment of unsurpassed bliss as well that is its fruit; thus he says: "Equal" (sama). Equal means devoid of the world's diversity. Unsupported means not dependent on anything else.
Kevalībhāvam means the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya). || 28 ||
Through its unwavering stability, its magnificence, and its manifest expansive splendor,
it arises from that state of desirelessness, like coolness produced by the moon.

He wards off the fear of its interruption by saying "unwavering" (*acala*). By that inquiry, through the brilliance—that is, the power—of the manifest expansion of unsurpassed bliss, ignorance, which is the cause of wavering, is destroyed; and thus, by virtue of its unwavering state, there arises a noble desirelessness characterized by the fullness of bliss. || 29 ||
By means of that great medicine of self-investigation, which is well-established within the mind and bestows excellence,
the virtuous person neither desires nor rejects anything.

The state of immovable stability itself is the highest excellence; by means of that aforementioned great medicine characterized by inquiry, the perfected person does not desire what has not been attained, nor does he relinquish what has been attained. The meaning is that he becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done. || 30 ||
The mind, having taken that state as its support, becomes expansive and luminous;
it neither sets nor rises, like the sky, having reached an exceedingly vast interior.
(31) Now, if the mind were to perish through the knowledge born of inquiry, then living would be impossible; if it does not...
Anticipating the objection that "if it were to perish, one would have to produce distraction once again; how, then, could the goal be accomplished?", he says:
"In the same way, the mind, having attained the state of appearance, reaches the internal nature of Brahman—which is like the sky, all-pervading and exceedingly vast."

The meaning is: that [mind] whose web of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—the seeds of distraction—does not set, that is, does not undergo destruction (for if it were destroyed, there would be no life), nor does it arise through mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*) such as attachment and aversion (for if it did, there would be distraction). Alternatively, the mind does not arise as a mere appearance, like a parched seed, which would lead to distraction; rather, it has expanded through beginningless latent impressions.
It does not undergo destruction due to the power of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of objects, being firmly established. || 31 ||
It neither gives nor takes, it neither rises nor subsides;
it remains merely as a witness, observing the world as it unfolds.

Why is that? Because he perceives the objects of the world merely with indifference, like a witness; thus, he does not apply his mind to them through passion, nor does he grasp or enjoy them as being real or as being the means to human goals.
He neither finds peace, nor does he abide within, nor does he abide without.
He does not cling to inaction, nor does he sink into action. || 33 ||

It does not become extinguished through the cessation of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) as in deep sleep; nor does it sink into that which consists of internal latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as in a dream;
nor does it remain dissolved in the external world as in the waking state of the deluded. || 33 ||
He remains indifferent toward what has passed and follows after what has arrived;
neither agitated nor unagitated, he shines like the full ocean.

In the case of the ocean, it neglects the objects such as Lakṣmī and the Kaustubha gem that have entered it and does not strive to obtain them. "Agitated" (kṣubdha) means being in a state of turmoil to the extent of overstepping its boundaries; "unagitated" (akṣubdha) means calm, which is to say, abandoning its natural course of conduct. The word "ca" (and) serves to conjoin the absence of results such as agitation. || 34 ||
Thus, with minds full [of contentment], these great-souled ones of noble disposition—yogins liberated while living—wander here in this world. (35)
Those who possess this yoga—which consists of the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman—experienced right here in this very body. || 35 ||
Having dwelt for a very long time, as long as they desired,
those wise ones finally abandon that [state] and proceed to the pervasive state of absolute oneness.
That which appears as the teacher is that very state—unlimited, absolute, and the liberation from the body (videhakaivalya). || 36 ||
Even in times of calamity, a wise person should diligently reflect with their own mind: "Who am I, and whose is this saṃsāra?"—and thus provide for themselves a remedy.

"Even in adversity," that is, even while occupied with family duties and the like; "with a remedy," meaning in such a way as to include the performance of hearing about and applying that remedy; "by oneself," by one's own self alone. || 37 ||
O Raghava, a king understands the doubt regarding the difficulty of a task—whether it will be fruitless or fruitful—only through deliberation, and not otherwise. (38)

That which must necessarily be done is the "kārya"; in times of crisis and financial distress, one hesitates—this hesitation is "saṃdeha," consisting of deliberations such as peace or war—and he knows that, meaning he determines it. || 38 ||
The established tenets of the Vedas and Vedānta, which are the cause of stability, are determined through inquiry, just as the features of the earth are discerned at night by means of a lamp. (39)

The established conclusions (*siddhāntasthitayaḥ*) of the ritual sections (*karmakāṇḍa*) and the Vedānta of the Vedas— characterized by the principles of *dharma* and *brahman* and serving as the ultimate resting points of their intended meaning—
are the cause, that is to say, the means of attaining, for the stability of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). And [the phrase] "by means of a lamp" refers to two things that are indeed equal.
[The reading is "samuccayaḥ" in the rule "tulyayoge samuccayaḥ"]. From the general rule that "samuccaya" [denotes conjunction], similarity is understood. || 39 ||
In the darkness, it is not lost; amidst many splendors, its own brilliance is not eclipsed—this is the reading favored by the commentator.
Even when obstructed, discernment, like an eye of exquisite beauty, perceives.

The meaning is that while the ordinary eye is as if lost in darkness, or is blunted and obstructed among the many splendors of the sun and other luminaries, and is incapable of perceiving what is hidden or distant, the eye characterized by discernment (*vicāra*) is not like that.
Indeed, one who is blind to discernment is like one born blind; such a person of evil intellect is an object of pity for all.
But he whose soul is endowed with discernment possesses divine vision and triumphs over all things. (41)

That person for whom discernment and reflection are as dear as the self, or who regards them as primary, conquers—that is, overcomes—calamities, destroys them, or attains the goals of human endeavor; such a person possesses divine vision. || 41 ||
Consisting of the Supreme Self, venerable, and the sole achiever of great bliss—
this wondrous power of discernment must not be abandoned for even a single moment. (42)

He speaks of that which is the essence even among these reflections, saying "the Supreme Self. The suffix *mayaṭ* is used here to indicate being predominantly composed of that through intense attachment, as in the expression "a fool who is full of women" (*strīmayo jālmaḥ*). Even for a moment, even for an instant. This is based on the Śruti: "He who makes even a slight distinction [between the Self and the world], then fear comes upon him. That is the loss; that is the great flaw; that is blindness.
And there is also deaf-muteness; for the meaning is that it is stated in the *Laiṅga-purāṇa*: "If for even a single moment or a single muhūrta one does not contemplate Śiva alone... (42).
A person who is beautiful in discernment is pleasing even to the great, just as a mango fruit that has reached full maturity is delightful.
The word "api" (even) is used for the purpose of indicating: "If this is so even for the great ones who have realized the truth, how much more so for those who merely desire to know it!
It refers to the fruit of the *sahakāra* mango tree, in which there is a "paripakva"—that is, fully matured—*camatkāra*, an excellence of sweetness produced by its ripening. || 43 ||
Men whose minds delight in reflection, who have repeatedly learned the ways of travelers, do not tumble again and again into the abysses of suffering. (44)
By those for whom the path of experience has been known through investigation alone,
even the account of the worldly traveler is understood through this concise expression.
Neither does a sick man nor one shattered by hundreds of misfortunes cry out as the ignorant man, whose soul is ruined by a lack of discernment, wails. (45)

Though his limbs are worn out and loosened by hundreds of calamities such as poison, weapons, and diseases, he does not cry out as much as that ignorant person who, having been ruined and nearly destroyed by a lack of discernment, weeps all around throughout the succession of births. || 45 ||
Better is the state of being mud, better is the condition of a worm in filth, and better is dwelling in a blind cave than the lack of reflection in a human being. (46)
One should abandon that which is the natural abode of all misfortune, despised by all the virtuous, the ultimate limit of all instability, and devoid of reflection.
A great-souled person must always be engaged in inquiry;
for those falling into a blind well, inquiry is indeed the support. 48.
For it is well known: that which blinds is "blind"; such a well—namely passion and the like—is described here as being identical to its fruit.
Having itself seized hold of itself through inquiry, one may cause the deer of one's own mind to cross over the ocean of delusion that is saṃsāra. (49)
Having seized it by force and stabilized it, even though it is being dragged away by the current of passion and other afflictions. || 49 ||
"Who am I? How has this defect called saṃsāra come upon me?"—such an inquiry into the underlying principle is called *vicāra* (investigation). (50)

He demonstrates the very nature of inquiry with the words "Who am I? The inquiry into the meaning of the term *tvaṃ* (you) is: "Is 'I' merely the body and so forth, or am I distinct from them? The inquiry into the meaning of the term *tat* (that) is: "How and by what cause has transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) come upon the substrate? [This is] by means of the reasoning shown by the Śruti, the sages, and the traditional teachers. || 50 ||
The heart of the evil-minded and thoughtless man has long been made like a stone—blinded by blinding delusion, utterly dense, and leading only to suffering. (51)

The heart and mind—the internal constituent—of a stone and of a wicked person are created by the Creator for the sake of suffering and pain, and for the sake of a "bad hole" (duṣṭakhāya), that is, a mere cavity, because they are produced through the hardship of being cut by chisels and the like. The meaning is that they have no utility other than this. The attainment of similarity is as explained previously.

For that [mind] is even more blind than a blind man who lacks sight, being exceedingly dense with delusion (*moha*). Indeed, a blind man falls into a well because he does not see; but the mind, even though it sees, falls even into the hells due to delusion.
In the sense of having a heart like stone, it is even more blind than a blind man due to its insentience (*jaḍatva*), and it is even denser than delusion.

The meaning is "because of its hardness. Alternatively, it is a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) that the heart of a man who is evil-minded and lacking in discernment is made from stone; for it is blind after blind, densely thick with delusion. Therefore, the sense is that such a heart leads only to suffering for a long time. || 51 ||
For here, O Rāghava, regarding those who hold views of grasping at existence and non-existence or of rejecting them, no reality whatsoever is properly known except through inquiry. 52.

Existence (*bhāva*) is that which is real; its grasping is appropriation (*upādāna*). Non-existence (*abhāva*) is that which is unreal; its relinquishing is renunciation (*tyāga*). For those who perceive these two correctly on this plane of worldly convention, the truth is not known properly without investigation;
from investigation, the truth is known, and from the truth comes rest in the Self.
Therefore, tranquility of mind is the complete destruction of all suffering. || 53 ||

Reality is the permanence of the object; from the knowledge of reality comes repose, which is the immobility of the mind. From this repose comes peace itself, which is the complete destruction of all suffering. || 53 ||
When examined with the eye of clear discernment, action indeed bears fruit upon this earth and attains its highest manifestation.
May it shine for you, who possess tranquility and existence. || 54 ||

He summarizes what was stated at length by saying, "saphalatām" (the state of being fruitful). For every person brings about (*phalate*), through the very vision of clear inquiry, the fruitfulness— that is, the accomplishment— of both worldly and Vedic actions, [leading] to the supreme, progressively ascending state of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) which will be described as the seventh stage (*bhūmikā*).

And it becomes manifest; that is, it is attained. Therefore, may such an investigated [truth] be pleasing to you, who possess the perfection of the means such as tranquility (śama) and so forth. In the phrase "it goes to the highest" (*gacchaty uttamām*), there is no sandhi because the application of sandhi in a sentence is not mandatory. 54.
Thus ends the fourteenth canto, titled "The Description of Inquiry," in the Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the Ṛṣi tradition.
Thus ends the fourteenth canto, titled "The Exposition of Inquiry," in the Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa.
Fifteenth Canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Contentment is indeed the supreme good; contentment is called happiness.
O destroyer of enemies, one who is content attains supreme rest.
Like the shade of the wish-fulfilling tree of dispassion, cool with happiness, the third gatekeeper here is described as contentment. (1)
He describes Saṃtoṣa, the third gatekeeper who follows in sequence, with the words beginning "Saṃtoṣa" and so forth.
Saṃtoṣa, whose characteristics will be described hereafter, is indeed the supreme good (*paraṃ śreyaḥ*), which is liberation (*mokṣaḥ*); it is also happiness (*sukham*).
This is a praise by superimposing the identity of the fruit upon the means, as in the expression "clarified butter is life."
Rest is the cessation of the distraction of ultimate suffering. || 1 ||
For those who are happy in the sovereignty of contentment, whose minds have long found rest,
and who are peaceful, even a universal empire is like a blade of withered grass. (2)

O Rāma, the intellect characterized by contentment becomes despicable amidst the activities of worldly existence; it acts like a mere fragment— a tiny bit— of withered, decayed grass, for its mind has long been rested and consoled by the sovereignty and power of happiness.
Even in adverse circumstances, he is never agitated, nor does he ever fall away from his state. || 3 ||

Even when circumstances in the world become adverse—meaning uneven, characterized by poverty, separation, and the like—if they occur through the power of fate, the intellect endowed with contentment does not decline; that is to say, one is not deprived of happiness. || 3 ||
For those who have attained peace and satisfaction by drinking the nectar of contentment, this incomparable splendor of enjoyments acts like a potent poison.
It behaves like an adverse poison; that is to say, it appears as such. || 4 ||
Neither do these waves of nectar’s essence bring such happiness as does contentment,
which possesses an exceedingly sweet taste and destroys all faults.
That which has an exceedingly sweet experience and relish, abundant with bliss, and which destroys defects such as the wretchedness of hope. || 5 ||

Having abandoned the desire for what has not been attained and having reached equanimity toward what has been attained, he who is free from distress regarding the unseen is called "contented" in this world. (6)

He characterizes contentment by its defining characteristic, [saying]: "When not obtained... Even when an object is obtained, because it is unreal, one has attained equality with what was not obtained, or equality with one's previous state, due to the absence of joy and other emotions caused by that acquisition. He states the reason for this: "Because it is unseen... (6).
As long as the mind does not attain contentment within itself by means of the Self,
calamities continue to arise like creepers from the hollow of the heart.
By itself, by its own nature, and not by another cause; in itself alone, and not in another object. || 7 ||
The mind, cooled by contentment, attains full blossoming through the vision of pure wisdom,
just as a lotus does under the rays of the sun.
In the case of the lotus, it was thoroughly refreshed and cooled by that water which brings complete satisfaction and quenches thirst. || 8 ||
In a mind that is helpless under the sway of desire and devoid of contentment,
knowledge does not reflect, just as it does not appear on a mirror obscured by a withered face.

"Vaivaśyam" means lack of self-control or dependence on others; therefore, in one who is helpless and agitated, [the truth] does not manifest—just as a face is not reflected in a faded mirror—even though it has been taught. This is the meaning. || 9 ||
The lotus of man does not undergo contraction through the night of dense ignorance for him,
in whom the sun of perpetual contentment has forever risen.
That lotus of a man for whose blossoming this previously mentioned sun of contentment has arisen does not undergo contraction due to the night of dense darkness characterized by ignorance.
Even though he possesses nothing, that person enjoys the happiness of sovereignty,
provided his mind is contented and free from mental and physical afflictions.
He who does not desire what has not been attained, eats in due order, and whose conduct is very gentle, is said to be "contented. (12)
Having restated the previously mentioned definition, he states another definition as well, beginning with "Not...

[na iti]. This refers to pleasure and pain as they occur in their respective order. He is gentle (*saumya*), the delighter of the world (*jagadānandana*), and one whose conduct (*ācāra*) or practice is perfect (*samyak*). || 12 ||
In the mouth of that great one who is devoted to contentment, fully satisfied, and whose mind is complete—
pure like the ocean of milk— the Goddess of Fortune shines resplendent.
He states that a specific luster of the face is also a characteristic of that [state], saying: "Contentment," etc. (verse 13).
Relying upon the stainless fullness within one's own self,
by means of one's own personal effort, one should abandon craving for everything.
Having resorted to and supported by experience the fullness within one's own self, which is of the nature of unsurpassed bliss. || 14 ||
For one who is filled with the nectar of contentment and possesses a mind that is peaceful and cool,
the mind itself attains eternal stability, like the moon.

For a person filled with the nectar characterized by contentment—like the moon—the intellect becomes peaceful and cool due to the absence of the causes for the torment of anger; through that intellect acting as the instrumental cause, the mind attains eternal stability. || 15 ||
With minds nourished by contentment, those of great prosperity attend upon him like servants,
having entered into a state of servitude.
To the question of how the maintenance of the body can be accomplished through mere contentment alone, without the acquisition of objects, he says:
"Contentment... Great riches and prosperities attend upon him, just as servants attend upon a king.
And so they say: "Those who are slaves to hope are slaves to the whole world; but those for whom hope is a slave..."
The world serves as their slave. Thus [it is said]. 16.
When a person remains established in themselves, self-abiding and content within their own self,
all mental afflictions are quickly pacified, like dust in the rainy season.
"Granted that the maintenance of the body may be thus, yet mental suffering, like that of the gods, is difficult to cure.
To this he replies: "By oneself alone," etc. "Pāṃśavas" means dust particles. As it is said: "The *tāla*, *tryā*, *dantī*, *śamba*, *śūkara*, and *pāṃśu* [are types of medicinal plants]. (17)
O Rāma, by means of a conduct that is eternally cool, stainless,
and pure, a person shines with fullness like the moon.

Nevertheless, since suffering would indeed arise from the seed of suffering— the veil of the stain of causality— he says "eternal" (nityam) in response to that. Just as on the new moon day (amā), the moon,
because it cannot be distinguished from the stain due to its waning, appears as if submerged in the stain.

And due to the proximity of the sun, it does not function with a cool mode of being; yet on the full moon day, because its digits are complete and because it illuminates even the spot, it shines with a pure mode of being distinct from that [spot]. In the same way, the Puruṣa also—when submerged as if in the stain of delusion through lack of contentment—becomes as if scorched by the threefold suffering.

The meaning is that he shines by means of a mental state (vṛtti) that is cooled by the bliss of one's own self and untouched by that [ignorance], because it is the witness of the stain of ignorance, being filled with a digit of the nectar of contentment. || 18 ||
The world finds such satisfaction in beholding a man’s face, beautiful in its symmetry, as it does not find through the accumulation of wealth. (19)
Equanimity is the state of mind free from partiality due to contentment with everything. || 19 ||
The sky-dwellers bow down to that stainless one, the king among men, who is here adorned by his equanimity, his wisdom, and his possession of virtuous qualities.
Even the great sages [do not know this], O descendant of Raghu.
He states his supreme excellence with the words "by equanimity": even the sky-dwelling gods and the great sages bow down and pay him homage. || 20 ||

Thus ends the fifteenth canto, titled "The Description of Contentment," in the Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the Ṛṣi tradition.
Thus ends the fifteenth canto, titled "The Description of Contentment," in the Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa of the Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa.
(111) The Sixteenth Chapter: A further [instruction],
O one of great intelligence, for the crossing over of the cycle of existence by men.
Everywhere in this world, the company of the virtuous brings benefit to the good.
Now the fourth gatekeeper is described here: association with the virtuous.
Even the service of each one among these four bears fruit as a human goal; indeed, even [the practice of] each one alone results in the attainment of the goals of human life. (1)

Describing the meeting with the virtuous as the fourth gatekeeper, and demonstrating that human effort reaches its fulfillment in each of the four goals of human life (puruṣārtha), Vasiṣṭha said: "In particular," etc.;
"everywhere" means in all circumstances. || 1 ||
Those great-souled ones who protect the white flower of discernment, born from the tree of association with the virtuous, are the vessels for the glory of its fruit.
They become vessels for the glory of the fruit—that is, for the perfection of the fruit of liberation; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 2 ||
An empty place becomes crowded; even death turns into a festival;
and misfortune appears like prosperity upon meeting with wise men. (3)
"Empty" means devoid of kinsmen, wealth, and so forth; "a place of suffering" means being crowded with or pervaded by them. (3)
The cool breeze that dispels the mist of delusion for the lotus-pond of the mind—victorious in this world is the singular excellence of association with the virtuous. (4)
The frost, that is, the hoarfrost, [is the enemy] of the lotus-plant, characterized by water; [the word] "sādhu" means excellent. || 4 ||

Know that association with the virtuous is the supreme nourishment for the intellect, the felling of the tree of ignorance [or, according to another reading, the destruction of the fever of ignorance], and the complete removal of mental anxieties. (5)
The specific increase of the intellect’s discriminative knowledge; its attenuation, which brings about dissolution. || 5 ||
From association with the virtuous, the supreme lamp of discernment arises—truly as radiant and captivating as a cluster of blossoms after being watered. (6)

It is captivating, radiant, and stainless. Through the watering of the garden, the cluster—namely the cluster of flowers and fruits—bestows unsurpassed, eternal, and ever-abundant bliss that is free from misfortune and free from affliction; such are the blessings of association with the virtuous. (7)

Whether it be described as eternally abundant, ever-increasing, or eternally unbounded— this association with the virtuous must not be abandoned even in the slightest by men who have attained a state of extreme suffering and have fallen into helplessness, for it is the very source of peace and happiness. (8)
"Manāk" means even slightly; that is to say, for even a moment. || 8 ||
In this world, associations with the virtuous are the illuminators of the true path;
they are the rays of the sun of knowledge that dispel the darkness within the heart.
It is a lamp for the true path and right conduct as long as the night of ignorance persists;
but after that time, it is the radiance and light of the sun in the form of knowledge. || 9 ||

For one who has bathed in the cool, white Gaṅgā of association with the virtuous, what need is there for gifts, what need for sacred fords, what need for austerities, and what need for sacrifices? (10)
The epithet "cool and white" is used as a qualification for the sake of attaining the destruction of heat and impurity; "adhvaraiḥ" means by sacrifices. || 10 ||
O sinless one, if there exist holy men who are free from passion, whose doubts are severed, and whose knots have been untied, what is the use of austerities or visiting sacred fords?
The "knot" (granthi) is the knot of consciousness and unconsciousness, characterized by the superimposition of identity and relation between the internal organ and its attributes.
Indeed, those fortunate ones whose minds are at rest must seek out the virtuous with great effort, just as a poor man must search for jewels. (12)
Like jewels, because they are obtained when otherwise unobtainable. || 12 ||
The intellect of the wise, graced by the beauty of association with the virtuous, shines forever like a lotus in the midst of a host of celestial nymphs. (13)

Kamalā is Lakṣmī; union with Viṣṇu on her side, as well as supreme beauty, do not belong even to the celestial nymphs who are her sisters (or, according to another reading, "the great sisters"). Therefore, she serves as the crest-jewel at the forefront of the station of pure discernment.
By that fortunate one, association with the virtuous was never abandoned, as is well known. || 14 ||
The term *padasya* refers to the reality of the Self as Brahman, which occupies the position of a crest-jewel (*cūḍāmaṇi*).
