Among the many striving for its attainment, "being the foremost crest" (*agrāvacūlitā*) means being made into a head-ornament by attaining it first.
It is "renowned" (*prathitā*), meaning celebrated. An *avacūḍa* is an ornament worn upon the crest (*cūḍā*).

The compound is formed according to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group; from the root *kṛ* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, followed by the suffix *ṇini* in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*), the abstract noun suffix *tal* is added.
Due to the non-distinction between *ḍa* and *la*, the letter *ḍa* becomes *la*. || 14 ||

Those virtuous ones who have severed the knots [of ignorance], who possess that knowledge, and who are honored by all—these should be served by every means, for they are the means for crossing the ocean of worldly existence. 15.
"By every means" means by all efforts such as giving, honoring, and serving; "means" refers to the methods of spreading [the teachings]. || 15 ||
These very people have become the dried fuel for the fires of hell—those by whom virtuous beings, who are like rain-clouds to the fires of hell, were viewed with indifference. (16)
Those by whom the virtuous have not been seen, even with indifference, become fuel for and nourishers of the fires of hell.
"Indifference" means disregard. Like clouds that cause the extinguishing of fire, they are the causes of the pacification of the fire characterized by hell.
[Furthermore,] there is the delusion regarding objects such as poverty, death, and suffering.
It is completely pacified by the medicines of association with the virtuous. || 17 ||
Delusion is a derangement of the humors; "without remainder" means by the total eradication of its root. || 17 ||
Contentment, association with the virtuous, inquiry, and likewise tranquility—these alone are the means for men to cross the ocean of worldly existence. (18)
Desiring to command all the gatekeepers simultaneously, he speaks again: "Contentment," [he says]. (18)
Contentment is the supreme gain; association with the virtuous is the supreme goal;
inquiry is the supreme knowledge; and tranquility is indeed the supreme happiness. (19)
In all cases, there is the superimposition of non-difference in the result. || 19 ||
These four are the stainless means for shattering cyclic existence;
those by whom they have been practiced have crossed over the ocean of existence, which has delusion as its water.
Delusion itself is the water; from such an ocean of existence... || 20 ||
Indeed, when even one [of these] has been practiced until pure realization arises,
there is an incapacity for all other practices. (Folio 112–113 is unclear)
In this way, it brings forth the world— consisting of words, forms, and objects— which is unreal in nature,
appearing like a garland of lotuses upon waves, or like a dance that has arisen before one's eyes. (24)
The world, which is unreal in nature, bears and accomplishes its appropriate meaning as "jagat" because it moves when investigated and does not remain [as it appears].
It is like a garland of lotuses imagined through delusion upon the waves; it is like a previously seen dance that, being remembered, seems to have arisen in the mind. 24.
It was like a mass of water rising up, filled with the whirring of wheels;
or like a sapless forest in summer, where the leaves have withered and fallen away, leaving nothing but decay.

*Cakra* means *cakravāka* (the ruddy sheldrake). A mass of frost accompanied by wind related to the mouth is *cītkāra*. Just as for a man lying on his back, or for a poet, upon seeing the sky filled with the cries of *cakravākas*, he imagines (*utprekṣita*) it to be like a lake with a rising mass of water. [The lotus] has fallen leaves, is sapless, dried up, and devoid of essence.
For this very reason, it is fallen, meaning deprived of the beauty of its luster and so forth, and ruined, meaning lacking the abundance of fruit and other qualities. || 25 ||
With minds distracted by the thought of death, dwelling in stone houses and mountain caves, they dance alone in dark caverns with the behavior of madmen. (26)
It is well known that at the time of death, the minds of those who are distracted become unsteady, prone to delusion and fainting;

like the interior of mountain caves—the abodes of rocky peaks—which are dark, empty, and terrifying, it is like a solitary dance within dark caverns, consisting mostly of the frantic behavior of a madman. (26)
With the mist of ignorance completely stilled, it is like the autumnal sky of pure consciousness;
it is as if carved upon a pillar, or, according to another reading, as if manifested upon the wall of the mind.

But from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is utterly tranquil—a mist of cognition and an autumnal sky of consciousness—like the form of a statue or the like, which is fashioned by being properly carved out through the strokes of a chisel and other tools. (27)
Just as [an image] fashioned from mud and so forth may be either sentient or insentient, the fourth chapter, concerning "Abiding," has thus been composed. (28)

The meaning is that the listener understands that the world has arisen—appearing in the forms of sentient and insentient beings fashioned from clay and mud, yet in ultimate reality having the nature of mere clay alone—and is thus devoid of any existence separate from its substratum. (Note: The reading is "śrotā" rather than "śrotraḥ.")
Then, immediately after that section on origination. || 28 ||
Three thousand verses consisting of commentaries and narratives—thus has the world come to exist in the form of the ego-sense (ahaṃbhāva). 29.
"Exegesis" (*vyākhyāna*) is the elucidation of the reality of the proliferation and its substratum; "narratives" (*ākhyāyikāḥ*) are stories, and [the work] abounds in them.

He states this very point with the four half-verses beginning with "In this way" (*ittham*). Thus, Brahman itself, while fully assuming the sequence of seer and seen that has thoroughly developed, [is described as follows].

"In the manner described—having attained its state as the world in the form of objective existence and the form of the ego (ahaṃbhāva), characterized by the enjoyer and the enjoyed, and continuous with agency"—this is to be connected with what follows: "is proclaimed here in this section on stability. || 29 ||
In this regard, it is proclaimed that the sequence of seer and seen is fully developed;
this delusion of the world shines forth, pervading the expanse of the ten directions. (30)
Thus, it is said therein that he has long attained growth;
thereafter follows the *Upaśāntiprakaraṇa* consisting of five thousand [verses]. (31)
The mention of "increase" (vṛddhi) is also an indication of "transformation" (vipariṇāma). It has been present for a long time, beginning from the beginningless past. || 31 ||
The fifth purifying stage is proclaimed as beautiful through the continuity of reasoning (or the lineage of sages).
This delusion has arisen: "This world," "I," and "you" are all "that. (32)

Thus, in this section on Quiescence (*upaśānti-prakaraṇa*), it is explained through a collection of verses how one attains complete peace; when this is heard, the cycle of existence (*saṃsṛti*) comes to rest.

In this chapter on "Peace" (Upaśānti), it is stated that [the mind] becomes tranquil through the process of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), being worn away until only a trace remains. This very remnant of a trace is clarified by means of the proclamation of the fruit of hearing [this teaching]. [The reading is *phalānukīrtana* instead of *phalakīrtana*.]
—From "upaśānti" and so forth, up to "saumyavārisaritsameta"—[verse 33].
Like a fallen painting whose details are only faintly discernible,
it remains with but a hundredth part remaining, its form appearing as if extinguished— or rather, its nature appearing as delusion.
Falling apart and nearly shattered, like an army depicted in a painting. || 34 ||
With her mind fixed on another's intention, she was like the illusory splendor of a city; standing beside an unattainable object, she was like the long-drawn-out clamor of a battle in a dream.

Regarding that, he states through examples—beginning with the words "anyā" and so forth—how, upon the successive conquest of higher stages, due to the excellence of the reduction [of afflictions], there remains only the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the perceptible and imperceptible.
Because it is created by the volitional constructs (*saṃkalpa*) of another, it resides in that [other's] mind. By these two, no object such as wealth and the like can be obtained.
In that [city], there were the sounds of battle and long-drawn-out cries belonging to another person standing beside the man who was imagining such things;

thus it was like the splendor of a city. Although the actions and sounds of others are equal to [one's own] in their falsity, [the city] did not become an object [of perception for them]; rather, it was as it would appear from the perspective of a dreamer.

The meaning is that just as something whose characteristics are slightly discernible through the seer’s vision—though barely perceptible—is itself pacified even while it is unreal, so it is here. || 35 ||
It is like the terrifying sound of a thunderbolt from a cloud filled with peaceful intentions;
it is comparable to a city created in a dream or through mental construction that has been forgotten.

Furthermore, in the section on tranquility (*upaśānti-prakaraṇa*), when [the mind] remains in an unperceivable state as the final residue, there are nine similes beginning with "tranquil" (*śānta*). It is like the terrifying sound of a thunderbolt— the crashing roar of a cloud that has become unrestrained like an intoxicated elephant— imagined by a volition (*saṃkalpa*) that has been stilled and ceased.
It is like a city whose manifestation has been forgotten through sleep or mental construction.
She whose limbs were darkened by the flowers blooming in the city gardens that were yet to come—
[the reading is *nagarodyānasotsavaśyāmalātmikāḥ*];
her [the reading is *naśyajjihvocyamāna*].
It is like the experience of the meaning of a discourse that is being uttered by the tongue and is intensely profound. || 37 ||

Just as a barren woman gives birth in the garden of a city that is yet to be built, so too, by the tongue of that "barren woman" whose very nature (aṅga) is pure, stainless, and indeed void, there are told those fierce matters concerning the battles and other events of her own sons, which are filled with the sentiment of heroism and the like. || 37 ||
Like a wall surface covered by a painting whose colors have not yet been applied,
it is like a city of mental construction whose objects are being forgotten.
It possesses the indistinct form of the movement of trees that have not yet sprouted in all seasons, yet it is colored by the essence of spring in the form of the forest of flowers yet to come. (39)

Like the unarisen vibration of a tree—[the reading is *vanaspandana*]—her form was indistinct and her appearance unperceivable; she was colored by aesthetic flavor (rasa) as if by the spring season. || 39 ||
Like a river whose flood of waves has subsided within and whose waters are tranquil, the sixth chapter, titled "Nirvāṇa," is thus proclaimed. (40)
It is gentle because of its immobility and serene. || 40 ||

The remaining portion of the text is its measure, which bestows great meaning through knowledge; when that is understood, there arises the supreme good—nirvāṇa, in which all conceptual constructions are stilled. (41)
The remainder, calculated from among the thirty-two thousand, is seventeen thousand five hundred;
that is to say, fourteen thousand five hundred. It is that in which all conceptual constructions have been stilled through the eradication of root-ignorance. 41.
p.
115) The self of consciousness is the nature of the light of the non-objective and the objective, free from affliction;
it is as pure as the sheath of the supreme ether, with all the delusions of existence stilled. || 42 ||

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that its nature would be described by the passage ending with "the hearer who is bodiless" (*śrotā akalevara*). It is unperceivable (*acetya*) and devoid of objects (*nirviṣaya*); for this very reason, it is free from affliction (*nirāmaya*). || 42 ||
Having brought to rest the worldly journey of the universe, he remains well-established, having accomplished all that was to be done;
he is like a diamond pillar for the undertakings of all people, resembling the sky. 43.

Just as a pillar of diamond, remaining unchanged itself, initiates all the people reflected within it and serves as the support for their activities and those initiated by them, so too is [the Self]. // 43 //
Fully satiated by having swallowed the entire web of the world according to its numerical order,
he has made his mental activity consist of the perception of all forms as being entirely transformed into space.
The poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is that he is ever-satisfied by the world-nets swallowed up with their well-known numbers;
the perception of forms through the external senses is enjoyment, while mental activity is mental enjoyment. (44)

Abandoned by the views of cause, effect, agency, and what is to be rejected or accepted, he is as if bodiless though possessing a body, and though in the midst of saṃsāra, he is beyond saṃsāra. || 45 ||
Regarding the state of being the agent of cause and effect— consisting of the forms of the objective, the subjective, and the divine—
it is viewed through the perspective of acceptance and rejection.
Consisting of consciousness, he is like the interior of a massive solid stone;
the sun of consciousness [illuminates] those worlds which are like a mass of darkness.
It is solid like the interior of a stone, thick, without gaps, full, and has other such similes as well.

The sun of consciousness (cid-āditya), heating the worlds imagined by its own ignorance with its own light ignited by its own mental modifications (vṛtti) in its own form, is of the nature of supreme illumination; yet, because of the absence of any object of sight, it is like a mass of darkness regarding the sphere of that [world’s] manifestation.

Because there is no distinction between the two [senses], it is connected with the following: "it has reached a state of supreme blindness, resembling dense darkness that has become solidified. || 46 ||

Though his nature is that of supreme illumination, he has entered as it were into a profound blindness; the wicked play of worldly existence is blocked for him, and the plague of desire has been destroyed. (47)
With the vampire of egoism destroyed, he remains as a mere embodied frame;
this Fortune of the world rests upon the tip of one of his pores,
like a bee upon a flower somewhere on Mount Mahāmeru.

"The embodied one is the non-corporeal" (dehavānakalevara). And so says the Śruti: "The wise man does not grieve, having realized the great, all-pervading Self which, though bodiless, dwells within bodies that are themselves unstable.
This is stated in order to establish the possibility of the world being sublated by the direct realization of that [Self].
He states its unlimitedness by virtue of being the substratum for the conceptualization of the universe with the words "in some [place]," and so forth.
Even though ignorance (*avidyā*) is limited like the tip of a hair, the splendor of the universe resides within it in one particular part.
Thus says the Śruti: "All beings constitute one foot of Him; His three feet are the immortal in heaven. And the Smṛti also says:
"Pervading this entire universe, I stand with but a single fraction of Myself. || 48 ||
Within the hollow of its own interior, the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) in every single atom sustains thousands of world-glories and, having created them, beholds them. (49)

Now, one might raise the objection: "How can there be the appearance of the exceedingly vast universe within a space that is not extensive? Anticipating this, and intending to show that nothing is impossible for ignorance—just as the sky with its clouds, planets, and stars is seen to enter within the interior of a mirror—it says: "In an atom," etc. "In its own cavity" means within the space imagined inside itself.
In the reading "of the space of consciousness" (cidākāśasya), by implication, the space of consciousness itself both sustains and perceives; the word "atha" (then/now) signifies conjunction. || 49 ||
O Mahāmati, even by hundreds of thousands of crores of Hari, Hara, and Añjanaja, the vastness of the heart of one who possesses liberation cannot be measured, for it is beyond comparison.
The unsurpassed reality is extensively unfolded. || 50 ||

The heart of the Great-minded One who is liberated while living is the Supreme Self itself; its expansion—that is, its vastness—does not admit of comparison or limitation even by hundreds of thousands of Hari, Hara, and others. Is that because they lack the capacity? No; for it is because [of the following reason] that no such comparison exists.
The meaning is that because it is the most excellent and supreme by virtue of its existence, its infinity, and its nature as bliss,
such a reality of the Self possesses that vast and undividedness which exists in the ultimate sense alone,
and is not— as in the case of space and so forth— merely imagined through the incapacity of the perceiving person. || 50 ||
Thus ends the seventeenth canto, titled "Description of the Number of Verses and Other Matters," in the Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vālmīki-Ārṣa-Vasiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa. 17.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Number of Verses and Other Matters," in the section on the Conduct of the Seeker of Liberation within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The eighteenth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Within this which is merely the mind, awakening proceeds.
Just as from a seed that exists and is sown, a good fruit necessarily arises. || 1 ||
The merits of this work, along with its primary, secondary, and incidental fruits, as well as the portions to be grasped within the similes herein, are now being set forth. (1)

Having thus described the division of the treatise according to its subject matter and purpose, and praising the merits of the entire work, he begins to state the essential points and the underlying intent found within the various examples introduced therein, for the sake of understanding the style of the composition, with the words beginning "In this [work]... and so forth.

Just as a good fruit necessarily arises from a seed that is intact in its potency and sown in an excellent field at an auspicious time, so too does the fruit of liberation necessarily arise from this compendium of the means to liberation (*mokṣopāyasaṃhitā*), which consists of these six treatises (*ṣaṭprakaraṇī*). || 1 ||
Even a human-authored treatise is to be accepted if it reveals sound reasoning; otherwise, even a work of the sages is to be rejected by one who adheres solely to what is logical. (2)

Now, one might ask: since there exist many Vedic recensions (śruti) divided into numerous branches, why is it said that this [work] alone—composed by human intellect—should be accepted, setting those aside? To this, he says: "api" (even/also).

It is "bodhaka" (illuminating), meaning it determines the truth through logical arguments (yukti). "Ārṣa" means that which originates from the Ṛṣi; here, "Ṛṣi" refers to the Veda, and thus it is "Vedic."

The meaning is that a person should strive to follow that which is "logical" (nyāyya), meaning that which does not deviate from reason, for that alone is primary. Although the Śruti scriptures are highly esteemed, they are nonetheless not sufficient for immediate realization because their underlying intent is profound; thus, they are not to be accepted by those who are ordinary candidates [for spiritual practice]. Rather, one should rely on that which is constructed through reasoning rooted in the experience of those who possess knowledge of its essence.
However, this treatise [is distinguished] by its clarity of intention.
(Folio 116–117; unclear on p. 118)
Listen to that introduction as this scripture is being heard, just as its true meaning is investigated according to the technical terminology. (49)
*Āpātanikā* is the introduction of the treatise, which consists of the means for its determination; it refers to that [introduction]. "In what manner" means by which illustration.

By "technical definition" (*paribhāṣā*), one should understand the form of the opening and the conclusion, and—by the inclusion of the word "etcetera"—repetition, novelty, result, explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), and logical justification.
And she is heard [described] according to the conventions employed for the sake of understanding those respective [meanings]. (49)

The wise know that to be an illustration (dṛṣṭānta) by which an object not experienced here [in this context] is made known through an observed object, yielding the fruit of assistance to understanding. (50)

Regarding that, he states the definition of an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) with the words "by which" (*yena*). That by which something is made known through similarity with a perceived object is "making known" (*bodhana*). He explains this very point: "yielding the fruit of assistance to understanding.
An illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) is that by which a determination of the subject matter at hand is seen (*dṛṣṭa*) through the power of similarity.
The wise are those who know its meaning. || 50 ||
O Rāma, without an illustration, a novel matter is not understood, just as household utensils and furnishings in a house at night cannot be seen without a lamp. (51)
"Apūrva" means something not previously seen, unseen, or marvelous. "Upaskaraṇa" means a high-quality instrument or accessory;
the suffix *suṭ* is applied here according to the rule *upāt pratiyatne*. || 51 ||
O descendant of Kakutstha, whatever examples I have used here to awaken your understanding,
may they all, though possessing their own causes, lead you to that which is truly without cause.

In order to distinguish the intended similarity within the illustrations, he shows the portion to be discarded with the words "by which": [the effects] are produced along with their causes, and therefore they are unreal; but that which is to be known is Being, the ultimate reality, causeless and eternal. By means of illustrations such as clay and gold, which are themselves illusory, [the nature of] Brahman, which is Being, [is shown].
The reason is made understood; thus, the meaning is that properties of the example (dṛṣṭāntadharma) such as being produced (janyatva) and unreality (anṛtatva) are to be abandoned. || 52 ||
The relationship of cause and effect between the objects of comparison and the things compared exists among all things whatsoever, with the exception of the Supreme Brahman. (53)

He states that this rule applies only to the analogies of the Supreme Brahman (parabrahma) and not to other analogies, using the words "upamāna" and so forth. The "state of being effect and cause" refers to the previously mentioned similarity by way of being an effect, a cause, and so on.
The meaning is as follows: just as it is said that through inquiry and other means, knowledge that apprehends the original object (bimba) arises.
Likewise, it should not be said that the reflection arises from knowledge, because the arising of Brahman cannot be asserted. || 53 ||
In this instruction on Brahman, whatever example is indeed stated by you here, it is accepted as possessing similarity only in a single respect. (54)
Having set aside the phrase "the Supreme Brahman," he clarifies what was said by stating "Brahman.
By taking up a partial similarity of attributes, the determination of the internal subject matter is made therein. This is the intended meaning:
in the communication that Brahman is the substratum of the world's illusory manifestation (*vivarta*).
The analogy of the rope perceived as a coiled serpent is an illustration only by virtue of the aspect of the substrate and its transformation;
it is not an illustration in every respect, such as the permanence or the state of happiness attributed to the subject of the comparison. 54.

Whatever illustration is given here for the sake of awakening to the reality of Brahman, each one should be understood as being like that which arises within a dream— the world perceived in a dream. 55.
If it is asked, "Why is that very example cited only with respect to a single part?

the answer is: it is because a similarity in all respects is unestablished; intending this, he says, "Whatever... [is like] what is born in a dream—false, existing only within the world, and not real.
The sense is that this is because the second ultimate reality—the entity consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss—is not established. || 55 ||
This being so, how could there be an example possessing form for Brahman which is formless? Thus, the speculative arguments of fools do not arise. (56)

These are merely optional statements arising from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*): "Is Brahman with a second (*sadvitīya*) or without a second (*advitīya*)? If it is with a second, there is a contradiction of one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). If it is without a second, then because of the absence of a teacher, scriptures, and so forth, knowledge would not arise. Thus, these optional statements do not hold up.
Through the refutation of examples characterized by unestablished, contradictory, and other such fallacies, nothing at all arises, because the world is like a dream. (57)
By this, [it is shown that] when the presentation of an example functions as a means of cognition by inducing an inference,

if the example, the reason (*hetu*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*), and so forth are unreal, there would be fallacies such as the unestablished nature of the pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) or the unestablished nature of the essence (*svarūpāsiddhi*); furthermore, if worldly reasons were used to prove [qualities like] reality, there would be fallacies such as contradiction (*viruddha*).
He says "anye" (others), meaning that the opportunity for the objection of logicians— that there would be defects acting as fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*)—

is also refuted; for, since the world, including the reasons and so forth which are to be refuted by the logicians who perceive defects such as the unestablished (*asiddha*) and the contradictory (*viruddha*), is like a dream, it does not exist in reality.

The meaning is that some refutation arises. The intention is that the linguistic usage between the knower and the known, persisting until the establishment of the probandum, is accounted for by mere conventional reality (*vyāvahārikasatyatā*).
It has been analyzed that the unreal exists neither in the past nor in the future, but only in the present;
thus, it is established—even for children—that the dream state is just like the waking state.
Having stated that [the world] is like a dream, he establishes this by demonstrating its similarity [to a dream] with the words "non-existent" (avastu).
It is non-existent—seized by absence—in the prior and posterior times, namely the periods before and after its production and destruction;
and even in the present time, it is unexamined when one investigates whether it exists as distinct from or identical to its material cause.
It is impossible even for a thousand disputants to determine [its nature]. However, when examined in the present time, it is established as a non-entity;
the meaning is that there is equality in its falsity, in that the dream is just like the waking object. || 58 ||

Through dreams, mental constructs, meditation, boons, curses, medicinal herbs, and so forth, examples are seen here that correspond to reality, because the existence of the world is of that same nature. (59)

If it is asked, "How can a dream, which possesses only apparent existence (*prātibhāsika-sattā*), be equal to that which possesses empirical existence (*vyāvahārika-sattā*)?", he replies with the word "svapne" (in a dream), stating that they are equal because their mutual relationship as cause and effect is observed and because of common worldly practice.

For instance, regarding one who is lying down, there may arise a doubt during waking life as to whether a journey or other such action should be undertaken; by means of praying to a deity and so forth, [the result is determined].
When a resolution arises in a dream that "this must be done," and one contemplates it accordingly—

thereby obtaining a boon favorable to that end through long-term worship, mantra-recitation, praise, and so forth characterized by such contemplation; or alternatively, when enemies are seen to suffer the curses of sages and the like, and one proceeds with a journey or other activities at dawn (the reading *karaṇena* is also found).

Because one sees the pacification of disease upon waking after obtaining a medicinal herb in a dream by visiting Śatruñjaya and other such places, and because the existence of the entire world is likewise of that same nature due to its similarity to that [dream experience], the examples of dreams are authentic. || 59 ||
Whatever other works have been composed by the author for the sake of the means to liberation,
this alone is the one systematic arrangement among them for the awakening of that which is to be known.

The meaning is that the established rule regarding the application of examples— namely, the understanding of a possible degree of similarity— is also well-known in those other works composed by Vālmīki for the sake of attaining liberation, such as the *Pūrvarāmāyaṇa* and others. || 60 ||
The dream-like nature of the world is understood through the sacred scriptures;
indeed, it cannot be explained quickly, for speech moves only step by step.
Now, one might object: "If the world is said to be similar to a dream, why do listeners not understand this immediately, or why do they even disagree?

Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states, "The state of being like a dream," explaining that it is because of the absence of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) from hearing the scriptures of spiritual science (*adhyātma-śāstra*) and due to the delusion regarding the reality of the world, that they cannot be made to understand or be awakened to this truth.
It is possible; the sense is that the destruction of the conflicting latent impressions (saṃskāra) of the listeners is something to be accomplished over a long period of time. || 61 ||
The world is like a dream, a mental construction, a city of the gandharvas, and so forth;
since these alone are the examples [given], no others exist here. (62)
Even in meditation, the visualization of a city is well-known in the context of mental worship. || 62 ||

When that which lacks a causal basis is compared for the sake of awakening to that which possesses it, a complete similarity of all attributes cannot possibly exist between them through the medium of comparison. (63)

If it is intended that there is similarity in every respect between the world and things such as dreams, then why is the fact of being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitā*) not likewise intended for Brahman, using the example of gold as the material cause of bracelets, crowns, and so forth? To this he replies: "In the non-cause. This very Brahman is without prior and without posterior.

By such scriptural passages as "One only, without a second," the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) is declared to be unchanging, non-transmigrating, pure, and infinite. Furthermore, by such traditional texts (*smṛti*) as "This is unmanifest, this is inconceivable, this is said to be immutable," because the consciousness— which is unattached and indifferent— is untouched by the causality of transformation, [it remains as such].

The meaning is that because transformation is impossible due to reasons such as the impossibility of the manifestation of the form of insentience (jāḍya), and because it is not a cause nor subject to modification, even with the efforts and exertions employed by means of metaphors— wherein something that undergoes transformation, like gold, is compared to the unchanging, uncaused [Brahman]— it is impossible to attain complete similarity in every respect. || 63 ||
The wise person, free from dispute, must accept that the object of comparison shares a common property with the standard of comparison in at least one respect, for the sake of understanding. (64)
He states that very point clearly: "Of the object of comparison," etc. (64).
In the illumination of an object, it is said that apart from the mere light of the lamp,
nothing else— such as its location, oil, or wick— is of any use.

He states [the following] with two verses beginning with "In the world, too, a gem is seen like a lamp," etc., because no cognition of similarity based on an unintended aspect is observed in such cases. The literal meaning of these two verses is clear.
[The term] "ābhāmātrāt" means from mere appearance, that is, from mere illumination. || 65 ||

O friend, because it possesses the capacity to convey only a single part [of its meaning], the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) brings about the cognition of the object of comparison (*upameya*), just as a lamp illuminates an object by means of its light. (66)
When the awakening of understanding arises through even a mere portion of an illustration,
the determination of the meaning of the Great Sentence (mahāvākya) should be grasped as something to be adopted.

He states the utility of all these scriptural illustrations with the words "of the illustration" (*dṛṣṭāntasya*). Through illustrations such as a dream for the world’s falsity, the illustration of space, the sun, and so forth for the inner self (*pratyak*), and the illustration of clay, iron, and so forth for Brahman, [the purpose is] the purification of the categories of meaning (*padārtha-pariśodhana*) for the sake of understanding the indicated object (*lakṣyārtha*). His—[meaning the text’s].

The meaning is that once the dawn of enlightenment has occurred, for the sake of severing ignorance along with its effects, one must necessarily adopt the certain realization of the meaning of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), "I am Brahman," which is the primary purport of all the Vedas and scriptures. || 67 ||
One should not, by falling into the state of a fallacious logician, destroy awakened consciousness through unholy conceptualizations that end in the denial of direct experience. 68.

Surely, [one knows] "I am fair-complexioned," "I am stout," and so forth, through direct perception; by the mark (liṅga) of observing the results of activity such as drinking medicine and attaining health; by analogy with the common usage of others; and by the words of all great people engaged in worldly affairs, one knows [oneself as] a Brāhmaṇa.
Through such scriptural injunctions as "one should sacrifice," through the Smṛtis, the Dharmaśāstras, and the reasonings of numerous logicians and others,
the Self is understood to have the nature of being an agent and an enjoyer, whether that Self is identified with the body or as distinct from it. How, then,
can a matter contradicted by direct perception and many other means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) be accepted based on the great Mahāvākya alone?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "No. Experience—that is, the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the wise—is either a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not, depending on whether Brahman is conceptualized by those who, having ended up in the denial of that experience, take as their object an impure self-identification with the body and so forth, which results in births as impure beings such as dogs or pigs. Thus, [Brahman] is conceptualized by the impure.

The awakened state—which is associated with the supreme human goal and consists of the specialized knowledge capable of awakening others—must not be destroyed through such conceptual alternatives as: "If it has a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), there is the loss of duality; if it lacks a means of valid cognition, there is the loss of the object of cognition (prameya)," and so forth.
The sense is that the impossibility of the body and other such things being the Self will be explained later. || 68 ||
Through investigation, even the verbal teachings of those who cause experience [of suffering] have followed us, such as ourselves; likewise,
that which was spoken by women, though contrary to the ultimate truth, has followed the Vedic path.
Speech is merely the utterance of words; it is not the sacred tradition (āgama). || 69 ||
Surely, since all people desire the happiness of unrestrained activity according to their own will, it is that which impels even a compassionate and most trustworthy person—
such as a Cārvāka— as well as one’s wife, sons, friends, and others,
toward objects of natural self-pleasure that are connected with the experience of manifold worldly enjoyments.
How can statements regarding the essence of saṃsāra and so forth be discarded?

For [renunciation] entails the pursuit of austerity, hardship, self-restraint, and the expenditure of wealth; it involves separation from beloved sons, wealth, wives, and the like; and it culminates in thousands of unforeseen misfortunes, such as wandering for alms and the practice of renunciation.

Anticipating the objection that the Vedic Mahāvākya— being insentient and resembling the speech of an enemy because it teaches the identity of Brahman and the Self as a secondary consequence of liberation characterized by the extreme poverty of nothing remaining but the objectless Self alone— is therefore not to be accepted, he says: "Because of [the need for] inquiry."

This is true because it is not through mere lack of inquiry, but rather through inquiry, that [the Veda] brings about the experience of the supreme human goal— the nature of the Self as eternal, unsurpassed bliss— even for an enemy known as such; thus,
among those like us who are established in experience, it is the most supremely authoritative.

It is indeed established that [the Veda] is the pinnacle of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). That speech or statement from which the ultimate human goal— the Vedic reality that has transcended [all else]— has departed, even if spoken by one’s most beloved woman,
is mere prattle, because it is followed by a succession of misfortunes such as death and hell.
The meaning is that it is merely idle chatter; it is neither scripture, nor the word of a reliable authority, nor a valid means of knowledge. || 69 ||
O dear one, our conviction is that this is so, for it is through this that the unification of all scriptures into a single voice bears fruit;
whereas that which [follows] the apparent meaning, nourished by its own limbs contrary to the scriptures—
Because there exists something other than self-awareness, that [other] is the means of valid cognition. || 70 ||

[Objection: "In that case, how is it that Kapila, Kaṇāda, Jaimini, and others—who were indeed knowers of the meaning of the Vedas—described the reality of the human goal and its means in one way, while you describe it otherwise?
What is the distinction in your statement? To this, he says: "asmākam" (of us). O dear friend, because for us... [the source from which it arises].

From the perspective of the intellect— that intellect which possesses such a virtuous method characterized by the direct realization of reality and liberation while living— thereby, in the manner previously described,
[is attained] that which is of such a nature: an object capable of immediate, intuitive experience, from which the supreme human goal arises.
The fruit of making all treatises—

including all the Vedas and the spiritual (adhyātma) scriptures— into a single coherent statement is their culmination in the meaning of one great sentence (*mahāvākya*). Consequently, an "unscriptural" work (*apaśāstra*) is that which does not fall within the purview of the intended meaning of the Vedas.

That which is nourished solely by its own limbs, such as logic (*tarka*) and so forth— namely, the cognition of Sāṃkhya, Kaṇāda, and others— is different from our means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which consists of the meaning of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), has a perceptual object, and is capable of yielding immediate experience (*aparokṣānubhava*). This is because their intellects have been impaired by fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*).
The meaning is: because they lack the mental capacity capable of ascertaining the intended purport of the sacred scriptures (śruti). || 70 ||

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Examples," in the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (sage-authored) tradition.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Examples," in the section on the Conduct of the Seeker of Liberation within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
Folio 120–121 is unclear. (p.
122) The world is agitated by forms, light, mental attention, and objects.
Just as there is an internal vibration within the wind, so too does sensation exist within. || 28 ||

Now, since it is impossible for a consciousness devoid of an object to be the cause of the movement of the mind, that [movement] must be said to have an object. In that case, an object already established prior to the movement of the mind must be asserted. Furthermore, since it was previously stated that objects consist of the mind (*manomaya*), the establishment of the mind must be asserted prior to the establishment of the objects; thus, there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*).

Anticipating this objection, he says "rūpa" (form), etc., to show that [the world] indeed manifests as existent by virtue of the reality of the substrate—the consciousness variegated by *māyā*—in the form of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). It is "disturbed" by those objects: the perception of objects through the external senses, which is the illumination of form (*rūpāloka*), and the mental engagement (*manaskāra*) which is the mental synthesis of objects; and the things (*padārtha*) which are the objects of both of these.
When the pure awareness of the self of all arises, it shines forth as that very essence, manifesting in forms that extend beyond space and time, both external and internal, including the body. 29.
[Objection: "In that case, how can there be an established order regarding its occasional arising and so forth? To this, he says: "All...

It arises according to the established order of the ripening of karma; it appears as if produced in the form of whatever manifests for the enjoyment of living beings, assuming the guise of external and internal objects extended across space and time.
[In ultimate reality, however, it is indeed bodiless. The long vowel in "antārūpa" is due to the rule regarding the elision of "ḍh". || 29 ||
Having seen the appearance of the visible, he remains abiding in his own essential nature;
whatever form appears to him, in whatever place, and in whatever manner, it is exactly so.

In that case—the meaning of the passage beginning with "tarhi" and ending with "caramam" (which is absent in some versions)—is as follows: having perceived his own final appearance as an object of sight, such as the body and so forth, and out of delusion maintaining the thought "that alone is my true nature," he remains as the universal Self in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*). And this is logical, as he says: "his own. (30)
In whatever manner and wherever that Universal Self attains manifestation,
it immediately abides there in that very way and shines as if it were of that very form.
He states that very point clearly: "He" (saḥ) || 31 ||
Because it consists of all things, it is logical for the Seer to appear as the object of sight;
yet, since the object of sight exists only when there is a Seer, even that state of being an object is not real.
He establishes the falsity of the object of perception as indicated by the word "iva" (as if): "The state of being perceived," etc.

If the seer, whose nature is pure consciousness (*dṛksvarūpa*), were to fall away from that conscious nature and attain the state of being perceived, then there would be no establishment of a perceived object without a seer. If, on the other hand, he does not fall away [from his nature], then how can this [object] possess the state of being perceived?

The meaning is that it is merely an illusory appearance (*vivarta*), like the state of a snake [superimposed] upon a rope without the rope’s own nature ever departing; thus, its falsity is established.
Therefore, Brahman is proven to be entirely without cause; this remains settled.
Perception alone is the creator, while inference and the other means of knowledge are but its parts. (33)

Therefore, since the falsity of the effect entails the falsity of the causal state which depends upon it, it is established that [the world] is without a cause. Thus, concluding that through the investigation of the reality of perception, non-dual Brahman alone is established, he says: "This very perception is established. As for inference and the other means of knowledge...

Because they are preceded by perception and because they culminate in that very [perception], they are merely its parts; thus, the meaning is that the reality of all means of valid cognition is the Self alone. || 33 ||
O virtuous one, that which a practitioner attains through mere self-effort alone— having cast far away the meaning of the word "fate"—
is the supreme state reached by the hero.
For indeed, the end is attained through one's own manly effort alone. || 34 ||
Recalling the refutation of fate (*daiva*) by means of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokana*) maxim, he states that this result belongs to human effort alone,
beginning with the word "sva": "In reality, having imagined that one's own past exertion alone is 'fate,' the person who,
thinking 'I am dependent on that,' becomes intent upon its worship— [the Lord] casts that person far away from the meaning of the word 'fate' as it is so imagined."

By a hero who has cast aside [worldly attachments] and possesses mastery over the senses and so forth, that supreme state is reached and attained within the very heart through one's own human effort alone. || 34 ||
Let it be considered, first of all, according to the true (or, as found in some readings of the root text and commentary: "existent") tradition of the lineage of teachers.
To whatever extent you yourself, through your own intellect, attain that which is utterly pure and of infinite form, so do you approach the Supreme.
By means of truth— that is,

by that which culminates in the ultimate reality (paramārtha)— and by means of purity— that is, by that which is thoroughly cleansed by valid cognition (pramāṇa)— investigate until you yourself, through your own intellect, reach and directly realize the state that is empty of the threefold conceptual determination.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Means of Valid Cognition," in the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* tradition. || 19 ||

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Means of Valid Cognition," in the section on the Conduct of the Seeker of Liberation within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Twentieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Through association with the noble and through the application of reasoning, one should forcefully increase wisdom;
thereafter, one attains the state of a Great Being by means of the marks of a Great Being. (1)
In this [work], the modes of wisdom and intellect constitute the characteristics of a Great Being (mahāpuruṣa);
and the sequences of right conduct have been described as mutually reinforcing one another. (1)

It has been stated that knowledge is established only in great beings (mahāpuruṣa) and not in others. And since the state of being a great being is accomplished through the conduct of the virtuous (sadācāra), which will be described hereafter, Śrī Vasiṣṭha, commencing the description of such conduct, said: "O Noble One" (ārya). First, [regarding] the noble ones...

Through associations and by means of the method of training in the practice of those instructions, one should lead wisdom to growth; thereafter, by means of the characteristics of a Great Being (mahāpuruṣa) which will be described hereafter, one should lead oneself to the state of a Great Being. || 1 ||
Whatever quality by which a person shines forth here, that very quality remains;
therefore, one should quickly increase one's intelligence.

In this regard, if all virtues were not found in a single person, then whichever person is known to be preeminent in whichever particular virtue would be taught by and distinguished from others precisely through that [virtue]. Therefore, having quickly learned each of those [virtues] from such a person, one should increase one's own intellect. (In the reading *śikṣeta*: "One should learn."
But this is clear. || 2 ||
For this state of being a Great Being, endowed with qualities such as tranquility and the rest,
O Rāma, does not attain any accomplishment whatsoever without perfect knowledge.
This very possession of qualities such as tranquility and wisdom constitutes the state of a Great Being. || 3 ||
Through knowledge, the qualities such as tranquility increase in those who follow the path of the virtuous; they are worthy of praise, like new sprouts within a rain shower that bears fruit. (4)

The "conduct of the virtuous" (satpuruṣakrama) refers to the practices followed and performed by the virtuous; these include such virtues as humility (amānitva) and others, which are praiseworthy and commendable because they result internally in the manifestation of the bliss of the Self. || 4 ||
Supreme knowledge increases from virtues such as tranquility,
just as an excellent rain of rice grows from sacrifices consisting of food offerings.

It is like rain, which is the cause for the production of rice and other grains. And so says the Smṛti: "An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun; from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings."
Thus [ends the fifth].
The virtues, such as tranquility and the rest, arise from knowledge, and from tranquility and the rest, wisdom likewise arises; these increase one another like a lotus and its pond.
To provide an illustration corresponding to their simultaneous mutual increase, he states once again what has already been said:
"The qualities... The phrase *te abjasarasī iva* (they are like a lotus and a lake) contains no sandhi (euphonic combination) because both words are *pragṛhya*.
Here, the intended meaning is that the lake increases through the qualities of the lotuses, such as coolness, fragrance, and beauty.
Knowledge arises from the conduct of virtuous persons, and the conduct of virtuous persons arises from knowledge;
thus, knowledge and the conduct of virtuous persons mutually increase one another.
Thus, he states that knowledge and right conduct are likewise causes for each other's growth: "Knowledge... (verse 7).
And by means of the sequence of the goals for a person skilled in tranquility, wisdom, and so forth,
the wise person should practice the sequence of knowledge and the conduct of true persons.

One who is skilled in the human goal consisting of tranquility, wisdom, the state of a Great Being, and so forth, should practice knowledge and right conduct through the sequence of effort such as hearing [the teachings]. 8.
As long as both the path of knowledge and the course of the true person have not been practiced equally,
my dear, not even one of these two will succeed for a man in this world.
Just as the joy of song is accomplished by a female guardian of the rice-ears through her singing with an extended rhythm, accompanied by the driving away of birds. || 10 ||

He states, with an illustration, that the fruit of their growth also occurs at the same time for both, using two verses beginning with "yathā": "Just as by a woman guarding a field of ripened rice, who, while engaged in another task, [sings] a song accompanied by the sound of her outstretched hands clapping, [the birds are driven away]."
Simultaneous with the incidental destruction of the birds, the joy of song proceeds. [1] || 10 ||
Through the application of knowledge and the effort of a true person, by means of one who is a non-doer yet appears as a doer, a man who is likewise free from desire attains that state.
Likewise, by one who is devoid of desire regarding the removal of obstacles to knowledge, such as attachment and pride, and who is therefore a non-agent,
through the performance of the means of knowledge— namely, listening [to scripture] and the practice of right conduct—
the removal of obstacles occurs incidentally for those persons whose nature is merely that of agents of those [means].
The supreme state is attained. || 11 ||
Thus, O descendant of Raghu, the sequence of right conduct has been proclaimed by me;
now, in this same manner, the sequence of knowledge is correctly taught.

"Just as this sequence of right conduct has been described by me in such a manner, so now the sequence of knowledge (jñānakrama) is taught in the subsequent section"—this is the formal promise of what is to be said. 12.
This [treatise] brings fame and longevity, and bestows the fruits of human goals; indeed, a wise person should listen to this true scripture from one who knows it and is trustworthy. (13)

He concludes the instruction on the collection of means for accomplishment (*sādhanakalāpa*) by stating "this," etc. The particle *kila* indicates the well-known status of the meaning according to the tradition (*sāṃpradāyika*). || 13 ||
Upon hearing this, through the purity of your intellect, you will by force attain that state,
just as turbid water becomes clear through contact with the *kataka* nut.
"By force" is an expression for the power of the means; "favor" means clarity. || 14 ||
O Sage, this mind, having known that which is to be known,
indeed goes helplessly to the supreme state,
once it has realized that which is indivisible and most excellent.
For indeed, by virtue of that realization, one does not abandon it. || 15 ||

The mind of the sage— one whose nature is reflection and who has attained the requisite means for practice— having known that which is to be known, becomes helpless through the power of that [knowledge] and goes to the supreme state, even if it does not desire it. He says "yad" (since) to show that this occurs not only due to the intensity of the means, but also due to the very nature of the reality to be known.

"By virtue of awakening" means being dependent upon awakening; that is to say, because it is sustained by the final mental modification (*vṛtti*) whose nature is awakening. Having shaken off ignorance and its effects, the mind does not abandon that state which is awakened, vigilant, undivided, and supreme. The meaning is that it shines forth together with the other [mental states] consisting of ignorance and its effects. This is indicated by the particle "hi."

This is well-known among the learned. Thus they say: "The knowledge of the Self, which sublates the notion that the body is the self, must arise regarding the Self itself; he in whom this occurs is liberated even against his will. (15)

Thus ends the twentieth canto, titled "The Description of Right Conduct," in the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra-prakaraṇa* (Section on the Conduct of those Seeking Liberation) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, a compendium of thirty-two thousand verses composed by Vālmīki according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. 20.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of Right Conduct," in the section on the Conduct of those Seeking Liberation within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
This chapter on the conduct of one seeking liberation is completed.
